label: Chapter 6 · Part A
title: The Nature of God I: Background Principles & the First Attributes
tagline: From “there is a First Cause” to “here is what it must be like”
oneSentence: Armed with three general principles — proportionate causality, “action follows being,” and the analogy of being — we can deduce from the conclusions of the five proofs that the First Cause is one, absolutely simple, unchanging, immaterial, timelessly eternal, and necessary, and that each proof reaches the very same God.
bigPicture:
Chapters 1–5 each ended with a cause of the world: a purely actual actualizer, an absolutely simple One, a divine intellect holding the abstract objects, subsistent existence itself, and a necessary being. A skeptic can fairly ask two things at this point: *why think these are one being rather than five?* and *why call any of them “God”?* This chapter answers both. It first lays out the general tools of reasoning that let us move from the world, considered as an effect, to the nature of its cause, and then it derives, one by one, the classical divine attributes.

The tools come first because the rest depends on them. The **principle of proportionate causality** (PPC) says a cause cannot give what it does not in some way have. **Agere sequitur esse** (“action follows being”) says what a thing does cannot outrun what it is. The **analogy of being** explains how words like “exists,” “power,” or “knows” can be applied literally to God without making him just a bigger version of us (univocal predication) and without emptying the words of all meaning (equivocal predication). Feser defends each principle independently of theism, and shows that even naturalist philosophers quietly rely on the first two.

With the tools in hand, Feser derives the first group of attributes: **unity** (there can be only one purely actual being, and the five proofs converge on it), **simplicity** (no parts of any kind — the attribute that anchors all the others and defines classical theism), **immutability**, **immateriality**, **eternity** understood as strict timelessness, and **necessity**. Along the way he answers a whole string of modern critics: Cottingham on proportionate causality; Plantinga, Morris, and the “theistic personalists” on simplicity; Swinburne, Pike, and Kenny on timelessness; Findlay, Russell, and Schrader on necessary being.

This part matters for persuasion as much as for understanding. Many objections to the five proofs (“Why only one God?”, “Isn’t your God just a cosmic superman?”, “Who made God?”, “How can a changeless God act?”) are really objections to the *nature* of the God concluded to. This module shows how tightly the attributes interlock: deny one — especially simplicity — and you lose the First Cause itself. Part B (module ch6b) continues with omnipotence, omniscience, goodness, will, love, incomprehensibility, and God’s ongoing relation to the world.
objectives: State the principle of proportionate causality, explain the formal/virtual/eminent distinction with the $20 example, and show how PPC follows from the principles of causality and sufficient reason.
Answer Cottingham’s “heirloom,” sponge-cake, triviality, and evolution objections to PPC.
Explain agere sequitur esse, its relation to formal causes, and how naturalists like Churchland and Searle implicitly rely on PPC and this principle.
Distinguish univocal, equivocal, and analogical predication, and within analogy distinguish attribution, proper proportionality, and metaphorical proportionality — with an example of each.
Reconstruct Feser’s seven-step argument that “being” is analogical and explain why confining God-talk to univocal or equivocal terms leads to agnosticism or atheism.
Derive God’s unity from pure actuality and explain why the five proofs must all reach one and the same God.

Explain why divine simplicity is nonnegotiable for classical theism and rebut Plantinga’s and Morris’s objections using the analogy of being, the essence/property/accident distinction, and Cambridge properties.

Derive immutability, immateriality, timeless eternity, and necessity, and answer the objections from acting, life, temporal causation, simultaneity, linguistic conventionalism, and Schrader’s “empty world.”
Identify when an objection commits the fallacy of accident or begs the question against the proofs, and explain why.

summary.heading: Opening: five proofs, one question left
summary.plain: The first five chapters argued that there is an ultimate cause behind everything. This chapter asks what that cause must be like, and whether the five arguments all point to the same thing. To answer, Feser first sets out some general rules of reasoning, then uses them to work out God’s characteristics one by one.
summary.takeaway: Each proof already reached a cause with a specific nature; this chapter systematically unpacks that nature and shows it is one and the same God, reasoning from the world as effect to God as cause.
summary.body:
Feser opens with a compact recap. The **Aristotelian proof** reasons from potentials being actualized to a purely actual actualizer. The **Neo-Platonic proof** reasons from composite things to an absolutely simple cause. The **Augustinian proof** reasons from abstract objects (universals, propositions, numbers, possible worlds) to a divine intellect in which they exist as ideas. The **Thomistic proof** reasons from the real distinction between essence and existence in things to a cause that is subsistent existence itself. The **rationalist proof** reasons from the principle of sufficient reason to an absolutely necessary being.

So far the focus has been on *that* God exists, with only glimpses of *what* he is and *how* he relates to the world. This chapter takes up those two topics. Because that requires reasoning from the world as effect to God as cause, Feser first sets out several general philosophical principles and only then applies them.

The chapter as a whole has two jobs, and this module covers the first half of both. One job is to say more about **God’s nature** — what the cause reached by the proofs must be like. The other is to say more about **God’s causal relationship to the world** — how such a cause acts on and sustains things (taken up mostly in Part B). Feser stresses that the earlier chapters already said something about both; the aim now is to be systematic. His method is to reason from the world *considered as an effect* to the nature of its *cause*, and since that kind of reasoning depends on general principles about causes and about language, he states and defends those principles before deriving a single attribute.
summary.deepDive:
The hardest idea in this opening is easy to miss: **how can we know anything about the nature of a cause we never observe?** Many people assume that cosmological arguments, at best, get you “some first cause or other,” and that a separate, shakier leap is needed to get from there to God. Philosophers sometimes call this the “gap problem.” Feser’s recap is quietly setting up his answer.

Notice what each proof actually concluded. The Aristotelian proof didn’t end with “something started things off” but with a *purely actual* actualizer — something with no unrealized potential. The Neo-Platonic proof ended with something *absolutely simple*. The Augustinian proof ended with an *intellect* in which necessary truths exist. The Thomistic proof ended with *subsistent existence itself*. The rationalist proof ended with an *absolutely necessary* being. These are not bare placeholders; they are descriptions with content. The work of this chapter is to draw out what that content implies, not to bolt new features onto an empty “first cause.”

A thought experiment helps. Suppose a detective finds that a safe was opened without force, by someone who knew the combination, left no fingerprints, and was inside a locked building overnight. She hasn’t seen the culprit, but the *features of the effect* sharply constrain what the cause could be. Feser’s approach is similar, only more rigorous: the relevant features are metaphysical (potency being actualized, composition, dependence of existence), and the constraints follow by strict reasoning.

Two nuances. First, Feser admits he has already said things about God’s nature in earlier chapters; this chapter is a systematic treatment, not a first attempt. Second, he announces that general principles must come first — proportionate causality, “action follows being,” and the analogy of being — because inferring from effect to cause and describing a cause radically unlike its effects both require them.

In the formal reasoning, this section supplies **step 1**: the five conclusions taken as data. Everything later — unity (step 21), convergence (step 26), simplicity (step 30), and the rest — is an unpacking of step 1 with the help of steps 2–13.

The usual confusion: people think that because the proofs are *about existence*, they say nothing about *character*. But “purely actual,” “simple,” and “necessary” are already characterizations. The question is only how far they reach — and the answer, this chapter argues, is: very far.

checks.q: Which of the five proofs, as Feser recaps them, begins from abstract objects such as numbers and propositions?
options: The Augustinian proof
The Aristotelian proof
The Neo-Platonic proof
The rationalist proof
checks.explanation: The Augustinian proof argues from abstract objects to a divine intellect in which they exist as ideas. The Aristotelian starts from change; the Neo-Platonic from composition; the rationalist from PSR.

checks.q: Why does Feser lay out general principles before deriving any divine attribute?
options: Because the principles are needed to prove God exists in the first place
Because inferring the nature of a cause from the world as its effect depends on general principles about causes and language
Because the attributes are arbitrary unless defined by convention
Because the attributes follow from Scripture, which the principles interpret
checks.explanation: The chapter reasons from the world, considered as an effect, to its cause; that requires principles like PPC and the analogy of being. God’s existence was already argued for in chapters 1–5.

summary.heading: The principle of proportionate causality: formally, virtually, eminently
summary.plain: A basic rule: a cause can’t give what it doesn’t have. But “have” can mean three things. I can give you $20 because I have the bill, because I have the money in the bank, or because I can print the bill myself. The cause doesn’t need to look like the effect; it just needs the resources to produce it.
summary.takeaway: PPC says an effect’s features must be in its total cause formally, virtually, or eminently — not that the cause must resemble the effect — and it follows from PC and PSR.
summary.body:
The PPC, first met in chapter 1, says that whatever is in an effect must be in its **total cause** in some way — because a cause cannot give what it lacks. The key refinement is that the effect’s features may be in the cause in one of three ways. Feser’s illustration: you end up with a $20 bill.

- **Formally**: I hand you a $20 bill from my wallet. I have the very “form” I give you.
- **Virtually**: I have no bill, but I have $20 in the bank and wire it so you can withdraw it. The total cause (me plus my account) contains the effect’s content in another mode.
- **Eminently**: I have neither bill nor funds, but I can get a genuine $20 bill printed on a Federal Reserve press. I have something causally *more* fundamental than a bill — the power to make bills.

PPC is not an arbitrary add-on. It follows from the **principle of causality** (PC) and the **principle of sufficient reason** (PSR), both defended in earlier chapters. An aspect of an effect that came from nothing in its total cause would be a potential actualized by nothing (violating PC) and a feature with no explanation (violating PSR).

Two features of the principle deserve emphasis. First, it concerns the **total** cause — all the factors that together produce the effect — not any single ingredient. Second, the three modes show that PPC is not a demand that causes *resemble* their effects. What is ruled out is only that the effect should contain something for which nothing in the total cause accounts. Applied to God, this will mean that the perfections found in creatures must be present in their First Cause — but eminently, in a higher way, not as the limited, material features we meet in things.
summary.deepDive:
The hardest idea here is the difference between **virtual** and **eminent** presence, and why neither is a cheat.

Start with the $20 example and ask, in each case, *what exactly does the cause have?* In the formal case, I have the very thing you get: a bill. In the virtual case, I have no bill but I have a *power or resource* — funds and a bank that will convert them into a bill in your hands. What is in the effect is in the total cause, but in the mode of a capacity rather than a finished feature. In the eminent case, I have something more fundamental still: control over the process by which bills are made at all. The eminent cause does not merely have *a* $20 potential; it has the source of all such bills.

A second worked example: a sculptor produces a statue with a certain shape. The sculptor doesn’t *have* that shape (formal presence fails — he isn’t shaped like a horse). But the shape is in the total cause — his idea and skill, the chisel, the marble’s capacity to be cut — virtually. And a being who could produce not just this statue but marble, sculptors, and shape itself would contain the statue’s perfection eminently.

Why isn’t this a trick to make PPC unfalsifiable? Because each mode still requires *something real* in the cause that accounts for the effect. A person with no bill, no funds, and no press cannot give you $20. That is exactly what PPC predicts. The principle rules out effects exceeding the resources of their total causes; it does not rule out causes that are richer than, or different in kind from, their effects.

The grounding is simple. If some feature of an effect had no source in its total cause, then a potential would have been actualized by nothing (against the principle of causality, from chapter 1), and that feature would have no explanation (against PSR, from chapter 5). That is the reasoning behind **step 3**; the three modes are the content of **step 2**.

The usual confusion: people hear “a cause can’t give what it doesn’t have” and conclude that a creator of material, changing things must itself be material and changing. But material and changeable features can be in God *eminently* — as the power to produce and sustain such things — without God being material. Later, PPC also helps explain why the First Cause must contain, in a higher way, perfections like intellect (a theme of Part B).

checks.q: A city council has no parks but has the legal authority and budget to create them. The parks it later creates were in the council:
options: Only metaphorically
Formally
Virtually (as power and resources), not formally
Not at all, so PPC is violated
checks.explanation: The council doesn’t have parks, but its budget and authority are a real capacity that accounts for them — the virtual mode, like my bank account in Feser’s example.

checks.q: Why does Feser think PPC follows from the principle of causality and PSR?
options: Because both principles say effects must resemble causes
Because PSR is defined as PPC applied to material things
Because PC applies only to God and PSR only to creatures
Because an effect-feature with no source in its total cause would be an actualization with no actualizer and a fact with no explanation
checks.explanation: That is the core of step 3. Neither PC nor PSR says effects resemble causes.

checks.q: What does the eminent case in the $20 example add beyond the virtual case?
options: The cause has something more fundamental than the effect’s feature: the power to make things of that kind
The cause has more $20 bills than in the formal case
The effect is only imaginary
The cause is identical to the effect
checks.explanation: Access to the press is not having money but having the power to make money — the mark of eminent presence.

summary.heading: Cottingham’s counterexamples and the triviality charge
summary.plain: A critic says the rule is obviously false: a sponge cake is spongy, but eggs, flour, and butter aren’t. Feser answers that the critic forgot the rest of the cause — the baker, the mixing, the oven. The ingredients don’t need to be spongy; the whole process just needs the power to make sponginess.
summary.takeaway: Cottingham refutes a straw man: PPC concerns the total cause and allows virtual and eminent presence, and explaining by potentialities is minimally informative, not trivial.
summary.body:
John Cottingham (criticizing Descartes’ version of the principle) says PPC presupposes an “heirloom” picture in which properties are handed down from cause to effect, and offers counterexamples: helium has properties absent in the hydrogen it fuses from; a sponge cake is spongy though no ingredient — eggs, flour, butter — is spongy.

Feser gives three replies. **First**, the examples consider only the *materials*, while PPC concerns the *total* cause (the baker, the oven’s heat, the chemistry of mixing and baking, and so on). Restricting PPC to material factors and then refuting the restricted version is a straw man. **Second**, the heirloom reading assumes the effect must be in the cause *formally*, which defenders of PPC explicitly deny. A Thomist writer (Coffey) notes that a boy need not have a black eye in order to give one; Aquinas says a hot body does not pass its own numerically identical heat to another but, by its power, actualizes a new heat that was potential in the thing heated. **Third**, Cottingham grants that sponginess doesn’t arise from nothing but says that calling it “potentially” present makes PPC trivial. Feser accepts the word *potentially* — the bank account’s potential to be drawn on, the printing press’s potential to print — but denies triviality: explanation in terms of potentialities may be only *minimally* informative, yet minimal is not the same as empty.

The shape of Feser’s reply is worth noticing. He does not deny that the cake’s sponginess is genuinely new, or that helium’s properties differ from hydrogen’s. He denies only that such novelty arises from nothing in the total cause. The objection works only by quietly replacing the principle defenders actually hold with a cruder one.
summary.deepDive:
The subtle part of this section is the **triviality charge**, because Feser partly agrees with it. Cottingham’s worry is a classic one: if every surprising effect can be “explained” by saying its features were potentially in the cause, hasn’t PPC become empty — true no matter what happens?

Feser’s answer has two layers. First, he openly accepts the language of potentiality. Aquinas himself said that the heat produced in a warmed body was previously in it potentially, and that the agent actualizes it. In the $20 cases, the virtual and eminent explanations *are* explanations in terms of potentialities — the account’s potential to be drawn on, the press’s potential to print. So the defender isn’t sneaking potentiality in to save the principle; it was always part of it.

Second, he distinguishes **minimally informative** from **noninformative**. A course illustration: Molière famously mocked doctors who said opium puts people to sleep because it has a “dormitive power.” The joke lands because the explanation is thin. But it is not empty: it tells you the sleepiness comes from something in the opium rather than from the patient’s mood or the weather, and it directs inquiry toward what in opium has that power. Likewise, saying the sponginess was potentially in the ingredients-plus-baking tells you where to look (the chemistry of eggs, flour, heat) and rules out that it came from nothing.

The most convincing evidence of non-triviality comes in the next section: philosophers on opposite sides (Churchland, dualists) draw substantive, disputed conclusions from PPC. A trivial principle can’t settle anything.

Notice also the **straw man** diagnosis. Cottingham’s examples consider only material ingredients. But PPC speaks of the *total* cause. Restricting the principle to ingredients, then refuting the restricted version, attacks something no defender holds. The heirloom reading makes the parallel mistake of assuming formal presence — as if the cook must be spongy. A Thomist writer’s quip about the black eye makes the point memorably.

This section protects **step 2** of the argument (the formulation of PPC) and **step 3** (its grounding).

The usual confusion: people think that because a new feature is *novel*, it must violate PPC. But novelty of instance — a new heat, a new sponginess — is exactly what PPC expects: the total cause actualizes something that was potential. What PPC forbids is only an effect-feature that nothing in the total cause accounts for.

checks.q: Which of Feser’s replies targets the fact that Cottingham’s examples mention only eggs, flour, butter, and hydrogen?
options: The reply that sponginess is an illusion
The reply that PPC concerns the total cause, not merely the material factors
The reply that analogy is literal
The reply from the second law of thermodynamics
checks.explanation: Restricting PPC to material ingredients and refuting that is a straw man; the total cause includes baker, mixing, and heat.

checks.q: What does Aquinas’ example of the hot body show?
options: That causes never resemble their effects
That heat is literally transferred from one body to another
That a cause produces a numerically new feature by actualizing a potential in the recipient
That PPC applies only to heat
checks.explanation: The heating body doesn’t hand over its own heat; it actualizes a new heat that was potential in the heated body.

checks.q: How does Feser respond to the claim that explaining sponginess as “potentially present” makes PPC trivial?
options: He denies that potentiality is involved at all
He concedes PPC is trivial but says trivial truths are useful
He replaces PPC with the principle of causality
He says explanations by potentialities may be minimally informative but are not noninformative
checks.explanation: Feser embraces the language of potentiality but rejects the slide from “minimally informative” to “trivial.”

summary.heading: PPC at work outside theology: Churchland, dualism, and evolution
summary.plain: Even philosophers who reject God use this rule. Some argue that because humans come from purely physical causes, humans must be purely physical — which assumes the rule. And evolution doesn’t break it: genes, mutations, and the environment together produce each new trait.
summary.takeaway: PPC is substantive and independent of theology: materialists and dualists both argue from it, and even the naturalistic account of evolution respects it.
summary.body:
That PPC is substantive shows up in the fact that naturalists use it. Paul Churchland argues that since human beings (individually and as a species) arise from purely material beginnings by purely material processes, the result must be purely material. That inference assumes that a wholly material total cause yields a wholly material effect — PPC. The mind-body dualist accepts the same principle but runs it the other way: since the intellect is not material, the total cause cannot have been wholly material. Both sides take PPC for granted.

Evolution is sometimes offered as a counterexample (simpler forms giving rise to more complex ones). But even on the standard naturalistic account, a simple organism does not just produce a more complex one out of nothing. Existing genetic material, a mutation (from a copying error in DNA replication or from radiation or chemical damage), and environmental conditions *together* produce a new variation — no one of them sufficing alone. That respects PPC. Feser adds the physicist Paul Davies’ point that denying that new biological information derives from some combination of prior factors (including the environment) would conflict with the second law of thermodynamics, according to which order and information tend to decrease in a closed system. Conclusion: PPC is well grounded independently of natural theology, yet highly useful for reasoning from the world to its divine cause.

Notice what Feser is and is not claiming. He is not using thermodynamics or biology to prove God’s existence. He is showing that PPC is a principle that scientific accounts themselves respect, and that naturalists employ when it suits them — so it can’t be dismissed as a theological invention or a triviality.
summary.deepDive:
The key move in this section is **dialectical**: Feser shows that a principle critics call medieval or trivial is actually shared ground.

Consider Churchland’s argument slowly. Premise: human beings, individually and as a species, arise from purely material beginnings (a fertilized egg; early organisms) through purely material processes (cell division; natural selection). Conclusion: human beings are purely material. What licenses that inference? Only the principle that if the *total* cause is wholly material, the effect must be too — a total cause can’t yield what isn’t in it in some way. Without PPC, Churchland’s argument would have no force: the effect might contain something non-material that simply appeared.

Now the dualist. She accepts the same principle but has a different premise: part of the effect (the intellect) is not material. By PPC, then, the total cause of a human being can’t have been purely material. The two sides disagree about the facts, not about the principle. That is Feser’s point: PPC is so far from trivial that it drives a central debate in philosophy of mind.

Next, evolution. The objection says complex organisms come from simpler ones, so the effect exceeds the cause. Feser patiently reconstructs the standard naturalistic account: every species is a variation on genetic material that has existed since life began; a mutation (from a replication copying error, or radiation, or chemical damage) produces a new trait; environmental conditions make it advantageous. The **total cause** of the new variation is the combination of all three. None alone would suffice — and so the new form is not something from nothing.

Feser then adds a supporting point from physicist Paul Davies: denying that a new life form’s information derives from some combination of prior factors, including the environment, would conflict with the second law of thermodynamics, according to which order and information tend to decline in a closed system. The point is about information bookkeeping, not about God.

Two nuances. Feser explicitly speaks of the *standard naturalistic* account, contrasting it with theistic evolutionary theories; he is showing that even the naturalist’s own story honors PPC. And he concludes that PPC is well founded *independently of natural theology*, while noting it will be very useful in reasoning from the world to its cause.

This secures confidence in **steps 2–3**. The usual confusion is to hear Feser as arguing that evolution needs God here. He isn’t; he is arguing that evolution is no counterexample to PPC.

checks.q: What does Feser think Churchland’s argument for materialism shows about PPC?
options: That PPC is implicitly assumed by naturalists as well as dualists
That PPC is false
That PPC applies only to evolution
That PPC entails materialism
checks.explanation: Churchland infers a material effect from a material total cause — PPC. The dualist runs the same principle the other way.

checks.q: On the naturalistic account Feser describes, which factors together form the total cause of a new biological variation?
options: Divine intervention and genetic material
Existing genetic material, a mutation, and environmental circumstances
The organism’s desire to adapt
Genetic material alone
checks.explanation: No one factor suffices; together they account for the variation, so PPC is respected.

checks.q: Why does Feser mention Paul Davies and the second law of thermodynamics?
options: To argue that the universe had a beginning
To prove that God must have designed life
To support the claim that new biological information must derive from some combination of prior factors
To show that evolution is false
checks.explanation: Davies’ point supports PPC’s application to evolution; it isn’t offered as an argument for God.

summary.heading: Agere sequitur esse: action follows being
summary.plain: What a thing does depends on what it is. Plants grow because they’re alive; rocks don’t, because they aren’t. Nothing can do, all by itself, something beyond its own nature — though something else can make it do so, the way a puppeteer makes a puppet dance.
summary.takeaway: What a thing does cannot outrun what it is (unless something else makes it); this is PPC’s counterpart for natures and follows from PSR.
summary.body:
The Scholastic principle *agere sequitur esse* says that what a thing does reflects what it is. Eyes and ears work differently because they are built differently; plants take in nutrients, grow, and reproduce while stones do none of these, because plants are alive and stones are not. Feser presents the principle as the counterpart, for **formal causes**, of what PPC says about **efficient causes**. An efficient cause brings about a thing’s existence or a change in it, and PPC says the effect cannot exceed that total cause. A formal cause is a thing’s nature — what makes it the kind of thing it is (for a human, rational animality). A thing’s characteristic attributes and activities flow from its nature (language flows from our rationality), and they cannot exceed that nature any more than an effect can exceed its cause. A stone that grew and reproduced would no longer be a stone.

Like PPC, the principle follows from PSR: an activity outrunning its nature would have no explanation. A footnote adds an important qualification: a thing can do what exceeds its nature when *something else* makes it do so, as a puppet’s wooden limbs move when the puppeteer moves them. What is ruled out is a thing doing so *on its own*.

The principle will matter a great deal later. It is what blocks the suggestion that a purely actual First Cause could nonetheless *act* in a way that involves unrealized potential (step 15), and it will return in Part B, where Feser argues that since creatures cannot even exist apart from God, they cannot act apart from him either.
summary.deepDive:
The key idea is that *agere sequitur esse* extends the logic of PPC from **efficient causes** to **formal causes**.

Recall the difference. An efficient cause is what produces a thing or a change in it: the baker, the heat, the sculptor. A formal cause is a thing’s nature — what makes it the kind of thing it is. For a human, that is rational animality; for water, whatever makes water water. PPC says an effect can’t exceed its total efficient cause. *Agere sequitur esse* says a thing’s characteristic activities can’t exceed its nature. Just as the effect is “contained” in the cause, a thing’s operations are “contained” in its nature — they flow from it.

Worked example: salt dissolves in water and a stone doesn’t, because of what salt and stone are. Language flows from rationality; you won’t find a dog composing sonnets. If a stone started, all by itself, to take in nutrients and grow, one of two things would be true: either it isn’t really a stone (it was a strange organism all along), or something is happening that nothing about it explains. The first option shows the principle at work (we revise our view of what the thing is); the second would violate PSR. That is exactly the reasoning Feser gives: an activity outrunning its nature would be unintelligible.

The qualification in Feser’s footnote is important. Things can do what exceeds their nature when *another* agent makes them. The puppet’s wooden limbs dance because the puppeteer moves them; a thrown stone flies because it was thrown. The principle is about what a thing can do *on its own*. So apparent exceptions always point to an outside cause — which confirms rather than refutes the principle.

In the formal argument this is **step 4**, and its big payoff is **step 15**: the First Cause’s being is purely actual, so its acting cannot involve potentiality either. There is nothing in a purely actual nature for merely potential activity to “follow” from.

The usual confusion: people read “action follows being” as determinism, as if everything a thing does is fixed by its nature. That’s not the claim. A free rational agent’s choices flow from its rational nature too, and the principle says only that its activities can’t exceed that nature. Another confusion is to think the principle is a mere definition. It isn’t: it is a substantive thesis, grounded in PSR, which even naturalists use (as the next section shows).

checks.q: How does Feser relate agere sequitur esse to PPC?
options: It is PPC applied to final causes
It is the converse of PPC
It replaces PPC for immaterial things
It applies to formal causes (natures) what PPC says about efficient causes
checks.explanation: PPC: effects can’t exceed their efficient causes. Agere sequitur esse: activities can’t exceed their agent’s nature.

checks.q: A thrown stone breaks a window, though breaking windows is not something stones do on their own. Does this violate agere sequitur esse?
options: No, because the principle concerns what a thing does on its own, and the thrower is acting on the stone
Yes, so the principle is only approximate
Yes, unless the stone is alive
No, because breaking windows is part of a stone’s nature
checks.explanation: Like the puppet, the stone exceeds its own powers only because another agent acts on it.

summary.heading: Agere sequitur esse among naturalists: Aquinas, Searle, and property dualism
summary.plain: This rule isn’t just old church philosophy. A famous argument that the soul survives death uses it, and so does a well-known non-religious philosopher, John Searle, when he criticizes a certain theory of the mind. The point is that many thinkers rely on the rule, whatever they believe about God.
summary.takeaway: Aquinas’ argument for the soul and Searle’s critique of property dualism both rely on agere sequitur esse, showing the principle is shared ground rather than a Scholastic relic.
summary.body:
Aquinas’ best-known use of the principle is his argument for the soul’s survival: intellectual activity is (on independent grounds) immaterial; a material thing cannot carry out an immaterial activity; so the soul is immaterial, and since immaterial things lack the natural tendency to decay that material things have, the soul does not perish with the body. A materialist will reject the premise that thought is immaterial, but can still accept the conditional: *if* intellectual activity were immaterial, its subject would have to be immaterial too.

In fact the naturalist John Searle argues along exactly these lines against **property dualism** (the view that mental properties are immaterial yet are properties of a material brain). Searle’s complaint is that the view is unstable: if a mental property is really something over and above the brain, it isn’t a property of the brain but a separate kind of entity; if it really is a property of the brain, it isn’t over and above it. Other critics find it mysterious how a wholly material brain could produce immaterial properties. Feser does not try to settle that debate; the point is that *agere sequitur esse*, like PPC, is not a Scholastic relic but something many secular philosophers are implicitly committed to.

The logic of Searle’s complaint is worth spelling out: a property is a way a thing is, so a genuinely immaterial property would require its bearer to be, in that respect, immaterial. That is agere sequitur esse (and PPC) applied to the mind. Whatever one concludes about the mind, the example shows that the principle is part of live contemporary debate rather than a museum piece.
summary.deepDive:
This section’s hardest move is recognizing that Feser is interested in the **conditional**, not the conclusion. He does not use the immortality of the soul as a premise for anything in natural theology. He uses Aquinas and Searle to show that “action follows being” is a principle people actually reason with.

Lay out Aquinas’ argument as a chain. (1) Intellectual activity is essentially immaterial — Aquinas has independent arguments for this, which Feser defends elsewhere. (2) A material thing cannot carry out an immaterial activity (agere sequitur esse). (3) So the human soul, which carries out intellectual activity, is immaterial. (4) Material things tend to decay by coming apart; immaterial things have no such natural tendency. (5) So the soul does not perish when the body does.

A materialist rejects premise 1. But — Feser’s point — she can accept premise 2, and so the conditional: *if* thinking were immaterial, the thinker would be too. The disagreement is over premise 1, not the principle.

Now Searle. Property dualism tries a middle way: no immaterial substance, but some immaterial properties of the brain. Searle presents a dilemma. Take “over and above.” If a mental property really is over and above the brain, it isn’t a property *of* the brain; it’s a separate thing or entity. If it really is a property of the brain, it isn’t over and above it. Other critics add that it’s mysterious how something wholly material could produce immaterial features. Both complaints rest on the idea that what belongs to a thing can’t exceed what that thing is — agere sequitur esse again (and PPC, for the “produce” version).

A worked comparison: imagine claiming that a stone has the property of understanding calculus but is in every respect just a stone. Everyone senses the incoherence — a property of that kind can’t belong to a bearer of that kind. Property dualism, according to its critics, makes the same kind of claim in a subtler way.

Feser explicitly says he isn’t settling the property-dualism dispute. The section supports **step 4** by showing that its principle is widely presupposed, making it unfair to dismiss it as Scholastic dogma.

The usual confusion: people think that invoking Aquinas’ soul argument commits Feser’s proofs to dualism. It doesn’t. The proofs of God don’t depend on the soul’s immateriality; the example is only an illustration of a principle.

checks.q: What does Feser say a materialist can accept about Aquinas’ argument for the soul?
options: The premise that intellectual activity is immaterial
The conditional that if intellectual activity were immaterial, its subject would have to be immaterial
Nothing, since materialists reject agere sequitur esse
The conclusion that the soul survives death
checks.explanation: The materialist denies that thought is immaterial but can grant the conditional, which is the principle at work.

checks.q: What is Searle’s dilemma against property dualism?
options: If the brain is material, thought is impossible
Either mental properties are physical or God exists
If a mental property is over and above the brain it is a separate entity, and if it is a property of the brain it is not over and above it
Either the mind is a computer or it is a soul
checks.explanation: Searle argues the view is unstable; Feser cites this as an implicit use of agere sequitur esse.

checks.q: Why does Feser discuss Aquinas and Searle in a chapter about God’s nature?
options: To prove the soul’s immortality as a premise for God’s existence
To argue that property dualism is true
To show that materialism is incompatible with evolution
To show that agere sequitur esse is a principle many contemporary philosophers implicitly accept
checks.explanation: The examples show the principle is live and shared, not a relic; Feser explicitly declines to settle the mind-body dispute.

summary.heading: The analogy of being: univocal, equivocal, analogical
summary.plain: We use words in three ways. Sometimes a word means exactly the same thing twice (“Fido is a dog,” “Rover is a dog”). Sometimes it means totally different things (a baseball bat versus a flying bat). And sometimes it means related but not identical things (“good wine,” “a good person”). That last way, called analogy, is still literal — and even the word “exists” works like that.
summary.takeaway: Besides univocal (same sense) and equivocal (unrelated senses) uses of words, there is a literal analogical use — and “being” itself is used that way.
summary.body:
Recalling chapter 2, Feser distinguishes three uses of terms. **Univocal**: “Fido is a dog,” “Rover is a dog” — the same sense. **Equivocal**: a “bat” flying in the attic and the “bat” you swing — unrelated senses. **Analogical**: “this wine is good,” “George is a good man” — not the same sense, but not unrelated either.

Talk of *being* or *reality* is analogical. A stone and its color and shape are all real, but not in the same way: the color and shape exist only *in* the stone, modifying and depending on it, while the stone doesn’t exist in another thing that way. Yet it isn’t that the stone is real and its attributes unreal (the way a baseball bat is simply not a flying mammal). So being is said of substance and attribute neither univocally nor equivocally, but analogically.

It helps to have a quick test for each use. If the two uses could be swapped in any sentence without changing what is claimed, they are **univocal**. If knowing one sense gives you no clue to the other, they are **equivocal** — the connection is an accident of the word. If understanding one sense helps you understand the other, because the things are really related, the use is **analogical**. Wine is good in being what wine should be; a man is good in being what a man should be. The same kind of relation holds, realized very differently.

Feser first introduced analogy in chapter 2. What is new here is his claim that the most basic concept of all — **being** — is analogical. That is illustrated by substances and their attributes. Attributes such as color and shape *modify* a substance and *depend* on it, while the substance does not modify anything else in that way. Both are real, but neither in the same way nor in unrelated ways.
summary.deepDive:
The difficult idea here is that **analogy is a third kind of literal meaning**, not a fuzzy halfway house or a polite name for metaphor.

Begin with how we actually talk. “Good” applies to wine, knives, arguments, people, and weather. Nobody thinks a good knife and a good man are good in *exactly* the same sense — a knife isn’t honest. But nobody thinks the word is a pun either, like “bat.” There is a common thread: in each case, the thing measures up to what that kind of thing should be. The thread is real, but it is realized differently in each case. That is analogy.

Now apply this to **being**, the most basic concept there is. Take a stone and its gray color. Both are real — the color isn’t an illusion. But the color exists *in* the stone: it modifies the stone and depends on it. The stone doesn’t exist in something else in that way. So “the stone is real” and “its color is real” don’t use “real” univocally. Yet it would be absurd to say the color is real only in the way a baseball bat is a “bat” in the mammal sense — i.e., not really at all. So “being” is said of substance and attribute analogically.

A thought experiment: imagine trying to make “being” univocal by insisting that to be real is to be a self-standing thing. Then colors, shapes, relations, and potentials would all be unreal. Imagine instead making it equivocal. Then saying a color “exists” would tell you nothing about what it is for a stone to exist. Neither fits how reality is structured.

This section supplies part of **step 5** (the three uses of terms) and prepares **steps 6–12**, which argue that “being” must be analogical. It also sets up **step 13** — that talk about God must be analogical — since if even substance and attribute have being analogically, we should hardly expect God and creatures to have it univocally.

The usual confusion: people hear “analogical” and think “not literally true” or “merely an analogy.” But when you say you “see” the solution to a problem, you are not speaking falsely or poetically — you really grasp it — even though your eyes aren’t involved. Analogical language says something true, in a way fitted to the reality described.

checks.q: “There was a bat in the attic” and “He swung the bat” use “bat”:
options: Equivocally
Univocally
Analogically
By analogy of attribution
checks.explanation: The meanings are completely unrelated; knowing one gives no clue to the other.

checks.q: Why does Feser say a stone and its color have being analogically?
options: Because color and stone belong to the same genus
Because both are real, but the color exists only in and dependent on the stone, while the stone does not exist in another thing that way
Because the word “being” is ambiguous like “bat”
Because the color is unreal
checks.explanation: Attributes modify and depend on substances; both are real, neither univocally nor equivocally.

summary.heading: Kinds of analogy: attribution and proportionality
summary.plain: There are different kinds of analogy. Sometimes a word really applies to one thing and to others only because of their connection to it: food is “healthy” because it makes people healthy. Sometimes it really applies to each thing in its own way: plants and animals are both truly alive. And sometimes it’s just a figure of speech: calling a brave man “a lion.”
summary.takeaway: Attribution names things by relation to one primary bearer; proper proportionality finds the perfection really in each; metaphorical proportionality finds it literally in only one — and only the first two are literal.
summary.body:
Feser distinguishes two main types of analogy.

**Analogy of attribution.** “George is healthy,” “this is healthy food,” “George’s complexion is healthy.” George is the **primary analogate**; the food and the complexion are **secondary analogates**. Health exists intrinsically only in George; the others are called healthy only because of their relation to him — the food as a *cause* of health, the complexion as an *effect and sign* of it.

**Analogy of proportionality**, which divides into two:

- **Proper proportionality**: “life” said of plants, animals, humans, and angels. Here the feature exists *intrinsically* in each analogate (unlike attribution) and *formally* in each — each really has the nature of being alive, though in very different ways.
- **Improper (metaphorical) proportionality**: “that is a lion” (at the zoo) versus “George is a lion.” Something intrinsic to George (his courage) grounds the usage, but the form of lionhood is literally present only in the animal.

Metaphor is one kind of analogy, but not all analogy is metaphor. And it is the analogy of proper — that is, nonmetaphorical — proportionality that is crucial for the concept of being.

Two questions sort the cases. **Is the perfection intrinsically in each thing it is said of?** In attribution, no — the food isn’t itself healthy the way George is. **Is the form or nature literally present in each?** In proper proportionality, yes; in metaphorical proportionality, only in one of them. Theology needs both of the literal kinds: proper proportionality lets us say being, goodness, and life are really in God as well as in creatures, each in its own way; attribution lets us see God as the primary analogate of being, with creatures called beings because of their relation to him as cause (Feser’s footnote).
summary.deepDive:
The difficulty in this section is keeping three kinds of analogy distinct, since the examples can blur. A patient way is to use two tests.

**Test 1: Is the perfection intrinsically in each analogate?** With “healthy,” it’s only in George. The food is called healthy because it *causes* health in things like George; the complexion because it is *caused by and a sign of* his health. Take George away and the food isn’t healthy in itself — it has nutrients, but health is a feature of living bodies. So “healthy” works by **attribution**: one **primary analogate**, several **secondary analogates** named by relation to it.

**Test 2: Is the form or nature literally present in each?** With “alive,” said of a plant, a dog, a human, and an angel — yes. Each really has the nature of a living thing, though plant life (nutrition, growth), animal life (plus sensation), human life (plus reason), and angelic life (pure intellect) are very different. This is **proper proportionality**: intrinsic *and* formal in each. With “lion,” said of the zoo animal and brave George — the courage that grounds the usage is intrinsically in George, but the *form* of lionhood is literally in the animal only. That is **improper or metaphorical proportionality**.

So: attribution fails test 1; metaphorical proportionality passes test 1 but fails test 2; proper proportionality passes both.

Why does this matter for God? Suppose we used attribution alone and said “God is good” means only “God causes goodness in creatures.” Then God wouldn’t intrinsically be good, any more than food is intrinsically healthy. Classical theists want more: goodness, being, and life are *really in* God, in the highest way. That is proper proportionality. Yet attribution also applies, because God is the source on which all creaturely being depends, so he is the primary analogate of being (Feser’s footnote 14).

This section completes **step 5** and is what makes **step 13** possible: literal, positive statements about God.

The usual confusion: “All analogy is metaphor.” Feser insists the reverse is the truth: metaphor is one kind of analogy, but the kinds that matter for metaphysics are nonmetaphorical. When Plantinga later describes Aquinas as treating language about God as nonliteral, this is the distinction he misses.

checks.q: “This food is healthy” is an example of which kind of analogy?
options: Univocal predication
Proper proportionality
Attribution, with the food as a secondary analogate
Metaphorical proportionality
checks.explanation: Health is intrinsically only in the living body (George); food is called healthy as a cause of it.

checks.q: What makes “life” said of plants and angels an analogy of proper proportionality rather than metaphor?
options: Life exists only in angels
Plants are called alive only because they cause life
The word “life” is ambiguous
The form of being alive is literally present in each, though realized differently
checks.explanation: Proper proportionality: the perfection is intrinsic and formal in each analogate.

checks.q: Why would the analogy of attribution alone be inadequate for saying “God is good”?
options: Because it would only mean God causes goodness, not that goodness is intrinsically in God
Because it would make “good” univocal
Because God is a secondary analogate
Because attribution is always metaphorical
checks.explanation: Attribution names secondary analogates by relation without intrinsic possession; classical theists hold that perfections are really in God (proper proportionality), with attribution also applying.

summary.heading: Why “being” is not a genus; proportional similarity
summary.plain: “Being” — the idea of existing — isn’t a category like “animal” that splits into subtypes, because there’s nothing outside existence to split it with. Instead, things exist in ways that are alike in pattern but different in detail, the way seeing a tree and “seeing” a math answer are both real seeing.
summary.takeaway: “Being” can’t be a genus because nothing outside being could divide it into kinds; it is said of things by proportional similarity — each thing’s existence is to its essence as another’s is to its own.
summary.body:
“Being” applies to substances, to attributes, to things whose essence and existence are distinct, and to that whose essence just is its existence — by an analogy of proper proportionality. The concept is applied to each in an indistinct, indeterminate way, on the basis of a real likeness among them, rather than in exactly the same way.

This differs from a univocal term applied to very diverse things. “Animal” applies to fish, birds, and reptiles in exactly the same way, naming a **genus**; what distinguishes them is their **specific difference**, which lies outside the genus (you can grasp rationality without grasping animality, or atomic number 79 without grasping metal). But being is not a genus. You cannot grasp substance or attribute *without* grasping them as beings, so their differences are not extrinsic to being. Indeed, the only thing outside being is nonbeing, and nothing cannot differentiate anything.

Instead, being is predicated by **proportional similarity**. Compare “I see the tree” and “I see that the Pythagorean theorem is true.” The seeing is radically different in the two cases, but eyes are to the tree as the intellect is to the theorem; that similarity of *relations* grounds using the one concept. In the same way, a man’s existence is to his essence as an angel’s existence is to its essence as God’s existence is to his essence — though the relation differs in each case (in God existence is *identical* to essence; in an angel it actualizes the potential essence of a wholly immaterial being; in a man it actualizes the essence of something with material and immaterial operations). A footnote adds that being is *also* predicated by analogy of attribution, with God, whose essence is existence, as the primary analogate and creatures as secondary analogates insofar as he causes them to exist.
summary.deepDive:
The hardest idea in this section is the argument that **being is not a genus**. It sounds like hair-splitting, but it does real work.

Start with how a genus works. Take “animal.” To mark off a species within it, you add a **specific difference**: “rational” marks off humans; other differences mark off dogs or sharks. Crucially, the difference comes from *outside* the genus. You can understand what “rational” means without already understanding “animal” — there could be rational things that aren’t animals (angels, say). Likewise “having atomic number 79” picks out gold within the genus metal, and you can grasp the atomic number without grasping metalhood.

Now try to treat being as the highest genus, with substance, attribute, and so on as its species. What would the specific difference be? It would have to be something outside being. But whatever is outside being is nothing — and nothing can’t differentiate anything, because it isn’t anything. Put another way: you can’t grasp “substance” or “attribute” without *already* grasping them as ways of being. Their differences are themselves ways of being. So being isn’t divided the way a genus is.

That is why “being” can’t be univocal. A univocal term like “animal” applies in exactly the same way to all its species, with differences added from outside. “Being” applies to everything, and its differences are inside it.

What takes the place of genus and species? **Proportional similarity.** Feser’s example: we “see” a tree and “see” that a theorem is true. The eyes are to the tree as the intellect is to the theorem. When we spell out each kind of seeing — light striking the eye versus grasping relations among concepts — they don’t turn out to be two species of one genus. The likeness is in the *relations*.

Applied to being: a man’s existence is to his essence as an angel’s existence is to its essence, and as God’s existence is to God’s essence. But the relation differs in each case. In a man and an angel, existence actualizes an essence distinct from it; in God, existence *is* the essence. Feser adds (footnote 14) that being is also said by attribution, with God as the primary analogate.

This section explains why **step 12** must come out as it does, and it lays the groundwork for **step 30**: God isn’t a member of any genus, which is exactly what theistic personalism denies.

The usual confusion: “Being is just the most general category, so everything is a species of it.” The argument shows that picture can’t be right.

checks.q: Why can nothing serve as a specific difference dividing being into species?
options: Because only God is a being
Because the only thing outside being is nonbeing, which cannot differentiate anything
Because species exist only in the mind
Because being is too simple to have species
checks.explanation: A differentia must be extrinsic to its genus, but whatever is extrinsic to being is nothing.

checks.q: What grounds calling both eyesight and intellectual insight “seeing”?
options: The word is used equivocally
They are two species of the genus “seeing”
The eyes are to the tree as the intellect is to the theorem — a similarity of relations
Both involve light
checks.explanation: Proportional similarity: the likeness lies in the relations, not in a shared generic nature.

checks.q: In Feser’s proportionality of existence to essence, how does God differ from a man and an angel?
options: God’s existence actualizes a potential essence
God has no essence at all
God’s essence is material
In God, existence is identical to essence
checks.explanation: In creatures existence actualizes a distinct essence; in God they are identical — so the relations differ and predication is analogical.

summary.heading: The argument that being is analogical
summary.plain: Feser gives a short argument for this. Both what a thing is and what it could become are real — a sleeping pianist really can play — but they aren’t real in exactly the same way. They aren’t real in totally unrelated ways either. So they are real in related ways, which is what analogy means.
summary.takeaway: Because potentiality and actuality are both real and really distinct, “real” must apply to them in analogous (neither identical nor unrelated) senses — so being is analogical, on grounds that don’t presuppose God.
summary.body:
Feser grounds the analogy of being in the act/potency distinction, which change forces on us (chapter 1). His seven-step argument, paraphrased: actuality is real; potentiality is real; they are really distinct; if potentiality were real in the same (univocal) sense as actuality, they would not be distinct; if it were real only in an equivocal sense, it would not be real at all; the three uses exhaust literal usage; so potentiality is real in a sense analogous to actuality’s.

He defends each premise. Denying premise 2 is **Parmenides’** denial of change, already shown incoherent. Denying premise 1 is the extreme **Heraclitean** view (on a traditional reading) that only change is real, with nothing stable. That is equally incoherent: there would be no persisting self to move from premises to conclusion, no single stable argument to repeat to critics or to oneself; change always heads *toward* some outcome (a melting ice cube moves toward liquidity and flatness — new actualities); and a thing changes as it does because it is actually a certain kind of thing (it melts because it is water, not wood or glass). Premise 3 holds because the real distinction of essence and existence (chapter 4) is already a case of real potency/act distinction, and because calling the distinction merely conceptual would amount to saying only one of the two is real — denying 1 or 2. Premise 4 holds because sameness of sense would make one a kind of the other; premise 5 because being in a wholly unrelated sense just means being unreal; premise 6 because the three uses exhaust literal predication.

This gives grounds for analogical predication, and for the analogical character of “being” in particular, that are independent of any argument for God — someone could accept act and potency without accepting the Aristotelian proof.
summary.deepDive:
The argument has a simple skeleton: it lists the only three options and eliminates two. The hard part is seeing why potentiality is **real but not actual**.

A worked example. Maria is a concert pianist, asleep. Right now she isn’t playing. Is her ability to play something real? Clearly: she differs from someone who has never touched a piano, and that difference is a fact about her now, not just about her past or future. Yet her playing isn’t actual. So her potential is *something* — not nothing — but not the same kind of something as actual playing. That is premise 2 (potency is real) and premise 3 (it is really distinct from act) in one picture.

Now the elimination. If “real” meant exactly the same for Maria’s ability and her actual playing (univocal), there would be no difference between being able to play and playing — potency would just be another actuality (premise 4). If “real” meant something wholly unrelated for her ability (equivocal), then saying her ability is real would be like saying a baseball bat is a “bat” in the zoological sense — i.e., it would really be unreal (premise 5). Since univocal, equivocal, and analogical exhaust literal usage (premise 6), the ability is real in a sense *analogous* to actuality (conclusion 7).

Feser’s defenses matter. Deny premise 2 and you are Parmenides, denying change — incoherent (chapter 1). Deny premise 1 and you are the extreme Heraclitean, for whom only flux exists. But then there is no persisting reasoner to go from premises to conclusion, no stable argument to repeat, no direction to change (a melting ice cube is heading *toward* liquidity and flatness), and no explanation of why things change as they do (ice melts because it is water, not wood or glass). Deny premise 3 by calling the distinction merely verbal, and you collapse into denying premise 1 or 2 — and chapter 4 already gave a real case (essence and existence).

Notice the nuance Feser underlines: the argument needs only act-potency theory, which one could accept *without* accepting any proof of God. That matters dialectically — analogy is not invented to rescue theology.

This section *is* **steps 6–12**. The usual confusion: “potential” means “merely logically possible,” like a unicorn’s being possible. But Aristotelian potency is a real capacity grounded in what something actually is — the ice’s potential to melt, not a mere lack of contradiction.

checks.q: Denying which premise amounts to Parmenides’ denial of change?
options: Potentiality is real
Actuality is real
The three uses exhaust literal usage
If potency were real univocally it wouldn’t be distinct
checks.explanation: Change is the actualization of potential; deny potency and you deny change.

checks.q: Why does Feser hold that if potentiality were real only in an equivocal sense, it wouldn’t be real at all?
options: Because potentiality is a kind of actuality
Because being “real” in a sense wholly unrelated to the ordinary one just means being unreal
Because Heraclitus proved it
Because equivocal terms are always false
checks.explanation: That is premise 5: total unrelatedness of sense leaves nothing of reality.

checks.q: What makes the argument for the analogy of being independent of theism?
options: It is a version of the ontological argument
It relies on revelation
It relies only on the act/potency distinction, which one can accept without accepting any proof of God
It assumes God is the primary analogate
checks.explanation: Feser stresses that the grounds come from act-potency theory alone, so analogy isn’t ad hoc.

summary.heading: Why this matters for God-talk: between silence and nonsense
summary.plain: This matters for talking about God. If words meant exactly the same for God as for us, God would just be a big version of us. If they meant something totally different, we’d be saying nothing. Analogy is the middle path that lets us say true things about God without shrinking him down to our size.
summary.takeaway: Univocal God-talk makes God a creature (or leaves only negations), equivocal God-talk leaves words empty — so only analogical predication lets us speak literally and positively about God.
summary.body:
The significance for natural theology is enormous. The proofs lead to something radically unlike anything we experience — purely actual, simple, immaterial, immutable, eternal. Words fitted to changeable, composite, material, temporal things cannot apply to such a being univocally; if to be a being *just meant* to be material and changeable, God would not be a being in that sense.

If we had only univocal language, we could say only what God is *not* — a purely **apophatic** or negative theology. But then we could not even say that God *exists* or that he *causes* the world, which are affirmative claims; the negative way is part of the story, not all of it, or it would undercut the very arguments that got us to God. Equivocal language is no escape: if God’s “power” means something wholly unrelated to power, what does it mean? Any attempt to fill in “God has ‘power’ in the sense that he ___” either uses a univocal term (reviving the first problem) or an equivocal one (compounding the second). Confined to these two options, we would end in agnosticism — or even atheism, if we couldn’t say what “God exists” means. The resolution is the third, independently motivated use: analogical predication — attribution and proper proportionality — lets us speak **literally and positively** about God.

Feser notes (as in chapter 2) that this is not special pleading: physics also stretches ordinary words — entities that are both wave-like and particle-like, *space itself* being curved — and seems intelligible only if understood analogically. We should expect the same when describing a level of reality more fundamental than physics.
summary.deepDive:
The hardest point here is why **negative theology can’t be the whole story**, even though Feser keeps it as part of the story.

Negative (apophatic) theology describes God by denial: not material, not changing, not in time, not composite. Many attributes in this very chapter are negative in form — immutability (not changing), immateriality (not material), timelessness (not in time). So Feser is not hostile to it. The problem comes if we say *only* negative things. Then we couldn’t say that God exists, or that he causes the world, or that he explains why there is anything at all — every one of those is affirmative. A purely negative theology would undercut the very arguments that led to God.

Why not just speak univocally? Because the proofs lead to something utterly unlike what our words were built for. If “being” *meant* “being a material, changeable thing,” God wouldn’t be a being in that sense. Univocal predication would turn God into one more item of the kind we already know — or, if we refuse that, leave us with only denials.

Why not equivocally? Feser’s fill-in-the-blank test is decisive. Say “God has ‘power’ in the sense that he ___.” Fill the blank with a univocal term, and the original problem returns. Fill it with an equivocal term, and you have a second word you can’t explain. So equivocation produces not a new meaning but no meaning. The upshot would be agnosticism — or even atheism, if we can’t say what “God exists” means.

A worked comparison: a physicist describing the electron. It isn’t a tiny billiard ball (univocal “particle” misleads), and it isn’t that “particle” means nothing here (equivocal emptiness). Physicists speak of particle-like and wave-like behavior, extending ordinary concepts analogically — just as relativity speaks of curved *space*, though curvature ordinarily belongs to objects in space. Feser draws exactly this parallel: if physics needs analogy, so does talk of the cause of there being a physical world at all.

This section supplies **step 13**, which is used throughout: in answering Plantinga (step 30) and in every positive attribute of Part B.

The usual confusion: “If God-talk is analogical, we don’t really know what we mean.” We know what we affirm (a real perfection of which ours is a limited likeness) and what we deny (the limits and composition it has in us). The concept is indeterminate, not empty.

checks.q: Why can’t negative theology be the whole story, according to Feser?
options: Because negative statements are always false
Because God has no negative attributes
Because negative theology is univocal
Because saying that God exists or causes the world is affirmative, so pure negation would undercut the proofs
checks.explanation: Feser keeps negative theology as part of the truth but notes it can’t express the proofs’ own affirmative conclusions.

checks.q: What is the point of Feser’s “God has ‘power’ in the sense that he ___” test?
options: To show that any attempt to explain an equivocal term either reintroduces univocity or multiplies unexplained terms
To show that God lacks power
To define power precisely
To show that power is a Cambridge property
checks.explanation: The equivocal option can never be given content, so it leaves God-talk meaningless.

checks.q: Why does Feser mention wave-particle duality and curved space?
options: To argue that God is a physical field
To show that science too extends language analogically beyond ordinary use
To prove the universe had a beginning
To show that physics disproves theology
checks.explanation: If physics needs analogy for strange entities, we should expect it when describing the cause of all physical reality.

summary.heading: Unity, step one: no potentiality even in God’s activity
summary.plain: The ultimate cause can have no untapped potential at all — not even in what it does. What a thing does reflects what it is, and a being with both a fully real side and an untapped side would be made of parts, which would need something else to hold them together. Then it wouldn’t be the ultimate cause.
summary.takeaway: The First Cause can’t have potentiality even in its activity: acting reflects being, and an actual-plus-potential being would be composite and caused.
summary.body:
Feser now turns to the attributes, starting with **unity**: there is, and in principle could be, only one God. Chapter 1 showed that things mixing act and potency depend at every moment on something purely actual. A critic might grant that the First Cause’s *existence* involves no actualization while suggesting that its *activity* (such as actualizing other things) does.

Feser gives two replies. **First, agere sequitur esse**: if a thing exists in a purely actual way, how could it act in a less than purely actual way? Existence is what is most fundamental in a thing; where in its nature would these less fundamental potentials for activity come from? **Second, composition**: a being with actual existence but potential activity would have parts — an actual part and a potential part. As chapter 2 showed, a composite needs a cause that unites its parts, and that cause must be extrinsic (an intrinsic one would be self-causing, which is incoherent). This holds even if the thing always existed: the question is why the parts are combined *at all*, which calls for an *ontologically* prior cause even if there is no *temporally* prior one. But a First Cause with a cause is not the first cause and cannot end the hierarchical regress. So God is purely actual, without qualification.

The significance is that “pure actuality” now holds without qualification. Everything that follows — uniqueness, simplicity, immutability, and the rest — depends on there being no potentiality in God *at all*. Had the loophole stayed open, a critic could say that God is unique in his being but changeable, composite, or multiple in his activity. Feser closes it by combining a principle from this chapter (action follows being) with a result from chapter 2 (composites need causes).
summary.deepDive:
The key idea is that **temporal questions and ontological questions come apart**, and the second kind is what matters.

The critic’s proposal: grant that the First Cause’s *existence* needs no actualizing — that’s how it ends the regress — but let its *activity* involve potential. Maybe it has unrealized capacities to do this or that.

Feser’s first reply uses **agere sequitur esse** (step 4). Existence is the most fundamental fact about a thing; everything else about it flows from its being. If a thing’s very being is purely actual, from what in it would merely potential activity arise? Its activities would outrun its nature, which the principle forbids.

His second reply uses chapter 2. A being that is actual in existence but potential in activity has two distinct components: an actual one and a potential one. It is composite. And a composite needs a cause of its composition — something that makes it the case that these parts are united. That cause can’t be one of the parts or the whole itself (that would be self-causation), so it must be external.

Here is where the temporal/ontological distinction enters. A critic may say, “Fine, but suppose the composite always existed — then nothing had to put it together.” Feser replies that the question isn’t *when* the parts were joined but *why they are joined at all*. Course illustration: a lamp has been lit all night. Asking “what’s keeping it lit right now?” is a real question even if it was never switched on (suppose it had always been on); the answer — the current — is **ontologically** prior, not temporally prior. The First Cause, by contrast, has to be what *ends* a hierarchical series of such present dependencies. A first cause that needs a cause isn’t first.

This section is **steps 14–17**. Step 17 — God is purely actual without qualification — is the premise from which unity (step 21), immutability (step 32), immateriality (step 40), and more are derived.

The usual confusion: “If God has no potential, he must be inert or unable to do different things.” Pure actuality means lacking no perfection, not lacking activity; how a purely actual God freely creates is taken up in Part B. Another confusion is to think the argument assumes the universe had a beginning. It doesn’t; it would work in a beginningless world.

checks.q: What is Feser’s first reply to the suggestion that God has potentiality in his activity but not his existence?
options: Activity is a Cambridge property
Activity is unreal
By agere sequitur esse, a purely actual being can’t act in a less than purely actual way
God has no activity
checks.explanation: Action follows being; there’s nothing in a purely actual nature for potential activity to derive from.

checks.q: Why doesn’t it help to suppose the composite First Cause had always existed?
options: Because nothing can always exist
Because the universe had a beginning
Because eternal things are simple by definition
Because the question is why its parts are combined at all, which requires an ontologically (not temporally) prior cause
checks.explanation: Everlastingness removes only a temporally prior cause, not the need for a present uniting cause.

summary.heading: Unity, step two: why there can be only one purely actual being
summary.plain: How can there ever be two of something? Two coins differ because they’re made of different metal; a penny and a dime differ by some added feature. Either way, you need parts. The ultimate cause has no parts, so there is nothing that could make a second one. There is, and could only be, one God.
summary.takeaway: There can be many of a kind only where individuals differ by parts, parts entail potency, and so a purely actual being is unique in principle.
summary.body:
For there to be more than one thing of a kind, there must be a distinction between an individual and its species, or (for a species) between the species and its genus — and any such distinction brings with it a distinction between potentiality and actuality.

Take the human species, with the essence *rational animal*. Animality and rationality are distinct metaphysical parts of that essence: rationality is one way of being an animal, not the only way, so it must be *added* to animality. Being an individual human adds a further part — the matter of one’s body, which distinguishes one human from another. Each part brings potentiality: the matter is potentially a human or some other kind of thing, and must be actualized as a human; the genus animal is, of itself, potentially rational or nonrational. Anything with parts of any kind is a mixture of act and potency, since parts only potentially compose a whole until actualized — even if the actualization never had a temporal beginning. (A footnote closes a loophole: one cannot distinguish two purely actual beings by other sorts of parts, such as substance and accidents, since *any* composition entails potentiality.)

So multiplicity within a kind requires composition, composition requires potentiality, and God has no potentiality. God is therefore not a member of a kind that could have other members: he is unique, and the theism the proofs reach is monotheism.

The conclusion is stronger than it first sounds. Feser isn’t claiming that, as it happens, we only find one God. He is claiming that a second purely actual being is impossible, because nothing could make it a *second* one.
summary.deepDive:
The central question is disarmingly simple: **what makes two things two?**

Take two pennies fresh from the mint, identical in design. What makes them two rather than one penny counted twice? Not their nature — both are pennies. Their matter: this lump of copper-coated zinc versus that one. That is how members of a species differ: by the matter in which the shared nature is realized. Now take a penny and a dime. They differ in species (within the genus coin) by some added specific difference — denomination, size, metal. That is how species differ: by a difference added to the genus.

Feser’s claim is that these are the only routes to plurality within a kind, and both require **metaphysical parts**: matter plus form, or genus plus difference. And parts bring **potentiality**. The matter of a penny could have been melted into a wire. The genus coin is, of itself, open to being a penny or a dime; one possibility must be actualized. More generally, parts only potentially make up a whole until something actualizes their union — even if the union never had a first moment.

Feser’s human example makes the same points: animality and rationality are distinct parts of human nature (rationality is one way, not the only way, of being an animal); individual humans differ by matter.

Now apply it. God is purely actual (step 17). So God has no such parts. So there is nothing that could distinguish God from a second God. Footnote 17 closes a loophole: you can’t distinguish two purely actual beings by some *other* kind of part, like substance and accident, because any composition whatsoever entails potency.

This section is **steps 18–21**. Step 21 isn’t just monotheism as a matter of fact — it is monotheism *in principle*. That difference becomes important in the simplicity section, where Feser argues that a God within a genus could be unique only by luck.

The usual confusion: “God is one” is heard as a count — one, like one apple rather than two. But the claim is that God isn’t the kind of thing that could be counted among others at all; he isn’t an instance of a kind. Another confusion is to think two gods could be told apart by location. Location is a feature of material things with parts, which a purely actual being lacks.

checks.q: According to Feser, what distinguishes individual members of a material species, such as two humans?
options: Their matter
Their specific difference
Their essence
