Their existence alone
checks.explanation: Members of a species share the nature; matter individuates them.

checks.q: Why does multiplicity within a kind require potentiality?
options: Because only material things can be counted
Because it requires parts (matter/form or genus/difference), and parts involve potentiality
Because PSR forbids plurality
Because many things are always in time
checks.explanation: Matter could be otherwise; a genus is open to several species; parts only potentially compose a whole.

checks.q: Why can’t two purely actual beings be distinguished by one having an accident the other lacks?
options: Because both would have all accidents
Because accidents are Cambridge properties
Because any composition, including substance and accident, involves potentiality
Because accidents exist only in material things
checks.explanation: Footnote 17: parts of any kind entail potency, so neither being would be purely actual.

summary.heading: One God, five paths
summary.plain: The five arguments describe the ultimate cause in five ways: fully real, having no parts, existence itself, the mind behind necessary truths, and a being that can’t fail to exist. Feser shows each description implies the others. So the five arguments aren’t pointing to five gods but to one God seen from five angles.
summary.takeaway: Pure actuality, simplicity, subsistent existence, and necessity each entail the others, so the five proofs are five routes to one and the same God.
summary.body:
Feser then shows that the five proofs reach the same God by showing that their key descriptions are mutually entailing.

- **Pure actuality ⇔ absolute simplicity.** Whatever has parts mixes act and potency, so the purely actual is simple. Conversely, something simple must be actual (or it would not exist) and can have no potentiality (or it would have an actual part and a potential part). So the Unmoved Mover of chapter 1 is the One of chapter 2.
- **Pure actuality ⇔ subsistent existence.** Essence and existence, where distinct, are related as potency to act, so the purely actual cannot have an essence distinct from its existence. Conversely, what just *is* subsistent existence cannot depend on some potential being actualized, or its existence would be derived, making it one more dependent thing. So chapter 1’s cause is chapter 4’s.
- **Simplicity ⇔ subsistent existence**, directly: a simple thing cannot have an essence distinct from its existence (that would be a metaphysical part), and subsistent existence can have no parts of any other kind either (parts entail potentiality).
- **All of these ⇔ absolute necessity.** A contingent being would need some potential actualized and would have parts (at least essence plus existence) needing combination; conversely, a necessary being can have neither potentiality nor parts, or its existence would depend on them.

So the necessary being of chapter 5 and the necessarily existing intellect of chapter 3 are the same as the purely actual actualizer, the One, and subsistent existence itself. These are not five deities but five routes to one God.
summary.deepDive:
The hard idea here is **mutual entailment** — and why it settles identity.

In logic, “A if and only if B” means each implies the other: whatever has A has B, and whatever has B has A. Feser establishes a web of such biconditionals:

- purely actual ⇔ absolutely simple;
- purely actual ⇔ subsistent existence itself;
- simple ⇔ subsistent existence itself;
- all three ⇔ absolutely necessary.

Why does this show the proofs reach one being? Because unity (step 21) says there can be only one purely actual being. If everything simple is purely actual, and everything that is subsistent existence is purely actual, and everything necessary is purely actual, then each of these descriptions picks out the one-and-only purely actual being. Five descriptions, one referent.

A course analogy: ancient astronomers named the bright “morning star” and the bright “evening star.” The discovery that both are Venus wasn’t a sixth observation of a new planet; it was the realization that two descriptions pick out one thing. Feser’s convergence works like that, except the identity is shown by reasoning rather than by telescope.

Look at one entailment in detail. Why must something simple be purely actual? It is actual — if it had no actuality it wouldn’t exist. Could it also have some potentiality? Then it would have an actual aspect and a potential aspect, two distinct constituents — and so it wouldn’t be simple. Conversely, why must the purely actual be simple? Because anything with parts has potency: the parts only potentially make up the whole until united.

And necessity: if something were contingent, some potential would need actualizing, or some parts (at least essence and existence) would need combining, for it to exist. Anything with neither exists necessarily. That entailment brings in chapter 5’s necessary being — and chapter 3’s necessarily existing intellect.

This section is **steps 22–26**. Notice that the convergence isn’t a new, sixth argument for God; it’s a consequence of what each proof already concluded plus the analysis of composition and potency.

The usual confusion: “The five proofs are five premises supporting one conclusion, so if one fails the case fails.” In fact each proof is meant to stand alone; convergence shows only that, if more than one succeeds, they reach the same God.

checks.q: Why must something absolutely simple also be purely actual?
options: Because it is material
Because it is in time
Because it is caused
Because if it had any potentiality it would have an actual part and a potential part, and so not be simple
checks.explanation: A simple thing must be actual (or not exist) and can’t mix potency without composition.

checks.q: Which attribute links the Augustinian proof’s divine intellect (ch. 3) to the other proofs’ conclusions?
options: Absolute necessity
Immateriality
Omnipotence
Timelessness
checks.explanation: The necessarily existing intellect of chapter 3 is identified via the entailments between necessity and pure actuality/simplicity/subsistent existence.

checks.q: What is the logical role of the convergence argument?
options: It shows that all five proofs depend on each other
It shows that the five proofs, if sound, reach one and the same being
It proves that the universe is necessary
It is a sixth independent proof of God
checks.explanation: Mutual entailment plus unity shows that the five descriptions pick out one referent.

summary.heading: Simplicity: the heart of classical theism
summary.plain: Saying God has no parts (“simplicity”) is the key to the whole picture. If God were made of parts, something would have to hold the parts together, and that something would be more basic than God. And God would be just one member of a “god” category — like Zeus being the last god left on Mount Olympus. That wouldn’t be God at all.
summary.takeaway: Simplicity is inseparable from God’s uniqueness and ultimacy; deny it and God becomes one of a kind and in need of a cause — a superangel, not God.
summary.body:
Feser stresses that unity cannot be separated from **simplicity**. If God contained a genus/difference or essence/existence distinction, there could in principle be more than one God. His status as First Cause also depends on it: any parts at all — act and potency, essence and existence, or others — would mean he needs a cause like everything else.

So to deny divine simplicity is implicitly to deny God’s uniqueness and ultimacy. Making God an instance of a genus turns him into a member of a pantheon, *even if the sole member* — Zeus and Odin would have the same nature even if they were the only residents of Olympus and Asgard. Making him something that needs a cause reduces him to a creature, even if the one creature that happens to lack a cause (and allowing an uncaused composite would undercut the proofs themselves). Insisting that he is immaterial doesn’t help: that yields a kind of superangel, and worshiping it would be idolatry. Denying that anything is simple amounts to atheism.

Hence the mainstream of Western philosophical theology — pagans (Aristotle, Plotinus), Jews (Maimonides), Muslims (Avicenna, Averroes), Christians (Athanasius, Augustine, Anselm, Aquinas) — treated simplicity as nonnegotiable. The Catholic Church taught it at the Fourth Lateran Council (1215) and the First Vatican Council (1869–1870); Luther and Calvin affirmed it. It is the core of **classical theism**.

Notice the structure of the claim. Feser is not saying simplicity is one more attribute to add to a list. He is saying it is the attribute on which God’s uniqueness and ultimacy depend — so that giving it up doesn’t produce a different conception of God but, strictly, gives up God.
summary.deepDive:
The hardest point here is Feser’s strong claim that **denying simplicity is implicitly atheism**. That sounds like an insult to theists who reject simplicity; it is actually a precise logical claim.

Recall what “God” means in this book: the ultimate explanation of things, the First Cause that terminates the regress of dependence. Now ask what composition would do. If God had parts of any kind — act and potency, essence and existence, genus and difference, really distinct attributes — then (by chapter 2 and step 16) something would have to account for those parts being united. That something would be more ultimate than God. So the “God” in question would not be the First Cause; the real First Cause would be whatever unites him. Hence: to deny that anything is simple is to deny that anything is ultimate — atheism in Feser’s sense.

Then the uniqueness point. If God fell under a genus, being God would be a kind of thing, and he would be an instance of it. Feser’s Zeus and Odin illustration nails this: even if every other Olympian vanished, Zeus would still be *a* god, the sole survivor of a pantheon. His nature wouldn’t change. So a God within a genus is unique only by luck.

Immateriality doesn’t save the situation. An immaterial being with parts is what Feser calls a **superangel** — powerful, perhaps without body, but still a creature: one of a kind, dependent on a cause. Worshiping it would be idolatry, the honoring of a creature as if it were the Creator.

Feser then notes the breadth of the tradition that held this: Aristotle and Plotinus; Maimonides; Avicenna and Averroes; Athanasius, Augustine, Anselm, Aquinas; Lateran IV (1215) and Vatican I (1869–1870); Luther and Calvin. The point isn’t an appeal to authority but a signal that simplicity is the core of classical theism, not a sectarian add-on.

In the formal reasoning, this is **steps 27–28**. Step 27 draws on steps 16 and 18–19; step 28 draws the consequence.

The usual confusion: “simple” heard as “simplistic” or “low in complexity.” Divine simplicity means lack of composition, and it is compatible with — indeed required for — God’s containing all perfections eminently. Another confusion: “Feser says theistic personalists are atheists.” His claim is about the implications of the view, not about anyone’s sincerity.

checks.q: What is the point of the Zeus-alone-on-Olympus illustration?
options: That God is immaterial
That pagan gods are material
That a god who falls under a kind would be unique only by fact, not in principle
That polytheism is incoherent
checks.explanation: Zeus’s nature wouldn’t change if he were the only god left; he’d still be one of a kind.

checks.q: Why does Feser say that denying simplicity implicitly amounts to atheism?
options: Because theistic personalists deny God exists
Because simplicity is defined by councils
Because composite things can’t be personal
Because a composite God would need a cause, so he wouldn’t be the ultimate First Cause
checks.explanation: Composition entails dependence on a uniting cause, which would be more ultimate than the composite ‘God.’

summary.heading: Theistic personalism and Plantinga’s critique
summary.plain: Some modern religious philosophers reject this and think of God as a person like us, only without limits. The philosopher Alvin Plantinga argued that if God had no parts, God would be just an abstract idea. Feser replies that Plantinga misunderstands the view: our words for God’s power and knowledge are different, but they can describe one undivided reality.
summary.takeaway: Plantinga’s objections come from reading simplicity through univocity, Platonic properties, and a flattened notion of “property”; drop those assumptions and the absurdities vanish, while the real stakes — dependence and uniqueness — remain.
summary.body:
Recently some theistic thinkers have rejected simplicity. They have been dubbed “neo-theists” (Norman Geisler) and “theistic personalists” (Brian Davies, who lists Alvin Plantinga, Richard Swinburne, and Charles Hartshorne). The label reflects their treating God as the unique member of a species under the genus *person*, alongside humans and angels, but without their limits. The dispute is *not* about whether God is personal — classical theists ascribe intellect and will to God — but about whether being personal puts God in a genus and makes him composite. (Some, like process theologian Hartshorne, even say God changes — which already implies potentiality and composition.)

**Plantinga** argues that simplicity says God is identical with each of his properties, so all his properties are one, contradicting the obvious fact that God has several (power, mercy), and makes God a property and hence an abstract object. Feser replies that Plantinga reads the doctrine through three assumptions of his own: (1) a very broad sense of “property” covering anything predicable (being human, wise, barefoot, married to Xanthippe, Plato’s teacher, even being Socrates and one’s essence); (2) properties as Platonic abstract objects in a “third realm”; (3) univocal predication.

Classical theists reject all three. (a) **Analogy**: power and knowledge are distinct *in us*, but what we call power and knowledge in God are only analogous to ours, so their distinctness needn’t carry over. Plantinga also misreads analogy as nonliteral — but attribution and proper proportionality are literal: nonunivocal does not mean nonliteral. And no classical theist says God is a “property” to begin with; that is Plantinga’s straw man. (b) **Metaphysics of essence**: we must distinguish a thing’s **essence** (rational animality), its **properties** in the strict sense that flow from the essence (the capacity to be amused), its **contingent accidents** (skin color — still intrinsic), and mere **relations** (being Plato’s teacher). And these are concrete constituents of the thing, not Platonic Forms it participates in — what Nicholas Wolterstorff calls a “constituent ontology.” The odd results — that creating humans would be as essential to God as wisdom, that God is an abstract object — come from Plantinga’s assumptions, not from the doctrine. When Plantinga replies that the word “property” doesn’t matter since these are all “characteristics,” he misses that Aquinas’ point is metaphysical, not verbal.

Plantinga also misses what is at stake. The worry isn’t just Platonic participation but **causal dependence** and **uniqueness**. Human rationality and animality can exist apart, so something must combine them; if God’s wisdom and power were distinct, something would have to combine *them*. A God who participates in a divine essence or belongs to a genus would be unique only as a matter of contingent fact. Such a being would be a quasi-divine ersatz, powerful but essentially creaturely — and nothing in the proofs supports even that, since each concludes to a wholly noncomposite cause. Classical theism and simplicity stand or fall together; denying simplicity is implicitly atheism; the proofs show atheism false; so simplicity is true.
summary.deepDive:
The hardest idea in this section is how God’s power, knowledge, and goodness can be **one reality** without our words becoming synonyms. Plantinga thinks simplicity makes God “one property” and therefore an abstract object. Feser’s reply has several layers; the key is to see how they fit together.

First, **analogy**. In us, power and knowledge really are distinct: you can know how to lift a piano and lack the strength. If “power” and “knowledge” meant exactly the same in God (univocity), their distinctness would carry over. But they are said of God analogically (step 13): God has something that is to his effects as our power is to ours, and something that is to truth as our knowledge is to it. There’s no reason those analogues must be distinct in a being with no parts.

Second, **concepts vs. reality**. Course analogy: “the morning star” and “the evening star” are different concepts, learned through different observations, yet both refer to Venus. Likewise, we form the concept “power” from God’s effects in producing things and “knowledge” from other features of those effects; the concepts differ, but what they apply to in God is one undivided reality.

Third, **constituent ontology**. Plantinga treats properties as abstract Platonic objects that things exemplify. On that view, if God *is* his wisdom, God is an abstract object. But for Aquinas, a thing’s nature and attributes are concrete constituents of it, not items in a third realm. And no classical theist says God is a “property” anyway.

Fourth, **distinguishing kinds of predicates**. Plantinga calls everything a property — being wise, being barefoot, being Plato’s teacher, being Socrates. Aquinas distinguishes essence (rational animality), proper properties (the capacity to be amused), contingent accidents (skin color), and relations (being Plato’s teacher). Lump them together and simplicity seems to make God’s creating humans as essential as his wisdom. Separate them and it doesn’t.

Finally, the **stakes**: a composite God would need a cause and would be unique only contingently — a quasi-divine stand-in, and nothing in the proofs supports such a being. That is why the conclusion of **step 30** holds.

The usual confusion: “simplicity means we can say only one thing about God.” We can say many true things; simplicity concerns what is in God, not how many concepts we use.

checks.q: Which is NOT one of the assumptions Feser says Plantinga reads into the doctrine of simplicity?
options: That God has intellect and will
That properties are Platonic abstract objects
That terms apply to God and creatures univocally
That anything truly predicable of a thing is a property
checks.explanation: Classical theists themselves attribute intellect and will to God; the three problematic assumptions are the other options.

checks.q: What does Wolterstorff’s “constituent ontology” contribute to Feser’s reply?
options: It proves God is a property
It captures the view that a thing’s nature and attributes are concrete constituents of it, so identifying God with his wisdom doesn’t make him abstract
It shows God has many real parts
It shows properties are abstract objects
checks.explanation: Only on a Platonic view would identity with one’s attributes make one an abstract object.

checks.q: How does Feser answer Plantinga’s fallback that it doesn’t matter what we call these features (“characteristics”)?
options: He denies God has any characteristics
He agrees it is merely verbal
He says Aquinas’ distinctions mark objective metaphysical differences, not preferences about words
He switches to calling them “attributes”
checks.explanation: Essence, properties, accidents, and relations really differ; relabeling doesn’t erase that.

summary.heading: Morris’s objection and Cambridge properties
summary.plain: Some new truths about you don’t involve any change in you. If your brother grows taller, you become “shorter than your brother” without shrinking. God becoming “Creator” is like that: the world changes by coming into existence, but God doesn’t change. This answers critics who say God must have changeable features.
summary.takeaway: Simplicity identifies only God’s real properties and rules out only contingent real properties; being Creator is a mere Cambridge property, so Morris’s necessary/contingent objection misses.
summary.body:
Thomas Morris (following a line also in Christopher Hughes) argues that God has some things true of him necessarily (omnipotence) and some only contingently (having created the world — he could have refrained), so he must have both necessary and contingent properties, which cannot all be identical.

Setting aside the loose use of “property,” Feser draws on Barry Miller, who builds on Peter Geach’s distinction between **real** properties and mere **“Cambridge” properties** (named for Cambridge philosophers like Russell and McTaggart who used the notion). If Socrates grows hair, that is a real change in him. If Socrates becomes shorter than Plato only because Plato grew, Socrates has undergone a mere Cambridge change and acquired a Cambridge property. Simplicity rules out God’s having contingent *real* properties, not contingent Cambridge ones; and it says his *real* properties are identical, not all his properties. Being Creator is a Cambridge property: it involves the world coming to be, not a change in God. So omnipotence (real, necessary) and being Creator (Cambridge, contingent) are indeed not identical — but simplicity never said they were. A footnote anticipates the rejoinder that creating is like Socrates *causing* Plato to change, which does involve change in Socrates; that assumes the changes agents like us undergo must belong to every agent — a fallacy of accident, taken up next.

A useful test for telling the two apart: ask whether anything *intrinsic to the subject itself* would have to be different for the new description to become true. For Socrates growing hair, yes. For Socrates becoming shorter than Plato, no — only Plato changed. For God becoming Creator, no — only the world, which begins to exist, is different. That is why Feser can say that God has contingent descriptions without having any contingent *real* features.
summary.deepDive:
The key idea is the **real vs. Cambridge** distinction, which does double duty in this module: it answers Morris here and the “creation is change” objection to immutability in the next section.

Start with the intuitive cases. When Socrates grows a beard, *he* is different: something about him has altered. When Plato grows taller and Socrates thereby becomes “shorter than Plato,” a new sentence about Socrates is true, but nothing about Socrates has changed. Peter Geach called the second kind a “Cambridge change,” after Cambridge philosophers (Russell, McTaggart) whose definition of change counted any new truth about a thing as a change in it.

Course examples make the pattern familiar. You become someone’s great-grandparent when a baby is born across the country. A mountain becomes “famous” when a travel writer praises it. A coin becomes “the oldest in the collection” when an older one is sold. In each case something true of the subject changes, but only because something else changed.

Now Morris. He argues: God is necessarily omnipotent but only contingently the Creator (he could have refrained). So God has both necessary and contingent properties. A necessary property can’t be identical with a contingent one. So simplicity, which identifies God’s properties, is false.

Feser (following Barry Miller) replies that simplicity never said *every* true description of God names a real feature identical with God. It identifies God’s **real** attributes, and it excludes only contingent **real** attributes. Being Creator is a Cambridge property: the difference between a world where God creates and one where he doesn’t is a difference in whether the world exists, not a further feature inside God. So omnipotence and being Creator are indeed distinct — but that’s no counterexample.

A footnote anticipates a rejoinder: isn’t creating more like Socrates *causing* Plato to grow, which would change Socrates? Feser answers that this assumes every agent changes when acting — a fallacy of accident, discussed under immutability.

In the formal reasoning this is **step 29**, and it’s used again at **step 34**.

The usual confusion: “A Cambridge property is fake or false.” No — it is true that God is Creator. The point concerns what *makes* it true: the existence and dependence of the world, not an extra intrinsic feature of God. Another confusion is to think this distinction settles every question about divine freedom; Part B carries that discussion further.

checks.q: Which of these is a Cambridge change in Anna?
options: Anna learns French
Anna grows two inches
Anna catches a cold
Anna becomes an aunt when her sister gives birth
checks.explanation: Nothing intrinsic to Anna changes when her sister gives birth; the new truth about her depends on a change in someone else.

checks.q: How does Feser (following Miller) answer Morris’s objection?
options: By noting that simplicity identifies only God’s real properties, and being Creator is a Cambridge property
By denying God has any contingent properties at all
By conceding that simplicity is false
By claiming God created necessarily
checks.explanation: Omnipotence (real, necessary) and being Creator (Cambridge, contingent) needn’t be identical.

checks.q: Who introduced the notion of “Cambridge change” that Miller builds on?
options: Nicholas Wolterstorff
Peter Geach
Alvin Plantinga
Thomas Morris
checks.explanation: Geach named it after Cambridge philosophers such as Russell and McTaggart.

summary.heading: Immutability
summary.plain: God can’t change: change means gaining something you lacked, and God lacks nothing. But that doesn’t make God inactive or lifeless. Acting just means making something happen, and being alive means acting from within yourself — and nothing acts more fully from itself than God.
summary.takeaway: God can’t really change (no potency, no parts), yet he acts and lives, because acting is producing effects and life is acting from within — neither essentially requires change.
summary.body:
Change is the actualization of potential; God has no potential to actualize; so God cannot change. Doesn’t creating involve a transition from not creating to creating? No: becoming Creator is a Cambridge change, like Socrates becoming shorter than Plato — the real change is in the world, not in God. Immutability means no *real* change in God, not no Cambridge change. Immutability also follows from simplicity: a real change is a change in one respect while remaining the same in others (a substance loses an attribute while keeping its identity and other attributes), which requires parts. A simple being has none.

**Objection: acting requires changing.** When I type, not only the screen changes; my fingers, nervous system, and thoughts change too. Feser replies that inferring that *every possible* agent must change in acting commits the **fallacy of accident** — like inferring that any possible professor must be under nine feet tall because every actual one has been. Following Brian Davies: what is essential to acting is producing an effect in another, not changing oneself; what is essential to teaching is causing someone to learn, not lecturing or writing books specifically. What is essential to creating is simply causing the world to exist.

**Objection: a changeless God couldn’t be alive.** Same fallacy. On the Aristotelian account, life is operating from an **internal principle** (immanent causation) rather than being wholly moved from outside (transient causation, as when a thrown stone breaks a window). God acts without being acted upon at all — unlike living things that must eat and breathe — so he has life in the fullest possible way.
summary.deepDive:
The hard idea here is separating **acting** and **living** from **changing**, because in our experience they always come together.

First, why God can’t change. Two derivations. (1) Change is the actualization of potential (chapter 1). A purely actual being has no potential to actualize (step 32). (2) Real change means changing in one respect while staying the same in another: a leaf goes from green to red while remaining the same leaf. That requires something that stays and something that goes — parts. A simple being has none (step 33).

Now the objection: when I type, my fingers move, my neurons fire, my thoughts shift. Acting involves the agent changing. So if God creates, God changes.

Feser’s diagnosis: **fallacy of accident**. Suppose someone reasons, “Every college professor who has ever lived has been under nine feet tall, so any possible professor must be.” The correlation is real but accidental: nothing about being a professor requires a height. Likewise, the correlation between acting and changing in the agents we know may be real but accidental. To find out, ask what acting *essentially* is. Brian Davies’ answer: bringing about an effect in something else. Teaching is essentially causing someone to learn — whether by lecturing, writing, or example; none of those specific means is essential. Creating is essentially causing the world to exist; nothing in that requires the Creator to undergo change.

A course illustration (imperfect, since the examples are material): the sun lights up a room without the room’s brightness being a change in the sun’s nature, and a magnet attracts iron filings that move while the magnet stays put. Such cases hint that producing change and undergoing change are different things.

Next, life. Living things grow, eat, move — isn’t life change? Again, fallacy of accident. On the Aristotelian account, life is operating from an **internal principle** (immanent causation), as opposed to being wholly moved by outside forces (transient causation). A stone does things only when acted on — it breaks a window only if thrown. An animal acts largely from within, but still needs food and air. God acts and is acted on by nothing at all. So God has life *most fully*.

This section is **steps 31–36**; step 34 reuses the Cambridge distinction from step 29.

The usual confusion: “immutable” heard as “frozen,” “inert,” or “passive.” It’s the opposite: things change because they lack something and acquire it; God lacks nothing.

checks.q: What two routes does Feser give to divine immutability?
options: PPC and the second law of thermodynamics
Revelation and religious experience
Pure actuality (no potential to actualize) and simplicity (no parts to lose while others remain)
Timelessness and omnipotence
checks.explanation: Steps 32 and 33 derive immutability from pure actuality and from simplicity respectively.

checks.q: According to Davies, what is essential to acting?
options: Undergoing a change oneself
Moving a body
Deliberating over options
Bringing about an effect in another thing
checks.explanation: Teaching is causing learning; creating is causing the world to exist — neither requires change in the agent.

checks.q: Why, on the Aristotelian account, can an immutable God be said to live?
options: Because life is operating from an internal principle, and God acts without being acted on at all
Because God grows in knowledge
Because God has a body
Because life is a Cambridge property
checks.explanation: Life is immanent activity; God’s activity is wholly from himself, so he lives most fully.

summary.heading: Immateriality and incorporeality
summary.plain: God isn’t made of matter. Physical things always have parts and can be rearranged, broken down, or changed — even the tiniest particles. Since God has no parts and nothing untapped in him, God can’t be physical, not even some invisible energy or force.
summary.takeaway: Whether matter is understood in Aristotle’s terms or physics’, material things have parts and potentialities, so a purely actual, simple God is wholly immaterial.
summary.body:
That God has no body and is wholly immaterial follows at once from pure actuality and simplicity, on either of two views of matter.

**Aristotelian view**: every material object is a composite of **substantial form** and **prime matter**, and matter just is the potentiality to take on form — prime matter by itself is pure potentiality. A simple being lacks the composition; a purely actual being lacks the potentiality.

**Any view**: material things have parts — the visible ones (the wood, plastic, or metal of furniture, an animal’s organs) and the microscopic ones (molecules, atoms, subatomic particles), which can be arranged and rearranged, implying potentiality. Even fundamental particles (fermions and bosons), though not made of smaller particles, have distinct attributes — parts in a broad sense — and they come into being and pass away. So nothing material can be purely actual and simple.

Two clarifications help. “Incorporeal” means having no body; “immaterial” is stronger, meaning not material in any way at all. God is both. And the argument doesn’t depend on any particular scientific picture of matter being final. Whatever physics eventually says matter is, as long as material things have distinguishable attributes, can be arranged differently, or can come to be and pass away, they involve composition and potentiality — which a purely actual, simple being cannot have. That is why Feser can say the conclusion follows “straightaway” from attributes already established.

This also rules out popular pictures of God as a kind of cosmic energy or field. Energy and fields are physical realities with measurable attributes and changing states, so they are exactly the sort of thing that needs a cause, not the sort of thing that could be the First Cause.
summary.deepDive:
The interesting move in this section is that Feser gives **two independent arguments**, one for each audience.

**For the Aristotelian.** Every material substance is a composite of substantial form (what makes it the kind of thing it is) and prime matter (what the form actualizes). Matter, as such, is the potential to take on form: a lump of bronze can become a statue or a bell; the bronze itself can become something else by chemistry; at the bottom, “prime matter” is sheer potentiality, never existing on its own. So anything material is (a) composite and (b) potential. God is neither (steps 30 and 17). Therefore God isn’t material.

**For everyone else.** You needn’t accept hylomorphism. Just look at what anyone would say about matter. Material things have parts — the legs and seat of a chair, an animal’s organs, and down through molecules, atoms, and subatomic particles. Those parts can be arranged and rearranged, which means potentiality. What about fundamental particles, like electrons, that aren’t made of smaller particles? Feser’s point is that they still have “parts” in a broad sense — distinct attributes such as mass, charge, and spin — and they exhibit potentiality in coming into being and passing away (particles are created and annihilated in physical processes).

A thought experiment: try to imagine a “simplest possible material thing.” Whatever you picture has a size or position (it could be elsewhere), some property distinguishing it from empty space, and some capacity to interact. Each of these marks composition or potency. There is no way to be material and purely actual at once.

This section is **steps 37–40**. It builds on step 17 (pure actuality) and step 30 (simplicity), and it will be presupposed in the necessity section, where Feser says you can’t form a mental image of God because God isn’t material.

The usual confusion: thinking of God as a very subtle or invisible kind of stuff — a spirit made of “spirit-matter,” or cosmic energy. Those are still material conceptions. Another confusion: supposing that because God is immaterial he is somehow less real or less powerful than matter. In Feser’s framework the reverse holds: matter is shot through with potentiality; God is pure actuality.

checks.q: On the Aristotelian view, why can’t a purely actual being be material?
options: Because matter is an illusion
Because matter is essentially the potentiality to take on form
Because only God is material
Because matter is too heavy
checks.explanation: Prime matter is pure potentiality; what has no potentiality can’t be material.

checks.q: Why don’t fundamental particles (fermions and bosons) count as simple in Feser’s sense?
options: Because physicists disagree about them
Because they are made of smaller particles
Because they have distinct attributes and come into being and pass away
Because they are purely actual
checks.explanation: Not being made of smaller particles isn’t enough; distinct attributes and generation/corruption still mean parts and potency.

summary.heading: Eternity: no beginning, no end — and no time
summary.plain: God never began and can never end. But more than that, God isn’t in time at all. Being in time means your life keeps adding new moments and you keep changing along with them. God doesn’t change, so God exists outside time rather than just living for an infinitely long time.
summary.takeaway: God can neither begin nor end, and since existing in time would mean change and temporal parts, his eternity is strict timelessness rather than endless duration.
summary.body:
God neither comes into being nor passes away. Whatever begins has parts needing combination — above all essence and existence — is merely potential until combined, exists contingently, and so needs a cause. God has no parts, no potentiality, exists necessarily, and just is existence; so he not only needs no cause but *could not* have one. Likewise, whatever ends has separable parts (its essence can come apart from existence), is potentially nonexistent, and is contingent; God, being existence itself, can hardly lose existence. What neither begins nor ends is eternal.

But divine eternity is not mere **longevity** (existing through all past and future time); it is **strict timelessness**. This follows from immutability: a God in time would keep adding days and years to his life, would act differently at different moments, and (since he has knowledge — argued in Part B) would keep learning new facts like “it is now t1,” then “it is now t2.” All that is change. It also follows from simplicity: a temporal life has distinct stages, i.e., parts. Feser notes that William Lane Craig, who rejects both immutability and timelessness, agrees that an immutable God would be timeless.

The two stages are worth keeping apart. The first — no beginning, no end — follows from God’s having no parts, no potentiality, and necessary existence. The second — no time at all — needs immutability and simplicity as well. Someone could accept the first and reject the second (as Craig does, since he rejects immutability); Feser’s point is that once immutability and simplicity are granted, the first leads to the second.
summary.deepDive:
The hardest idea in this section is the difference between **everlasting** and **timeless**, and why immutability pushes us from the first to the second.

Stage one: no beginning or end. Whatever begins to exist has parts needing combination — above all an essence and an act of existence — and so is merely potential until combined, contingent, and in need of a cause. God has no parts, no potentiality, exists necessarily, and just *is* existence. So he doesn’t merely lack a cause; he *couldn’t* have one. Similarly, whatever ends has separable parts (its essence can come apart from existence) and is potentially nonexistent. Existence itself can hardly lose existence. So God doesn’t end. That’s eternity in a minimal sense.

Stage two: timelessness. Picture a God who has existed through every past moment and will exist through every future one. Is that enough? Feser says no. A temporal God would *keep adding* moments to his life — Tuesday gets added to Monday. He would act one way at one time and another way later. And, since God has knowledge (Part B), he would keep acquiring new knowledge: “it is now noon,” then “it is now 12:01.” Each of these is a change, and God is immutable (step 36). Moreover, a temporal life has distinct stages — God-on-Monday, God-on-Tuesday — which are parts, and God is simple (step 30).

A thought experiment: think of how much of your own identity is spread out in time — memories of the past, plans for the future, a present that keeps slipping away. Temporal existence is fragmented existence: you never have your whole life at once. A being who lacks nothing couldn’t exist that way.

Feser notes that William Lane Craig — who rejects immutability and timelessness — nonetheless agrees that *if* God were immutable, he would be timeless. That concession shows the inference is not a quirk of Thomism.

This section is **steps 41–47**. Steps 42–44 secure “no beginning/no end”; steps 45–46 secure timelessness; step 47 concludes.

The usual confusion: “eternal” heard as “very old” or “infinitely long.” Another confusion: thinking a timeless God couldn’t know what happens in time. How God knows temporal events belongs to Part B; the author analogy in the next section offers a first picture of how timelessness and the temporal world relate.

checks.q: Why can God not have a cause, according to the eternity section?
options: Because he existed before the Big Bang
Because causes must be material
Because he is timeless
Because he has no parts, no potentiality, exists necessarily, and just is existence
checks.explanation: What begins has parts needing combination and is contingent; God has none of these features, so a cause is impossible.

checks.q: Which is a reason Feser gives for thinking a temporal God would change?
options: He would constantly acquire new knowledge, such as that it is now t1 and then t2
He would grow physically older
He would need food
He would be caused by time
checks.explanation: Adding moments, acting differently at different times, and acquiring new knowledge are all changes.

checks.q: What is significant about Craig’s position as Feser reports it?
options: Craig invented the simultaneity objection
Although Craig rejects immutability, he agrees an immutable God would be timeless
Craig denies that God exists
Craig proves God is everlasting and immutable
checks.explanation: Even a critic of timelessness grants the inference from immutability to timelessness.

summary.heading: Two objections to timelessness
summary.plain: Critics ask: if God keeps things existing today and tomorrow, isn’t he acting today and tomorrow? Feser says no. Think of an author who dreams up a whole novel at once: inside the story, chapter 10 comes after chapter 1, but the author didn’t think of them one after the other. God creates the whole timeline in a single act from outside it.
summary.takeaway: “God causes X at t1” doesn’t mean “at t1 God causes X,” and eternity isn’t a point in time, so neither temporal causing nor the simultaneity puzzle puts God in time.
summary.body:
**Temporal causing.** Feser has argued that God causes the existence of things at every moment. If God causes something to exist at t1 and at t2, doesn’t he act at t1 and then again at t2 — and so exist in time (Swinburne, Pike)? No. Following Davies, from *God causes it to be the case that X exists at t1* it does not follow that *at t1 God causes X to exist*. God does not perform a string of successive acts — creating at t1, conserving at t2, conserving again at t3. From outside time, in a single act, he causes a temporal world in which the object exists at t1, t2, t3, and so on. Compare (with Stephen Barr) an author who conceives a whole story in one flash of insight: for the characters, the middle comes after the beginning, but the author didn’t devise the beginning first and the ending later.

**Simultaneity.** If Socrates’ existence in 469 B.C. is simultaneous with God’s eternity, and Obama’s existence in A.D. 1961 is too, then by the transitivity of simultaneity Socrates and Obama would be simultaneous — absurd (Swinburne, Kenny). Feser (citing Davies and Paul Helm) replies that this treats eternity as a *point in time*, since only a point in time can be simultaneous with another. The whole claim is that God is not at any point in time but outside time altogether.

Both objections, at bottom, make the same mistake: they picture eternity as if it were a stretch or point of time located alongside the moments of history. Once eternity is understood as outside time altogether, God’s relation to temporal things is one of causal dependence — each moment exists because God causes it — rather than one of before, after, or at-the-same-time.
summary.deepDive:
The key tool here is a **scope distinction** — a matter of where the time-phrase attaches.

Compare two sentences:

1. God causes it to be the case that [X exists at t1].
2. At t1, [God causes X to exist].

In (1), the time-phrase is inside the brackets: it describes *the effect*. In (2), it modifies *God’s act*: it says when God acts. Swinburne and Pike reason from something like (1) to (2). Feser, following Brian Davies, points out that (2) doesn’t follow from (1). God’s causing can have a temporally located effect without the causing itself being located in time.

An everyday analogy (course): an architect’s single design fixes that the east wing is built before the west wing. The design includes an order of construction; it doesn’t follow that the architect designs the east wing first. Feser’s own image, borrowed from Stephen Barr, is sharper: an author conceives a whole story, beginning to end, in a single flash of insight. Inside the story, chapter 1 precedes chapter 10. But the author didn’t invent chapter 1 first and chapter 10 later. Similarly, God doesn’t perform a sequence of acts — creating at t1, conserving at t2, conserving again at t3 — but by one timeless act causes a temporal world in which things exist at t1, t2, t3.

Now the **simultaneity objection** (Swinburne, Kenny). If Socrates’ existence in 469 B.C. is simultaneous with God’s eternity, and Obama’s existence in A.D. 1961 is too, then since simultaneity is transitive, Socrates and Obama would be simultaneous — absurd. Feser (with Davies and Helm) replies that the argument treats eternity as a point in time, since only a point in time can be simultaneous with another. The whole claim of timelessness is that God is not at any point in time. The premises are therefore false as stated.

This section defends **step 47**. It also shows how steps 45–46 are compatible with Feser’s earlier claim (chapters 1–5) that God causes things to exist at every moment.

The usual confusion: thinking of eternity as a very long present moment “stretched over” all of time. That image invites both objections. Better: the author isn’t located at any page of the book, though every page depends on him.

checks.q: Which inference do Swinburne and Pike make that Feser rejects?
options: From “Socrates exists” to “Obama exists”
From “God is timeless” to “God is immutable”
From “God causes X to exist at t1” to “at t1 God causes X to exist”
From “God is simple” to “God is one”
checks.explanation: The time-phrase can describe the effect without locating God’s act in time.

checks.q: What does the author-and-story image illustrate?
options: That God learns the plot as it unfolds
That God is one of the characters
That time is an illusion
That a single act can fix a whole temporal sequence without the agent acting successively
checks.explanation: The author conceives beginning, middle, and end at once; within the story they are successive.

checks.q: Why does the simultaneity objection fail?
options: Because it treats timeless eternity as if it were a point in time
Because simultaneity is not transitive
Because Socrates and Obama are simultaneous
Because God did not cause Socrates
checks.explanation: Only a point in time can be simultaneous with another; God isn’t at any point in time.

summary.heading: Necessity: the conventionalist objection
summary.plain: Some philosophers say “necessary” only applies to word definitions, like “bachelors are unmarried,” so a being can’t exist necessarily. Feser replies that truths like 2 + 2 = 4 are necessary without being about words, and that the arguments for God already explain what makes God’s existence necessary.
summary.takeaway: Necessity isn’t merely linguistic: propositions aren’t sentences, mathematical truths aren’t conventions, and the objection simply assumes the proofs’ extralinguistic account of God’s necessity is wrong.
summary.body:
The rationalist proof argues directly for a necessary being, and the other proofs imply it. Some reject the very idea. J. N. Findlay (and Bertrand Russell, in his 1948 BBC debate with Frederick Copleston) held that necessity is purely a matter of linguistic convention: “all bachelors are unmarried” is necessary only because it is analytic — true by the meanings of words — and tells us nothing about reality. Extralinguistic reality can’t be necessary; God would be part of extralinguistic reality; so a “necessary being” makes no sense.

Feser replies in two ways. **First**, conventionalism fails on independent grounds. It confuses **sentences** (linguistic items) with **propositions** (not linguistic). “Snow is white” and “Schnee ist weiss” express one proposition, which would be true even if no language had ever existed. So the conventionality of sentences doesn’t make propositions or their necessity conventional. That example is contingent, but mathematical and logical truths — 2 + 2 = 4, everything is identical to itself — are necessary and notoriously hard to treat as mere conventions (see chapter 3). **Second, and deeper**, the objection begs the question. The proofs claim to show there is an extralinguistic, necessarily existing cause, and they give an account of that necessity with nothing to do with language: pure actuality, absolute simplicity, identity of essence and existence. Simply asserting that all necessity is conventional presupposes the arguments are wrong without showing it.

It matters what kind of necessity Feser claims for God. It is not that the sentence “God exists” is true by definition, as “bachelors are unmarried” is. It is that the being whose existence the proofs establish has a nature that makes nonexistence impossible for it: it has no potentiality that might go unactualized and no parts that might fail to be combined. That is a claim about extralinguistic reality, so the conventionalist can’t simply rule it out by fiat.
summary.deepDive:
The key distinction in this section is between **sentences** and **propositions**, and it unlocks why conventionalism about necessity fails.

Conventionalism says: all necessity is linguistic. “All bachelors are unmarried” is necessary because it is **analytic** — the meanings of the words guarantee it. Since necessity lives only in language, it makes no sense to call a real being “necessary.” Findlay pressed this, and Russell raised something similar against Copleston in 1948.

Feser’s first reply: a sentence is a string of words in some language; a proposition is what the sentence says. “Snow is white” (English) and “Schnee ist weiss” (German) are different sentences expressing one proposition. And that proposition would be true even if English and German had never existed — snow would still be white. So while *sentences* are conventional (we could have used “snow” for coal), it doesn’t follow that *propositions* are, or that their truth or necessity is.

But “snow is white” is contingent. Are there necessary propositions that aren’t conventional? Feser points to mathematics and logic: 2 + 2 = 4; everything is identical to itself. Chapter 3 argued at length that these aren’t mere conventions. A thought experiment: suppose a culture used “4” to name the number five. Then their sentence “2 + 2 = 4” would be false, but only because it would express a different proposition. The proposition we express by “2 + 2 = 4” would be as necessary as ever. Changing words changes which proposition a sentence expresses, not what is necessary.

Feser’s second, deeper reply: the objection **begs the question**. The proofs claim to show that there is an extralinguistic cause of the existence of things that exists of necessity, and they explain that necessity without any reference to language: pure actuality, simplicity, identity of essence and existence. To reply “but all necessity is linguistic” is to assume the proofs fail, not to show it.

This section supports **steps 48–51**, especially step 51’s claim that God’s necessity is real and extralinguistic.

The usual confusion: thinking “necessary being” means “a being whose existence follows from a definition,” as in an ontological argument. Feser’s route is different — existence first, from the world; necessity second, from the nature of what was found.

checks.q: What does the “Snow is white” / “Schnee ist weiss” example show?
options: That German is more precise than English
That one proposition can be expressed by different sentences and would be true even without language
That all truths are analytic
That snow is necessarily white
checks.explanation: Propositions are not linguistic items, so the conventionality of sentences doesn’t make propositions conventional.

checks.q: Why does Feser say the conventionalist objection begs the question?
options: Because Russell debated Copleston
Because it asks a question without answering it
Because it assumes all necessity is linguistic, which the proofs claim to have shown false by giving an extralinguistic account of God’s necessity
Because it relies on mathematics
checks.explanation: Asserting conventionalism presupposes the proofs are wrong without showing it.

summary.heading: Necessity: Schrader’s empty world
summary.plain: Another critic says, “I can imagine a world with nothing in it, not even God, so God doesn’t have to exist.” Feser replies that you can’t picture God at all, any more than you can picture the number four itself. And what must be true of a thing is learned from what the thing is — not from what we can imagine.
summary.takeaway: Picturing an empty world tells us nothing about a being that can’t be pictured, and modal truths about a thing flow from its essence, so Schrader’s argument assumes rather than shows that God isn’t necessary.
summary.body:
David Schrader argues that we can imagine a world containing only a single green marble, and then imagine even the marble gone — a world with nothing at all, not even God. So God doesn’t exist in every possible world and is not necessary.

**First reply**: this works only if everything that exists or could exist, God included, is the sort of thing one can form a **mental image** of. It isn’t. Picture “2 + 2 = 4” chalked on a board as the only existing thing, then picture it erased; that does nothing to show 2 + 2 = 4 is not necessary, because numbers aren’t imageable objects. You can picture numerals (“2,” “4,” or Roman “II,” “IV”), but numerals are labels, not numbers. What we can picture is irrelevant to what we can strictly conceive. The same goes for God, who is not material: you can’t picture God existing, let alone not existing (Feser cites Brian Leftow).

**Second reply**: even setting imagery aside, the method of settling necessity by consulting what we can conceive in possible worlds — common in contemporary philosophy — gets things backward from the Aristotelian-Thomistic point of view. We start from *actual* things, discover their essences, and from there infer what is possible or necessary for them. In God’s case: first establish that he exists, then determine his nature (purely actual, simple, subsistent existence depending on nothing), and from that infer that he exists necessarily — and so, if we use possible-worlds talk, in every possible world. That is exactly what the previous chapters did. Schrader’s objection doesn’t refute this; it assumes it is wrong, and so begs the question. With necessity established, the chapter turns to omnipotence (covered in Part B).
summary.deepDive:
Two ideas carry this section: **imagining vs. conceiving**, and **essence-first modality**.

First, imagining vs. conceiving. To imagine is to form a mental picture. To conceive, strictly, is to grasp something intellectually. The two often go together, but not always. You can understand a figure with a thousand sides (and prove things about it) though you can’t picture it distinctly — a classic example from Descartes. You can understand the number seven, though what you picture is only a numeral, “7” or “VII.”

Schrader’s procedure is to picture a lone green marble, then picture it gone, and to conclude that he has conceived a world where nothing — not even God — exists. Feser’s reply: this assumes that everything that exists or could exist is the kind of thing whose presence or absence can be pictured. God isn’t. He isn’t material (step 40), so you can’t picture him existing, let alone not existing. The chalkboard parallel makes the absurdity vivid: picture a world containing only the chalked equation “2 + 2 = 4,” then picture it erased. Have you shown arithmetic is contingent? Obviously not — you erased numerals, not numbers.

Second, the method. Even if Schrader drops imagery and says he can *conceive* an empty world, much contemporary philosophy tests necessity by asking what is conceivable in “possible worlds.” From the Aristotelian-Thomistic standpoint, that’s backward. We don’t first list possible worlds and then learn what things can do. We learn what things *are* — their essences — and infer what is possible or necessary for them. Water can be boiled because of what water is; the possibility is grounded in the nature.

Applied to God: first show that God exists (chapters 1–5); then determine his nature (purely actual, simple, subsistent existence, dependent on nothing); then infer that he exists necessarily — and so, in possible-worlds talk, in every possible world. Schrader’s argument doesn’t find a flaw in that chain; it assumes there is one. So it begs the question.

A thought experiment: someone claims to conceive that a certain complicated arithmetic sum is false. Until they work it through, it may *seem* conceivable. Apparent conceivability is overturned by understanding the thing in question. So too for an “empty world,” once one understands a being whose essence is existence.

This section secures **step 50** and completes **step 51**.

The usual confusion: “If I can imagine it, it’s possible.” Imagination tracks picturable things; it is silent about numbers and God.

checks.q: What is the point of Feser’s chalkboard example?
options: That mathematics is conventional
That God is a number
That imagination is always reliable
That erasing imagined numerals shows nothing about the necessity of numbers — and likewise imagining absence shows nothing about God
checks.explanation: Numbers, like God, aren’t imageable; picturing their symbols gone proves nothing.

checks.q: What does Feser say is the proper order of inquiry into what is necessary for a thing?
options: Start with actual things, determine their essences, then infer what is possible or necessary for them
Survey possible worlds first, then infer essences
Consult linguistic conventions
Rely on imagination
checks.explanation: Essence-first modality: possibility and necessity are grounded in natures.

checks.q: A critic says, “I don’t picture it — I conceive a world with nothing in it.” What is Feser’s best reply?
options: Then God does not exist
Conceivability tested via possible worlds gets things backward; from God’s established nature it follows he exists necessarily, so the claim assumes what it must prove
The critic must be imagining after all
Conceiving is impossible
checks.explanation: Feser’s second reply: the objection begs the question against the essence-first derivation.

argument.name: From the First Cause to the first divine attributes
argument.overview:
This module is not a single proof but a chain of derivations. It starts from what chapters 1–5 established — a purely actual, simple, self-subsistent, necessary cause — and adds three general principles: **proportionate causality** (a cause cannot give what it lacks), **agere sequitur esse** (activity cannot outrun nature), and the **analogy of being** (terms can apply literally to very different things by proportional likeness). Feser’s one explicitly numbered argument in this stretch — the seven-step case that “being” is analogical — is included in full (steps 6–12).

The stages then run attribute by attribute. First the loophole of “potential activity” is closed, so God is purely actual *without qualification* (Stage 3). **Unity** follows, together with the proof that all five routes reach one being (Stage 4). **Simplicity** is shown to be the linchpin, with the real/Cambridge property distinction that deflects its critics (Stage 5). **Immutability**, **immateriality**, **eternity** (as timelessness), and **necessity** each follow from pure actuality and simplicity, with a key premise answering the main objection to each (Stages 6–9).

Notice the pattern: almost every attribute is derived twice — once from pure actuality (no potency) and once from simplicity (no parts). That redundancy is deliberate; it shows the attributes are aspects of one reality rather than a list of separate add-ons.

stages.title: Stage 1 — Starting points and tools
stages.gist: Recall what the five proofs established and set out the three background principles: PPC, agere sequitur esse, and the three uses of terms.

stages.title: Stage 2 — Being is said analogically
stages.gist: Feser’s seven-step argument that potentiality and actuality are real in analogous senses, and the consequence that positive, literal talk about God must be analogical.

stages.title: Stage 3 — Pure actuality without qualification
stages.gist: The First Cause cannot have potentiality even in its activity, by agere sequitur esse and because such a mix would make it composite and caused.

stages.title: Stage 4 — Unity and the convergence of the five proofs
stages.gist: Multiplicity within a kind requires parts and hence potency, so the purely actual is unique; and pure actuality, simplicity, subsistent existence, and necessity mutually entail one another.

stages.title: Stage 5 — Simplicity
stages.gist: Any composition would make God one of a kind and in need of a cause; simplicity identifies God’s real attributes, while contingent relations to creatures are mere Cambridge properties.

stages.title: Stage 6 — Immutability (and life)
stages.gist: No potency and no parts means no real change; creating is a Cambridge change in God; acting and living do not essentially require changing.

stages.title: Stage 7 — Immateriality and incorporeality
stages.gist: Matter, on the Aristotelian view or any view, involves parts and potentiality, so God cannot be material.

stages.title: Stage 8 — Eternity as timelessness
stages.gist: God can neither begin nor end, and being in time would mean change and temporal parts, so he is strictly timeless, causing the whole temporal world in one act.

stages.title: Stage 9 — Necessity
stages.gist: A contingent God would need potency actualized and parts combined; reasoning from God’s established nature (not from imagined worlds) shows he exists necessarily.

steps.text: The five proofs have established a cause of the world that is (ch. 1) a purely actual actualizer, (ch. 2) an absolutely simple One, (ch. 3) a necessarily existing divine intellect, (ch. 4) subsistent existence itself, and (ch. 5) an absolutely necessary being.
steps.why: These are the conclusions of chapters 1–5, recapped at the start of the chapter. This module takes them as its data and asks what else follows.
steps.example: Chapter 1 ended with a purely actual actualizer, chapter 4 with subsistent existence itself — each a description with real content, not a bare placeholder.
steps.challenge: Why take the conclusions of five contested arguments as data at all?
steps.answer: This chapter is conditional on the earlier chapters, which defended each proof at length; its question is what follows if they succeed. Chapter 7 then answers general objections.

steps.text: Principle of proportionate causality (PPC): whatever is in an effect is present in its total cause in some way — formally, virtually, or eminently.
steps.why: Illustrated by the $20 bill: handed over from my wallet (formally), wired from my bank account (virtually), or printed on demand by one with power over the printing press (eminently). The principle concerns the total cause, not merely the material ingredients.
steps.example: You get $20 from me because I hand you a bill (formally), wire it from my account (virtually), or have one printed on a press I control (eminently).
steps.challenge: Sponge cake is spongy though no ingredient is, so effects can contain what causes lack.
steps.answer: The ingredients aren’t the total cause; the baker, the mixing, and the heat also count, and the feature may be in the total cause virtually rather than formally.

steps.text: PPC is not an independent assumption but follows from the principle of causality and the principle of sufficient reason.
steps.why: An aspect of an effect not traceable to its total cause would be a potential actualized by nothing (against PC) and a feature lacking any explanation (against PSR). Its non-triviality is shown by naturalists like Churchland relying on it.
steps.example: If a $20 bill appeared in your hand with no wallet, account, or press behind it, a potential would be actualized by nothing and the event would have no explanation.
steps.challenge: Explaining an effect by saying its features were “potentially” present makes PPC trivially true (Cottingham).
steps.answer: Explanations by potentialities may be minimally informative but aren’t empty; naturalists like Churchland and their dualist critics draw substantive conclusions from PPC.

steps.text: Agere sequitur esse: a thing’s characteristic activities and attributes flow from, and cannot exceed, its nature (unless something else makes it act beyond its nature).
steps.why: It is the formal-cause counterpart of PPC and likewise follows from PSR: an activity outrunning the agent’s nature would be unexplained. Stones don’t grow; puppets move only when moved. Searle uses the same principle against property dualism.
steps.example: Plants take in nutrients, grow, and reproduce because they are alive; a stone can’t, and anything that could wouldn’t be a stone.
steps.challenge: A puppet’s wooden limbs dance, which goes beyond the nature of wood.
steps.answer: The principle concerns what a thing does on its own; the puppet’s limbs move only because the puppeteer moves them.

steps.text: Terms can be used univocally (same sense), equivocally (unrelated senses), or analogically (related but not identical senses); analogy includes attribution, proper proportionality, and metaphorical proportionality, and the first two are literal.
steps.why: “Dog” of Fido and Rover; “bat” of the mammal and the club; “good” of wine and of George. Health is in George intrinsically and in food only by relation (attribution); life is formally in plants and angels alike (proper proportionality); lionhood is formally only in the zoo animal, figuratively in brave George (metaphor).
steps.example: “Dog” of Fido and Rover (univocal); “bat” of a mammal and a club (equivocal); “good” of wine and of George (analogical).
steps.challenge: Analogy is just a polite name for metaphor, so analogical talk isn’t literally true.
steps.answer: Metaphor is only one kind of analogy (improper proportionality); attribution and proper proportionality are literal — plants and angels really are alive.

steps.text: Actuality is real — it has being.
steps.why: Denying it is the extreme Heraclitean view that only change is real. That is self-undermining: there would be no persisting reasoner and no stable argument; change is always toward some new actuality (the melting ice cube); and a thing changes as it does because of what it actually is (water, not wood).
steps.example: An ice cube on hot pavement is actually solid and actually made of water; that actual nature explains why it melts rather than burns.
steps.challenge: Heraclitus: only flux is real; nothing is stably actual.
steps.answer: Then there’d be no persisting reasoner and no stable argument; change is always toward new actualities; and things change according to what they actually are.

steps.text: Potentiality is real — it has being.
steps.why: Denying it amounts to Parmenides’ denial of change, which chapter 1 showed cannot coherently be maintained.
steps.example: A sleeping pianist really can play — she differs now from someone who has never learned — though she isn’t playing.
steps.challenge: Parmenides: potentiality is unreal, because change is an illusion.
steps.answer: Denying potency means denying change, which chapter 1 showed cannot coherently be done — even the passing experience of the illusion is a change.

steps.text: Potentiality is really (not merely conceptually) distinct from actuality.
steps.why: The real distinction of essence and existence (ch. 4) is already one case of real potency/act distinction; and treating the distinction as merely a way of talking would mean only one of the two is real — denying step 6 or step 7.
steps.example: Knowing what a dodo is doesn’t tell you whether any dodo exists: essence (potency) and existence (act) are really distinct in creatures.
steps.challenge: Act and potency are just two ways of describing one thing.
steps.answer: Then that one thing would be only actual or only potential, which amounts to denying step 6 or step 7.

steps.text: If potentiality had being in exactly the same (univocal) sense as actuality, it would not be really distinct from actuality.
steps.why: Being real in precisely the same sense could only mean that potentiality is really a kind of actuality, or actuality a kind of potentiality.
steps.example: If the pianist’s ability were real in exactly the way her actual playing is, being able to play would just be playing.
steps.challenge: Why not say potency and act are both simply “real,” full stop?
steps.answer: Sameness of sense would make potency a kind of actuality or vice versa, erasing the real distinction secured at step 8.

steps.text: If potentiality had being only in an equivocal sense, it would not have being at all.
steps.why: To be “real” in a sense wholly unrelated to the ordinary sense is just to be unreal — like a baseball bat being a “bat” but not in the mammal sense.
steps.example: A baseball bat is a “bat” only in a sense unrelated to the mammal — which is to say it isn’t a mammal-bat at all.
steps.challenge: Maybe potency is real in its own wholly different sense.
steps.answer: Being “real” in a sense with nothing in common with the ordinary sense just means being unreal.

steps.text: Univocal, equivocal, and analogical usage exhaust the literal uses of terms, so the only sense left is the analogical one.
steps.why: Analogy is precisely the middle ground between sameness of sense and unrelatedness of sense; there is no fourth literal option.
steps.example: Every literal use of “good” is either the same sense, an unrelated sense, or a related-but-different sense; there is no fourth option.
steps.challenge: Couldn’t there be some further kind of literal usage?
steps.answer: Univocal and equivocal are the two extremes (identical vs. unrelated), and analogy covers everything in between, so the three exhaust the options.

steps.text: Therefore potentiality has being in a sense analogous to the sense in which actuality has it — “being” is an analogical term.
steps.why: Follows from 6–11. Note that this conclusion rests only on act/potency theory, not on any argument for God, so appealing to it in theology is not special pleading. Being is not a genus (nothing outside being could serve as a differentia), so it is predicated by proportional similarity: each thing’s existence is to its essence as another’s is to its.
steps.example: A man’s existence is to his essence as an angel’s is to its essence and God’s to his — proportionally similar relations, grounding one analogical concept of being.
steps.challenge: This is special pleading invented to rescue theology.
steps.answer: The argument uses only act-potency theory, which one can accept without accepting any proof of God, so it is independently motivated.

steps.text: Since God is radically unlike the composite, changeable, material, temporal things our words were formed to describe, positive and literal talk about him must be analogical — by attribution and proper proportionality.
steps.why: Univocal-only language would leave pure negative theology, unable even to say that God exists or causes; equivocal language leaves the terms empty (“God has ‘power’ in the sense that he ___” can’t be filled in), ending in agnosticism or atheism. Analogy, independently motivated by step 12, avoids both — much as physics speaks analogically of curved space and wave-particles.
steps.example: “God has power” is true, but not in the sense that God has muscles or a will that effortfully overcomes resistance.
steps.challenge: If our words don’t apply in the same sense, we don’t know what we mean when we speak of God.
steps.answer: Analogical concepts are indeterminate, not empty: we affirm a real perfection and deny the limits it has in us; otherwise we could not even say that God exists.

steps.text: The first cause’s existence involves no actualization of potential; it is always already actual and so need not and cannot be actualized by anything else.
steps.why: This is what lets it terminate the otherwise vicious regress of actualizers argued for in chapter 1.
steps.example: The hand-stick-stone series needs a first member that moves without being moved; that member’s existence can’t await actualization.
steps.challenge: Perhaps the regress simply has no first member.
steps.answer: In a hierarchical series each member acts only by borrowed causal power, so without a first member nothing would act at all (chapter 1).

steps.text: By agere sequitur esse, a being that exists in a purely actual way cannot act in a less than purely actual way; its activity cannot involve potentiality any more than its existence does.
steps.why: From step 4: action reflects being, and existence is the most fundamental thing about a being. There is nothing in a purely actual nature from which (less fundamental) potentials for activity could derive.
steps.example: Water’s behavior flows from what water is; a being whose very existence is pure act has nothing from which merely potential activity could flow.
steps.challenge: Why can’t something purely actual in existence still have unrealized options in its activity?
steps.answer: Existence is what is most fundamental in a thing and activity follows it; potency for activity would need a source in the nature, and there is none.

steps.text: Moreover, a being with purely actual existence but potential activity would be composite — an actual part plus a potential part — and every composite needs an extrinsic cause of its composition, even if it has always existed.
steps.why: From chapter 2: the whole is merely potential until something unites its parts; an intrinsic uniter would be self-causing, which is incoherent; everlasting existence removes only a temporally prior cause, not an ontologically prior one. A first cause that has a cause is not first.
steps.example: A lamp that has always been lit still needs the current flowing now; everlasting duration doesn’t explain why the parts are joined.
steps.challenge: A composite that always existed needs no cause.
steps.answer: The issue is ontological, not temporal priority: something must account for the parts being combined at all, and a first cause with a cause isn’t first.

steps.text: So God is purely actual without qualification — devoid of potentiality in his activity as well as in his existence.
steps.why: From 14–16. This closes the critic’s loophole and supplies the premise from which unity and the other attributes will be derived.
steps.example: The Unmoved Mover not only exists without being actualized; it also acts without any of its activity being actualized by anything.

steps.text: For there to be more than one thing of a kind, there must be a distinction between the individual and its species (e.g., matter plus species-essence) or between the species and its genus (genus plus specific difference).
steps.why: Two humans differ by their matter while sharing the essence rational animal; the human species differs from other animal species by adding rationality to animality. Without some such distinction there is nothing to make two of the same.
steps.example: Two identical pennies differ by their metal (matter); a penny and a dime differ by an added specific difference within the genus coin.
steps.challenge: Couldn’t two things differ in some other way, such as location?
steps.answer: Location presupposes material parts and potency; any genuine intrinsic difference brings composition, and footnote 17 rules out substance/accident parts too.

steps.text: Having such metaphysical parts — indeed parts of any kind — entails having potentiality.
steps.why: Matter is potentially a human or something else; the genus animal is of itself potentially rational or nonrational; and parts in general only potentially compose a whole until actualized (even with no temporal beginning). Substance/accident composition would not help either (footnote 17).
steps.example: The bronze of a statue could have become a bell; the genus animal is, of itself, open to being rational or nonrational.
steps.challenge: Parts that have always been united have no unrealized potency.
steps.answer: Parts only potentially compose a whole until their union is actualized, and that remains true even if the union had no temporal beginning.

steps.text: A purely actual being can have none of the parts that multiplication within a kind requires.
steps.why: From 17 and 19.
steps.example: Pure act has neither matter to individuate it nor a genus to be specified — there is nothing to add or to receive.

steps.text: Hence God does not belong to any kind that could have more than one member: he is unique, and the theism the proofs reach is monotheism — true in principle, not by accident.
steps.why: From 18 and 20. There could not even possibly be a second God.
steps.example: Unlike Zeus, who would still be one god among a possible many even if alone on Olympus, God couldn’t have a rival even in principle.
steps.challenge: Maybe there just happens to be one God, but there could have been more.
steps.answer: Feser’s conclusion is stronger: nothing could distinguish a second purely actual being, so monotheism is true in principle, not by accident.

steps.text: Pure actuality and absolute simplicity entail each other, so the Unmoved Mover of chapter 1 is the One of chapter 2.
steps.why: What has parts mixes act and potency, so the purely actual is simple; and a simple thing, being actual (or it would not exist), cannot have any potency without having an actual part and a potential part.
steps.example: The Unmoved Mover (ch. 1) and the One (ch. 2) turn out to be a single reality described by its lack of potency and its lack of parts.
steps.challenge: Couldn’t something be simple yet have some potential?
steps.answer: Then it would have an actual aspect and a potential aspect — two constituents — and so not be simple after all.

steps.text: Pure actuality and being subsistent existence itself entail each other, so the cause of chapter 1 is the cause of chapter 4.
