steps.why: Where essence and existence differ they relate as potency to act, so the purely actual cannot have an essence distinct from its existence; and what just is existence cannot depend on a potency’s actualization, or its existence would be derived and it would be one more dependent thing.
steps.example: A dodo’s essence needs existence added; a being whose essence is existence needs nothing added and so has no potency to be actualized.
steps.challenge: Why can’t the purely actual have an essence distinct from existence?
steps.answer: Where essence and existence differ they relate as potency to act (ch. 4), so such a being would not be purely actual.

steps.text: Simplicity and subsistent existence also entail each other directly, so the One of chapter 2 is the cause of chapter 4.
steps.why: A simple thing can’t have essence and existence as distinct metaphysical parts; and subsistent existence can have no other parts either, since parts bring potency and it must be purely actual.
steps.example: A simple being can’t be “essence plus existence”; and existence itself can’t be “existence plus anything else,” since that would bring in potency.

steps.text: Whatever is purely actual, simple, or subsistent existence exists with absolute necessity, and whatever exists with absolute necessity is all three.
steps.why: A contingent being would need some potential actualized and some parts (at least essence and existence) combined in order to exist; a being with any potency or parts would depend on their actualization or combination, and so be contingent.
steps.example: You exist contingently because your essence had to be joined to existence by causes; a being with no parts and no potency has nothing that could fail to be supplied.
steps.challenge: Couldn’t a simple, purely actual being just happen to exist, contingently?
steps.answer: Contingency means depending on some potential being actualized or parts being combined; a being with neither can’t exist contingently.

steps.text: Therefore the purely actual actualizer, the One, the necessarily existing intellect, subsistent existence itself, and the necessary being are one and the same God: the five proofs are five routes to one God, not proofs of five deities.
steps.why: From 22–25 and 21: all five descriptions pick out the same unique reality.
steps.example: Like “morning star” and “evening star” both naming Venus, the five proofs’ descriptions pick out one referent (a course analogy).
steps.challenge: Why not five ultimate beings, one per proof?
steps.answer: The descriptions entail one another and pure actuality entails uniqueness, so all five pick out the one purely actual being.

steps.text: If God had parts of any kind — genus and difference, essence and existence, act and potency, or distinct attributes — there could in principle be more than one God, and God would require a cause of his own.
steps.why: From 18–19 and 16. Human rationality and animality can exist apart, so something must unite them; if God’s wisdom and power were really distinct, something would have to unite them too.
steps.example: Human rationality and animality can exist apart, so something must combine them; if God’s wisdom and power were distinct, something would have to combine them too.
steps.challenge: Why assume distinct attributes need something to unite them?
steps.answer: A whole of distinct parts is only potentially that whole until its union is actualized (ch. 2); so a God of parts would depend on a uniting cause.

steps.text: So denying divine simplicity implicitly denies God’s uniqueness and ultimacy, reducing him to a member of a pantheon (even if its sole member) or to a creature (even if the one uncaused creature) — a superangel, not God.
steps.why: Zeus or Odin would have the same nature even if alone on Olympus or in Asgard. And since every proof concludes to a wholly noncomposite cause, nothing in them would support even this ersatz god; denying simplicity is implicitly atheism.
steps.example: Zeus and Odin would keep their natures even as sole occupants of Olympus and Asgard; a composite God would be such a figure, a superangel.
steps.challenge: Isn’t it uncharitable to call theists who reject simplicity implicit atheists?
steps.answer: The claim concerns implications, not sincerity: a composite being would need a cause and so wouldn’t be the ultimate First Cause the proofs conclude to.

steps.text: Simplicity identifies God’s real (intrinsic) attributes with one another and with God; it does not identify his mere Cambridge properties — contingent relations such as being Creator — with them.
steps.why: Following Geach and Miller: Socrates growing hair is a real change; Socrates becoming shorter than Plato because Plato grew is a Cambridge change. God’s being Creator involves a real change only in the world. Omnipotence (real, necessary) and being Creator (Cambridge, contingent) need not be identical.
steps.example: When Plato grows, Socrates becomes shorter than Plato without any change in Socrates; when the world begins, God becomes Creator without change in God.
steps.challenge: Being Creator is a contingent property of God, so God has contingent properties (Morris).
steps.answer: He has contingent Cambridge properties, not contingent real ones; simplicity identifies only God’s real properties (Miller, building on Geach).

steps.text: Therefore God is absolutely simple — and the standard objections (Plantinga, Morris) arise from reading univocal predication, Platonic “properties,” and a flattened notion of property into the doctrine rather than from the doctrine itself.
steps.why: From 17, 21, 27–29, with steps 12–13 (analogy) showing why distinct attributes in us need not be distinct in God, and the essence/property/accident/relation distinctions showing why simplicity does not make God a property or make creation essential to him.
steps.example: Our concepts of God’s power and knowledge are distinct, but they apply analogically to one undivided reality, not to two parts of God.
steps.challenge: Simplicity makes God one property and therefore an abstract object (Plantinga).
steps.answer: That follows only on univocity and Platonic properties; classical theists hold a constituent ontology and never say God is a property.

steps.text: Change is the actualization of potential.
steps.why: The analysis of change from chapter 1.
steps.example: Coffee heating up is its potential for heat being actualized.
steps.challenge: Is all change really actualization of potential, or just rearrangement?
steps.answer: Chapter 1 argued that even rearrangement is a case of potential (to be arranged otherwise) becoming actual.

steps.text: A purely actual being has no potential that needs to be, or could be, actualized, so it cannot undergo real change.
steps.why: From 17 and 31.
steps.example: A being with no unrealized capacities has nothing that could become actual, so nothing about it could change.

steps.text: Independently, real change requires that a thing alter in one respect while remaining the same in others, which presupposes parts; a simple being therefore cannot change.
steps.why: From 30: a substance that loses one attribute while keeping its identity and other attributes must be composed of what stays and what goes.
steps.example: A leaf turns from green to red while remaining the same leaf: something stays and something goes, which requires parts.
steps.challenge: Couldn’t a simple thing change all at once, entirely?
steps.answer: Total replacement wouldn’t be the thing changing but one thing ceasing and another beginning; real change needs a subject that persists through it.

steps.text: God’s becoming Creator is a mere Cambridge change: the real change is in the world, not in God.
steps.why: From 29, applied to the apparent transition from not creating to creating.
steps.example: The world’s coming to be is a real change in the world; “God is Creator” becomes true without anything new in God.
steps.challenge: Creating is like Socrates causing Plato to grow, which involves change in Socrates.
steps.answer: That assumes the changes we undergo when acting must occur in every agent — a fallacy of accident (footnote 32).

steps.text: Neither acting nor living essentially requires the agent to change: acting essentially is producing an effect in another, and living essentially is operating from an internal principle rather than being wholly moved from outside.
steps.why: Inferring otherwise from the agents we know is a fallacy of accident (like concluding all possible professors must be under nine feet tall). Davies: teaching is essentially causing another to learn, not lecturing specifically. God acts without being acted on at all — life in the fullest sense.
steps.example: Every professor so far has been under nine feet tall, but no possible professor has to be; likewise every agent we know changes, but acting doesn’t require it.
steps.challenge: When I type, my fingers and brain change; acting always changes the agent.
steps.answer: What is essential to acting is producing an effect in another (Davies); life is acting from an internal principle, which God does most fully.

steps.text: So God is immutable — without any real change — yet genuinely active and living.
steps.why: From 32–35.
steps.example: God acts on everything and is acted on by nothing — unlike animals, which must eat and breathe.
steps.challenge: An unchanging God would be frozen and lifeless.
steps.answer: Things change because they lack something; God lacks nothing, and acting from oneself without dependence is life in the fullest sense.

steps.text: On the Aristotelian view, every material thing is a composite of substantial form and prime matter, and matter as such is potentiality for form (prime matter is pure potentiality).
steps.why: The hylemorphic analysis of material substance favored by classical theists.
steps.example: Bronze can become a statue or a bell; underneath, prime matter is sheer potency for form.
steps.challenge: Hylomorphism is outdated metaphysics.
steps.answer: Feser gives a second argument (step 38) that doesn’t depend on it.

steps.text: On any view, material things have parts that can be arranged and rearranged — organs, molecules, atoms, subatomic particles — and even fundamental particles have distinct attributes and come into being and pass away.
steps.why: This needs no controversial philosophy of matter; it is the common picture from ordinary experience and physics (fermions and bosons included).
steps.example: A chair’s legs, a dog’s organs, molecules, atoms — all rearrangeable; even an electron has mass, charge, and spin, and can be created or annihilated.
steps.challenge: Fundamental particles aren’t made of smaller particles, so they are simple.
steps.answer: They still have distinct attributes (parts in a broad sense) and come into being and pass away, which shows potentiality.

steps.text: So anything material is composite and has potentiality.
steps.why: From 37 or 38, whichever account of matter one prefers.
steps.example: Whether you picture matter as form plus matter or as particles and fields, it has distinguishable aspects and can be otherwise.

steps.text: Therefore God, being purely actual and simple, is immaterial and incorporeal.
steps.why: From 17, 30, and 39.
steps.example: God can’t be a cosmic energy or field, since those are physical realities with attributes and changing states.
steps.challenge: Couldn’t God be some very fine, invisible kind of matter?
steps.answer: Any matter, however fine, is composite and potential, so it would need a cause rather than being the First Cause.

steps.text: Whatever comes into being has parts needing to be combined (above all essence and existence), is merely potential until they are combined, exists contingently, and so requires a cause.
steps.why: From the analyses of chapters 2 and 4–5.
steps.example: A tree begins when its matter and form — and its essence and existence — are joined by causes; before that it was only potential.
steps.challenge: Couldn’t something just pop into existence uncaused?
steps.answer: That would be an actualization with no actualizer and no explanation, against PC and PSR.

steps.text: God — without parts or potency, necessary, existence itself — not only needs no cause but could not have had one, so he never came into being.
steps.example: Existence itself doesn’t need existence added to it, so there’s nothing a cause could supply to it.
steps.challenge: Maybe God began to exist without a cause.
steps.answer: What begins has parts needing combination and is contingent; God has no parts, is necessary, and just is existence, so he couldn’t begin.

steps.text: Whatever passes away has separable parts (its essence can come apart from existence), is potentially nonexistent, and is contingent; God has none of these features and, being existence itself, cannot lose existence.
steps.why: The mirror image of 41–42.
steps.example: A tree ends when its parts come apart; subsistent existence has no parts to separate and can hardly lose existence.

steps.text: What neither begins nor ends is eternal, so God is eternal at least in the sense of being without beginning or end.
steps.why: From 42 and 43.
steps.example: God neither comes into being nor passes away — eternity at least in this minimal sense.
steps.challenge: Isn’t that just saying God is very old?
steps.answer: It is only the first stage; steps 45–47 show God’s eternity is timelessness, not endless duration.

steps.text: If God existed in time, he would keep adding moments to his life, act differently at different times, and keep acquiring new knowledge (“now it is t1,” “now it is t2”) — all of which is change.
steps.why: From 36: an immutable being cannot undergo such succession. Even Craig, who rejects immutability, agrees that an immutable God would be timeless.
steps.example: A temporal God would learn “it is now noon,” then “it is now 12:01,” and keep adding moments to his life.
steps.challenge: God could be in time without changing in any important way.
steps.answer: Any succession — new moments, different acts, new knowledge — is change, and God is immutable; even Craig grants an immutable God would be timeless.

steps.text: If God existed in time, his life would have distinct stages, and so distinct parts.
steps.why: From 30: a simple being has no temporal parts any more than spatial or metaphysical ones.
steps.example: God-on-Monday and God-on-Tuesday would be distinct stages of a life — temporal parts.

steps.text: Therefore God’s eternity is strict timelessness, not mere endless duration; from outside time he causes, in a single act, a temporal world in which things exist at t1, t2, t3, and so on.
steps.why: From 44–46. That God causes X to exist at t1 does not mean that at t1 God causes X (Davies) — compare an author conceiving a whole story at once (Barr). And eternity is not a point in time, so the simultaneity objection fails.
steps.example: Like an author who conceives a whole story in one flash, God by one act causes a world in which things exist at t1, t2, t3 (Barr).
steps.challenge: If God causes things at t1 and t2, he acts at t1 and t2 (Swinburne, Pike).
steps.answer: “God causes X to exist at t1” doesn’t entail “at t1 God causes X” (Davies); and eternity isn’t a point in time, so the simultaneity objection fails.

steps.text: If God were contingent, some potentiality would have to be actualized for him to exist, and he would have parts — at least an essence distinct from his existence — needing to be combined.
steps.why: From 25: contingency just is dependence of existence on something’s being actualized or combined.
steps.example: You could fail to exist because your existence depended on causes joining an essence to existence.
steps.challenge: Couldn’t something be contingent without having parts or potency?
steps.answer: Contingency just is dependence of existence on some potency’s actualization or some parts’ combination; remove those and nothing remains to depend.

steps.text: Since God is purely actual, absolutely simple, and subsistent existence itself, he is not contingent.
steps.example: The being whose essence is existence has no unactualized potency and no parts that could fail to be combined.

steps.text: The proper way to settle what is possible or necessary for a thing is to start from what actually exists and its essence, not from what we can imagine or conceive in “possible worlds.”
steps.why: The Aristotelian-Thomistic method: essence grounds modality, not the reverse. Also, God (like numbers) is not imageable, so picturing an empty world is irrelevant to his necessity; and necessity cannot be dismissed as linguistic convention, since propositions are not sentences and mathematical truths are not conventions.
steps.example: Water can be boiled because of what water is; possibility is grounded in essence, not read off imagined scenarios.
steps.challenge: I can imagine a world with nothing in it, so God might not exist (Schrader).
steps.answer: God, like numbers, can’t be pictured, so imagining absence is irrelevant; and modal truths come from essences, so the objection assumes the proofs fail.

steps.text: Therefore God exists with absolute necessity — in possible-worlds idiom, in every possible world — and this necessity is a real, extralinguistic feature grounded in his nature.
steps.why: From 49 and 50. Findlay’s conventionalism and Schrader’s empty world both simply assume the proofs are wrong, and so beg the question.
steps.example: God exists in every possible world, not by definition but because of the nature the proofs uncovered: pure act, simplicity, essence identical to existence.
steps.challenge: Necessity belongs only to statements, by linguistic convention (Findlay, Russell).
steps.answer: Propositions aren’t sentences, mathematical necessity isn’t conventional, and the objection begs the question against the proofs’ extralinguistic account of God’s necessity.

keyTerms.definition: Whatever is in an effect must be present in some way — formally, virtually, or eminently — in its total cause, since a cause cannot give what it does not have.
keyTerms.example: You cannot get $20 from me unless I have the bill, the funds, or the power to produce the bill.
keyTerms.origin: A Scholastic principle used by Aquinas; Descartes’ version is known to scholars as the “Causal Adequacy Principle.” Feser first introduces it in chapter 1.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Principle of causality (PC): PC says any actualized potential needs an actual actualizer; PPC adds that the actualizer must contain what it produces formally, virtually, or eminently.

keyTerms.definition: The complete set of factors that together produce an effect — not just its material ingredients but agents, powers, and conditions.
keyTerms.example: A cake’s total cause includes the eggs and flour but also the baker, the mixing, and the oven’s heat.
keyTerms.origin: Scholastic *causa totalis*, the whole of what produces an effect, as opposed to a partial cause.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Material cause: the ingredients are only one factor in the total cause, which is why Cottingham’s ingredient-only counterexamples miss PPC.

keyTerms.definition: The cause has the very same kind of feature it produces in the effect.
keyTerms.example: Handing you a $20 bill from my wallet; a hot stove heating a pan.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *formaliter*, “according to the form”: the cause has the very form it communicates.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Numerical identity of the feature: even formal causation produces a new instance (a new heat), not the same heat handed over.

keyTerms.definition: The cause has the effect’s content in a different mode — a power or resource that can yield it — rather than having the very feature itself.
keyTerms.example: Wiring $20 from my bank account so you can withdraw a bill I never held.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *virtualiter*, from *virtus*, “power”: present as a power or capacity.
keyTerms.confuseWith: “Virtual” in the modern sense of simulated or not real: virtual presence in the Scholastic sense is a real power to produce the effect.

keyTerms.definition: The cause possesses something more fundamental than the effect’s feature, such as the power to make things of that kind.
keyTerms.example: Having access to the Federal Reserve press that prints $20 bills.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *eminenter*, “in a surpassing or higher way.”
keyTerms.confuseWith: Having more of the same feature: eminent presence is possession of something more fundamental (the power to make bills), not a larger stack of bills.

keyTerms.definition: “Action follows being”: a thing’s characteristic activities and attributes flow from and cannot exceed its nature, unless something else makes it act beyond it.
keyTerms.example: Plants grow and reproduce because they are alive; a stone cannot do these things on its own.
keyTerms.origin: Latin: *agere* (“to act”) *sequitur* (“follows”) *esse* (“to be”). A Scholastic axiom used throughout Aquinas.
keyTerms.confuseWith: PPC: PPC concerns effects not exceeding their efficient causes; agere sequitur esse concerns activities not exceeding the agent’s nature (formal cause).

keyTerms.definition: An efficient cause brings about a thing’s existence or a change in it; a formal cause is a thing’s nature, what makes it the kind of thing it is. PPC governs the first; agere sequitur esse is its counterpart for the second.
keyTerms.example: The sculptor is the statue’s efficient cause; rational animality is a human’s formal cause.
keyTerms.origin: Two of Aristotle’s four causes (material, formal, efficient, final).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Final cause: the final cause is the end or goal a thing is directed toward, not its nature (formal) or its producer (efficient).

keyTerms.definition: Applying a term to different things in exactly the same sense. Adverb: used “univocally.”
keyTerms.example: “Dog” in “Fido is a dog” and “Rover is a dog.”
keyTerms.origin: Latin *univocus*, “having one voice”: one word, one meaning.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Literal predication: analogical predication is also literal, so “nonunivocal” does not mean “nonliteral.”

keyTerms.definition: Applying a term to different things in completely different, unrelated senses. Adverb: used “equivocally”; the ambiguity is called “equivocation.”
keyTerms.example: “Bat” for the flying mammal and for the baseball club.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *aequivocus*, “equal voice”: the same word used with unrelated meanings (Aristotle, Categories 1).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Analogical predication: analogical senses are related by a real relation or proportion; equivocal senses share nothing but the word.

keyTerms.definition: Applying a term to different things in senses that are neither identical nor unrelated, because of a real relation or likeness between them. It is literal, not metaphorical (except in the metaphorical subtype). Adverb: used “analogically”; the things so related are “analogates.”
keyTerms.example: “Good” said of wine and of a good man.
keyTerms.origin: Greek *analogia*, “proportion”; developed by Aristotle and Aquinas and classified by Cajetan (De Nominum Analogia, 1498).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Metaphor: metaphor is only one (improper) kind of analogy; attribution and proper proportionality are literal.

keyTerms.definition: A term applies intrinsically to one primary analogate and to secondary analogates only because of their relation (as cause, sign, or effect) to the primary one.
keyTerms.example: George is healthy (primary); food is healthy as a cause of his health; his complexion as a sign of it.
keyTerms.origin: Scholastic terminology (systematized by Cajetan); the stock example of “healthy” goes back to Aristotle.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Analogy of proper proportionality: in attribution the perfection is intrinsic only to the primary analogate; in proper proportionality it is intrinsic to every analogate.

keyTerms.definition: A term applies intrinsically and formally to each analogate, though in proportionally different ways, grounded in a similarity of relations.
keyTerms.example: “Life” said of plants, animals, humans, and angels; “being” said of substances, attributes, creatures, and God.
keyTerms.origin: Cajetan’s classification of Thomistic analogy; “proportionality” means a likeness of proportions (A:B :: C:D).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Metaphorical proportionality: in the proper kind the form is literally present in each analogate; in the metaphorical kind, in only one.

keyTerms.definition: A term applies formally to one analogate but only figuratively to another, grounded in something intrinsic that resembles it.
keyTerms.example: “Lion” of the animal at the zoo vs. “George is a lion” because of his courage.
keyTerms.origin: Cajetan’s term for metaphor treated as a kind of analogy.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Analogy in general: all metaphor is analogy, but not all analogy is metaphor.

keyTerms.definition: A likeness of relations (A is to B as C is to D) that grounds applying one concept, indeterminately, to very different cases.
keyTerms.example: Eyes are to the tree as the intellect is to the Pythagorean theorem — both are “seeing.”
keyTerms.origin: From the mathematical sense of Greek *analogia*: equality of ratios.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Direct resemblance: things proportionally similar need not share any quality; what is alike is the relation (eyes:tree :: intellect:theorem).

keyTerms.definition: A genus is a general kind; a specific difference is what marks off a species within it, and it lies outside the genus. Being is not a genus, because nothing outside being could differentiate it. The specific difference is also called the “differentia.”
keyTerms.example: Human = animal (genus) + rational (difference); gold = metal + atomic number 79.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *genus* (“kind”) and *differentia specifica*; Aristotle’s logic and Porphyry’s Isagoge (the “Porphyrian tree”).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Being as a supreme genus: being is not a genus, because nothing outside being could serve as its differentia.

keyTerms.definition: Describing God by saying what he is not (immaterial, immutable). Feser holds it is part of the truth but cannot be the whole, since “God exists” and “God causes” are affirmative. Adjective: “apophatic.”
keyTerms.example: “God is not in time” is apophatic; “God causes the world to exist” is not.
keyTerms.origin: Greek *apophasis*, “denial”; associated with Pseudo-Dionysius and Maimonides.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Equivocal predication or agnosticism: negative theology denies limitations of God; it becomes self-defeating only if made the whole story.

keyTerms.definition: There is, and in principle could be, only one God, because a purely actual being cannot have the parts that multiplication within a kind requires. Also called God’s uniqueness.
keyTerms.example: Two humans differ by their matter; nothing could distinguish two purely actual beings.
keyTerms.origin: Classical theism’s affirmation that God is one; in Feser derived from pure actuality (chapter 6).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Divine simplicity: unity means there is only one God; simplicity means there are no parts within God (though each entails the other).

keyTerms.definition: God has no parts of any kind — no matter/form, genus/difference, essence/existence, act/potency, or really distinct attributes. His real attributes are identical with each other and with him. Adjectives: God is “simple” or “noncomposite.”
keyTerms.example: God’s power and his knowledge are, in reality, one and the same act of being, only analogous to power and knowledge in us.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *simplex*, “without fold,” i.e., uncompounded. Affirmed by Aristotle, Plotinus, Augustine, Anselm, Maimonides, Avicenna, Aquinas; defined at Lateran IV and Vatican I.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Simplicity as “easy to understand” or as low informational complexity: it means lack of composition, and a simple God is incomprehensibly rich rather than simplistic.

keyTerms.definition: The mainstream tradition (Aristotle, Plotinus, Maimonides, Avicenna, Averroes, Augustine, Anselm, Aquinas, and others) for which divine simplicity is nonnegotiable and the core of the conception of God.
keyTerms.example: Taught by the Fourth Lateran and First Vatican Councils; affirmed by Luther and Calvin.
keyTerms.origin: A modern label for the mainstream tradition of philosophical theology from Plato and Aristotle through the medieval Jewish, Muslim, and Christian thinkers.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Theism in general, or deism: classical theism is defined by simplicity and by God’s continual causing of the world’s existence, not merely by belief in a creator.

keyTerms.definition: The modern view (labels from Brian Davies and Norman Geisler) that treats God as the unique member of a species under the genus person, lacking our limits but not simple.
keyTerms.example: Plantinga, Swinburne, and Hartshorne are classified this way by Davies.
keyTerms.origin: “Theistic personalism” is Brian Davies’ label; “neo-theism” is Norman Geisler’s.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Belief in a personal God: classical theists also affirm divine intellect and will; the difference is whether personhood puts God in a genus and makes him composite.

keyTerms.definition: Aquinas’ distinctions: the essence (what a thing is); a property in the strict sense (a feature flowing necessarily from the essence); a contingent accident (an intrinsic feature not flowing from the essence); a mere relation to something else.
keyTerms.example: Rational animality; the capacity to find things amusing; skin color; being Plato’s teacher.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *essentia*, *proprium*, *accidens*, *relatio*; from Aristotle’s Categories and Porphyry’s five predicables.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Plantinga’s broad sense of “property” (anything truly predicable of a thing): Aquinas’ “property” is only what flows necessarily from the essence.

keyTerms.definition: Wolterstorff’s term for the view, held by defenders of simplicity, that a thing’s essence and attributes are concrete constituents of the thing, not abstract Platonic entities it participates in.
keyTerms.example: Socrates’ rationality is part of Socrates, not a Form floating in a third realm.
keyTerms.origin: Term coined by Nicholas Wolterstorff (“Divine Simplicity,” 1991) to characterize the metaphysics behind the doctrine of simplicity.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Relational (Platonic) ontology: there a thing stands in a relation of exemplifying abstract properties outside it; in constituent ontology its nature is inside it.

keyTerms.definition: A change in what can be truly said of a thing that involves no real change in the thing itself, only in something related to it (Geach’s term).
keyTerms.example: Socrates becomes shorter than Plato when Plato grows; God becomes Creator when the world begins.
keyTerms.origin: Peter Geach’s term, named for Cambridge philosophers such as Bertrand Russell and J. M. E. McTaggart who worked with the notion; applied to simplicity by Barry Miller.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Real change: in a real change something intrinsic to the thing itself alters; in a Cambridge change only something related to it does.

keyTerms.definition: Treating a feature that merely happens to accompany things of a kind as if it were essential to that kind.
keyTerms.example: Every professor so far has been under nine feet tall, so no professor could be taller.
keyTerms.origin: One of the fallacies catalogued in Aristotle’s Sophistical Refutations.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Fallacy of composition: composition infers a whole has a property because its parts do; accident treats a merely accompanying feature as essential.

keyTerms.definition: Immanent causation originates from within the agent (the mark of life); transient causation passes from one thing to another, as when a thing acts only because acted on. Adjectives: “immanent,” “transient.”
keyTerms.example: An animal feeding vs. a thrown stone breaking a window.
keyTerms.origin: Scholastic *actio immanens* (action that remains in the agent) and *actio transiens* (action that passes into another).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Inner vs. outer in a spatial sense: immanent causation is about the source of activity (the agent’s own nature), not location.

keyTerms.definition: In Aristotelian metaphysics, the two principles composing every material substance: the form that makes it the kind of thing it is, and matter as the pure potentiality to take on form. The theory that material things are form-matter composites is called “hylomorphism” (adjective “hylomorphic”).
keyTerms.example: A dog is canine form actualizing matter; matter by itself is just potential.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotle’s hylomorphism (Greek *hyle*, “matter,” + *morphe*, “form”); Latin *materia prima*.
keyTerms.confuseWith: “Matter” in physics: physical matter is already formed stuff (atoms, fields); prime matter is the pure potentiality underlying any material substance.

keyTerms.definition: God’s mode of existence outside time altogether — not endless duration through all past and future time, but no succession at all. Adjectives: “eternal,” “timeless.”
keyTerms.example: Like an author conceiving a whole story in one flash rather than day by day.
keyTerms.origin: The classical conception articulated by Augustine and Boethius and adopted by Aquinas.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Everlastingness (sempiternity): existing at all times without beginning or end, still with succession, which Feser argues is not enough for an immutable, simple God.

keyTerms.definition: The view (Findlay; Russell against Copleston) that all necessity is a matter of linguistic convention, so a necessary being is nonsense.
keyTerms.example: “All bachelors are unmarried” is necessary only because of what “bachelor” means.
keyTerms.origin: Associated with logical positivism; in the theistic debate, J. N. Findlay (1948) and Russell in his BBC debate with Copleston.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Analyticity: some necessary truths may be analytic, but conventionalism claims all necessity is merely a matter of linguistic rules.

keyTerms.definition: A sentence is a linguistic item; a proposition is what it expresses, which can be expressed in many languages and would be true or false even if no language existed.
keyTerms.example: “Snow is white” and “Schnee ist weiss” express one proposition.
keyTerms.origin: A distinction central to modern logic since Frege; Feser cites Plantinga for it here.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Utterance or statement: an utterance is a speech act; a proposition is the language-independent content that can be true or false.

keyTerms.definition: Forming a mental picture versus strictly grasping something intellectually. Only imageable things can be pictured present or absent.
keyTerms.example: You can picture the numeral “4,” not the number four; nor can you picture God existing or not existing.
keyTerms.origin: Classic distinction (Descartes’ thousand-sided figure, which can be understood but not distinctly pictured); Feser cites Brian Leftow.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Conceivability as a sure guide to possibility: even genuine conceiving is, for Feser, secondary to knowledge of essences.

keyTerms.definition: Any potential that is actualized is actualized by something already actual; nothing moves itself from potency to act.
keyTerms.example: Water does not heat itself; the stove’s actual heat actualizes its potential to be hot.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotelian-Scholastic principle defended in Feser’s chapter 1.
keyTerms.confuseWith: PPC: PC says there must be an actualizer; PPC says the actualizer must contain the effect’s perfection in some way.

keyTerms.definition: There is an explanation for the existence of any being and for any attribute it has, either in its own nature or in something else.
keyTerms.example: If a coin appears on your desk, there is some explanation — even if you never learn it.
keyTerms.origin: Named by Leibniz; defended by Feser in chapter 5.
keyTerms.confuseWith: “Everything has a cause”: PSR requires an explanation, which in a necessary being is found in its own nature, not in an external cause.

keyTerms.definition: Actuality with no admixture of potentiality: nothing about it is waiting to be realized, so it neither needs nor can have an actualizer. Adjective: “purely actual.”
keyTerms.example: The Unmoved Mover of chapter 1, which actualizes everything else without itself being actualized.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *actus purus*; Aristotle’s unmoved mover as developed by Aquinas.
keyTerms.confuseWith: “Very active” or “always busy”: pure act means lacking no perfection, not engaging in constant change.

keyTerms.definition: That whose essence just is its existence, so that it exists of itself rather than having existence added to an essence.
keyTerms.example: The conclusion of the Thomistic proof: the cause of the existence of everything whose essence differs from its existence.
keyTerms.origin: Latin phrase from Aquinas, *ipsum esse subsistens*.
keyTerms.confuseWith: “Existence in general” or the sum of existing things: it is not an abstraction or the world’s total, but the one being whose nature is to exist.

keyTerms.definition: A distinction between two principles that are really different in the thing, not merely two ways of thinking about it; in creatures, essence relates to existence as potency to act.
keyTerms.example: Knowing what a dodo is does not tell you whether any dodo exists.
keyTerms.origin: Aquinas, De ente et essentia; defended in Feser’s chapter 4.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A merely conceptual distinction (like “morning star” vs. “evening star”), which reflects our ways of thinking rather than distinct principles in the thing.

keyTerms.definition: In an analogy of attribution, the primary analogate is the thing in which the perfection is intrinsically found; secondary analogates receive the name by relation to it.
keyTerms.example: George is the primary analogate of “healthy”; his food and complexion are secondary.
keyTerms.origin: Scholastic terminology of analogy.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Better and worse instances of the same quality: secondary analogates of attribution do not intrinsically have the perfection at all.

keyTerms.definition: Really distinct principles that compose a thing even when they are not physically separable pieces: matter and form, genus and difference, essence and existence, substance and accidents, act and potency.
keyTerms.example: A human’s animality and rationality are metaphysical parts of the human essence, though you can’t cut them apart.
keyTerms.origin: Scholastic metaphysics; in Feser, chapters 2 and 6.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Physical or integral parts (arms, atoms): simplicity denies both, but the key arguments turn on metaphysical parts.

keyTerms.definition: The view that what makes two members of the same material species two individuals is their distinct matter.
keyTerms.example: Identical twins share a nature but differ as individuals because each is made of different matter.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotle and Aquinas; Feser points to Oderberg and his own Scholastic Metaphysics.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Distinction by specific difference, which separates species (human vs. dog), not individuals within a species.

keyTerms.definition: A cause is temporally prior if it comes earlier in time; it is ontologically prior if the effect depends on it for its being here and now, regardless of time.
keyTerms.example: A lamp’s light depends at this moment on the current flowing, whether or not the lamp was switched on long ago.
keyTerms.origin: Scholastic distinction between priority in time and priority in nature; central to hierarchical (per se) causal series.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Temporal beginning: showing that something always existed removes only a temporally prior cause, not an ontologically prior one.

keyTerms.definition: The picture, attributed to PPC by Cottingham, on which causes pass their own properties down to effects the way heirlooms are handed on.
keyTerms.example: Thinking a cook must be spongy to make a spongy cake.
keyTerms.origin: Cottingham’s label, in criticizing Descartes’ “Causal Adequacy Principle.”
keyTerms.confuseWith: PPC itself: PPC allows virtual and eminent presence and does not require the same feature to be handed over.

keyTerms.definition: The view that mental properties are immaterial yet are properties of a material thing, the brain, so there is no immaterial substance.
keyTerms.example: Saying pain is a nonphysical property that the physical brain has.
keyTerms.origin: A contemporary position in philosophy of mind; criticized by John Searle as unstable.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Substance dualism: substance dualism holds that the mind (or soul) is itself an immaterial thing, not just that brains have immaterial properties.

keyTerms.definition: A form of theistic personalism, associated with Charles Hartshorne (and Whitehead), which holds that God changes and develops in response to the world.
keyTerms.example: Saying God grows in experience as history unfolds.
keyTerms.origin: Alfred North Whitehead and Charles Hartshorne, 20th century.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Classical theism with an active God: classical theism holds God is active and personal without undergoing real change.

keyTerms.definition: The picture of properties as abstract objects existing apart from concrete things, which the things exemplify or participate in.
keyTerms.example: On Plantinga’s view, Socrates exemplifies an abstract property, wisdom, that exists whether or not anyone is wise.
keyTerms.origin: Plato’s Forms; modern Platonism about properties.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Constituent ontology, on which a thing’s nature and attributes are concrete ingredients within it.

keyTerms.definition: A statement true by virtue of the meanings of its terms.
keyTerms.example: “All bachelors are unmarried.”
keyTerms.origin: Kant’s analytic/synthetic distinction, later central to logical positivism.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Necessary truth in general: conventionalists identify the two, but Feser holds that mathematical and metaphysical necessities are not mere matters of meaning.

keyTerms.definition: A way of speaking about modality: a necessary truth is true in every possible world, a possible one in at least one.
keyTerms.example: Schrader claims there is a possible world with nothing at all in it.
keyTerms.origin: Leibniz; formalized in twentieth-century modal logic (Kripke, Plantinga, Lewis).
keyTerms.confuseWith: The source of modal truth: for the Aristotelian-Thomist, possible-worlds talk is a convenient idiom, while what grounds modality is the essences of actual things.

keyTerms.definition: God’s lack of any real change, following from pure actuality and simplicity; Cambridge changes (like becoming Creator) are compatible with it. Adjective: “immutable” (unchangeable, changeless).
keyTerms.example: The world beginning to exist is a real change in the world, not in God.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *immutabilis*, “unchangeable.”
keyTerms.confuseWith: Inertness or impassive indifference: immutability means lacking no actuality, not lacking activity or life.

keyTerms.definition: Incorporeal: having no body. Immaterial: not material in any way. God is both, since matter involves parts and potentiality.
keyTerms.example: Neither atoms nor fields nor bodies of any kind can be God, since all have rearrangeable parts.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *in-* (“not”) + *corpus* (“body”) / *materia* (“matter”).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Being made of a very fine or invisible substance (like a gas or energy): that would still be material.

keyTerms.definition: A contingent being could fail to exist and depends on causes; an absolutely necessary being cannot fail to exist because of what it is. Nouns: “contingency,” “necessity.”
keyTerms.example: You exist contingently; the being whose essence is existence exists necessarily.
keyTerms.origin: Avicenna and the Scholastics; the rationalist proof of chapter 5.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Physical or relative necessity, e.g., water necessarily boiling at a given pressure, which still depends on conditions.

keyTerms.definition: Refuting a weaker or distorted version of a view than the one its defenders actually hold.
keyTerms.example: Restricting PPC to material ingredients, then refuting that restricted principle with a sponge cake.
keyTerms.origin: Informal logic.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Fallacy of accident: a straw man misstates the opponent’s view; the fallacy of accident misgeneralizes from contingent features.

keyTerms.definition: Assuming, in an argument, what is at issue.
keyTerms.example: Rejecting a necessary being by assuming all necessity is linguistic, when the proofs claim to show otherwise.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *petitio principii*, “assuming the starting point.”
keyTerms.confuseWith: Raising a question: in logic, “begging the question” does not mean “prompting” one.

keyTerms.definition: Feser’s term for what God would be if he were not simple: an immaterial, very powerful but essentially creaturely being, one of a kind and in need of a cause.
keyTerms.example: A God with really distinct wisdom and power, which something would have to combine.
keyTerms.origin: Feser, chapter 6.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The God of classical theism, who is not one being among others but subsistent existence itself.

keyTerms.definition: Actuality (act) is the way a thing really is right now; potentiality (potency) is a real capacity to be or do otherwise. To actualize a potential is to make it actual; change is exactly that. Things are “actual” or “potential” in these respects.
keyTerms.example: A cold cup of coffee is actually cool and potentially hot; heating it actualizes that potential.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotle’s *energeia* / *entelecheia* (act) and *dynamis* (potency); Latin *actus* and *potentia*. Defended in Feser’s chapter 1.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Mere logical possibility: a potency is a real capacity grounded in what a thing actually is (ice can melt), not just the absence of contradiction.

keyTerms.definition: The uncaused cause that terminates a regress of causes, above all a hierarchical series of things depending here and now on something else for their existence or activity. Also called the uncaused cause.
keyTerms.example: The purely actual actualizer of chapter 1, on which everything that changes depends at every moment.
keyTerms.origin: A standard term of classical natural theology (Latin *causa prima*).
keyTerms.confuseWith: The first event in time (e.g., the Big Bang): “first” here means first in the order of dependence, not earliest in time.

keyTerms.definition: A substance is a thing that exists in its own right (a stone, a dog); an accident or attribute is a feature that exists only in a substance and modifies it (its color, shape, size).
keyTerms.example: The stone is a substance; its gray color and round shape are accidents that exist only in the stone.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotle’s Categories; Latin *substantia* (“standing under”) and *accidens* (“what befalls”).
keyTerms.confuseWith: “Substance” in the chemical sense (a material like water or salt) and “accident” in the sense of a mishap.

keyTerms.definition: Saying something of something: the predicate is what is said (“is wise”), the subject is what it is said of (“Socrates”). Univocal, equivocal, and analogical are ways of predicating.
keyTerms.example: In “God is good,” “good” is predicated of God.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *praedicare*, “to proclaim”; Aristotelian logic.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A property: a predicate is a linguistic or conceptual item; whether it corresponds to a distinct property in the thing is exactly what the simplicity debate is about.

keyTerms.definition: Made up of parts of any kind — physical pieces or metaphysical principles (matter and form, essence and existence, act and potency). Composition is the state of being composite; its opposite is simplicity (“noncomposite”).
keyTerms.example: A chair is composite in its pieces; a human is composite in body and soul, and in essence and existence.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *compositum*, “put together.” Central to the Neo-Platonic proof of chapter 2.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Complicated: a thing can be composite without being complicated (a two-piece object), and simplicity doesn’t mean poverty of perfection.

keyTerms.definition: A series in which each member causes only because it is being caused right now by the one before it, so the whole series depends at every moment on a first member that causes without being caused. A regress of such dependencies with no first member would be vicious — nothing would ever be explained.
keyTerms.example: A hand moves a stick that moves a stone: the stone moves only while the hand moves the stick (chapter 1).
keyTerms.origin: Scholastic *causae per se ordinatae*; contrasted with per accidens (linear) series like parents and grandchildren.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A linear (per accidens) series extending back in time, like generations of ancestors, which the proofs do not need to deny could be infinite.

keyTerms.definition: Materialism: everything that exists is material. Naturalism: reality is exhausted by the natural world studied by science, with no God or immaterial realm. Materialists and naturalists deny that minds or causes are immaterial.
keyTerms.example: Paul Churchland’s argument that humans are purely material because they arise from purely material processes.
keyTerms.origin: Modern philosophical positions with roots in ancient atomism (Democritus, Epicurus).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Science itself: naturalism is a philosophical thesis about what exists, not a scientific finding.

keyTerms.definition: The view that a human being includes an immaterial mind or soul, distinct from the body, not merely immaterial properties of a material brain. Dualists hold the intellect is not material.
keyTerms.example: Aquinas’ argument that since thinking is immaterial, the soul that thinks is immaterial and survives death.
keyTerms.origin: Plato, Descartes; Aquinas holds a distinctive hylomorphic version.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Property dualism, which denies an immaterial substance while positing immaterial properties of the brain.

keyTerms.definition: The physical law that in a closed system disorder (entropy) tends to increase, so order — and thus information content — tends to decrease.
keyTerms.example: A tidy room left alone becomes messier, not tidier; Davies uses the law to argue biological information must come from prior factors.
keyTerms.origin: Nineteenth-century physics (Clausius, Kelvin); cited by Feser via Paul Davies.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A claim that order can never increase locally: it can, in open systems drawing on outside energy — which is why the environment matters in Davies’ point.

keyTerms.definition: Two opposite Pre-Socratic extremes. Parmenides denied that change (and hence potentiality) is real; Heraclitus, on a traditional reading, held that only change is real, with nothing stable (denying actuality). Feser argues both are incoherent.
keyTerms.example: The Heraclitean can’t coherently reason from premises to conclusion, since on his view there is no persisting self to do it.
keyTerms.origin: Parmenides of Elea and Heraclitus of Ephesus, 5th–6th centuries B.C.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Ordinary observations that things change or stay the same: these are claims that *only* permanence or *only* flux is real.

keyTerms.definition: Belief that there is only one God. Feser distinguishes monotheism in principle (there could not be another God) from monotheism as mere fact (there happens to be only one).
keyTerms.example: If God were one member of a genus, monotheism would be true only as a matter of fact, like Zeus alone on Olympus.
keyTerms.origin: Greek *monos* (“alone, one”) + *theos* (“god”).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Henotheism (worshiping one god while allowing others exist): classical monotheism holds that a second God is impossible.

keyTerms.definition: God’s being all-powerful — the source of all power, with nothing outside the range of his power. Treated in detail in Part B (ch6b); in this module it appears as an example of a real attribute God has necessarily.
keyTerms.example: In Morris’s objection, omnipotence is the necessary property contrasted with the contingent property of having created.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *omni-* (“all”) + *potens* (“powerful”).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Being able to do literally anything, including contradictions: the classical notion is power to do whatever is possible (see Part B).

keyTerms.definition: The ways something can be true or exist: necessarily, possibly, contingently, impossibly. Modal questions ask not just what is but what must or could be.
keyTerms.example: Asking whether God exists necessarily or only contingently is a modal question.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *modus*, “manner”; Aristotle’s modal logic.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Probability: modal claims concern what must or could be, not how likely something is.

keyTerms.definition: A number is an abstract object; a numeral is a symbol used to name it. Different numerals (“4,” “IV,” “four”) name the same number.
keyTerms.example: You can picture the numeral “2” on a chalkboard, but not the number two itself.
keyTerms.origin: Standard distinction in philosophy of mathematics (Frege).
keyTerms.confuseWith: The idea that erasing or imagining away numerals affects the numbers themselves — Feser’s reply to Schrader turns on this.

keyTerms.definition: Existing at all times, without beginning or end, but still within time and with a before and after. Everlasting things are “sempiternal.”
keyTerms.example: A God who had lived through every past moment and would live through every future one would be everlasting, not timeless.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *sempiternus*, “always-lasting.”
keyTerms.confuseWith: Timeless eternity, in which there is no succession at all — the view Feser defends.

keyTerms.definition: Describing God in human terms as though he were a bigger or better version of us. Univocal predication tends toward anthropomorphism.
keyTerms.example: Picturing God as a very wise person who deliberates and changes his mind.
keyTerms.origin: Greek *anthropos* (“human”) + *morphe* (“form”).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Analogical predication, which attributes perfections to God without importing human limitations.

keyTerms.definition: An argument that tries to prove God’s existence from the concept or definition of God alone (Anselm, Descartes). Feser’s proofs are not ontological arguments.
keyTerms.example: Reasoning that since God is the greatest conceivable being, he must exist in reality.
keyTerms.origin: Anselm’s Proslogion (11th century); named by Kant.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Feser’s claim that God exists necessarily, which is derived from what the proofs show about the world’s cause, not from a definition.

keyTerms.definition: The charge, pressed by some contemporary critics, that if God is simple and his act of creating is identical with his necessary essence, then everything God does — and the world itself — would be necessary.
keyTerms.example: “If creating is identical to God, and God is necessary, then creating is necessary.”
keyTerms.origin: Contemporary philosophy of religion (e.g., R. T. Mullins); not raised in this chapter.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Morris’s objection: Morris argues that necessary and contingent properties can’t be identical; modal collapse argues simplicity forces everything to be necessary. Both are addressed with the real/Cambridge distinction.

keyTerms.definition: The most basic entities in current physics, not composed of other particles. Fermions make up matter (like electrons and quarks); bosons carry forces (like photons).
keyTerms.example: Feser notes that even an electron has distinct attributes (mass, charge, spin) and can come into being and pass away — so it involves composition and potency.
keyTerms.origin: Named after physicists Enrico Fermi and Satyendra Nath Bose.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Simple beings in Feser’s sense: not being made of smaller particles is not the same as having no parts or potentialities at all.

keyTerms.definition: Giving to something created the worship due only to God. Feser says worshiping a non-simple “god” would be idolatry, since such a being would be a creature.
keyTerms.example: Worshiping a powerful superangel as if it were the ultimate source of all being.
keyTerms.origin: Greek *eidolon* (“image”) + *latreia* (“worship”).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Merely having an inadequate concept of God: idolatry concerns what is worshiped, not how precisely it is understood.

keyTerms.definition: The position that we cannot know whether God exists or what God is like. Feser argues that confining God-talk to univocal and equivocal terms would force us into agnosticism (or even atheism). Adjective/noun: “agnostic.”
keyTerms.example: Someone who says “God, if there is one, is so beyond us that nothing we say about him means anything” has slid into agnosticism.
keyTerms.origin: Coined by T. H. Huxley (1869) from Greek *a-* (“without”) + *gnosis* (“knowledge”).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Apophatic theology, which denies limitations of God while still affirming that he exists and causes the world.

keyTerms.definition: The view that God created the world but does not continually sustain or act in it, like a watchmaker who winds the watch and walks away. Adjective/noun: “deist,” “deistic.”
keyTerms.example: Picturing God as the one who lit the Big Bang’s fuse and then left.
keyTerms.origin: Seventeenth–eighteenth-century Enlightenment thought.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Classical theism, on which God causes the existence of things at every moment (the hierarchical causation of chapters 1–5).

distinctions.name: Formal vs. virtual/eminent presence in a cause

left.label: Formal presence
left.desc: The cause has the very feature it produces — the heirloom picture: the $20 bill in my wallet that I hand over, the hot body warming a colder one.

right.label: Virtual or eminent presence
right.desc: The cause has the effect’s content as a power or a more fundamental reality: funds in the bank (virtually), control of the printing press (eminently). The effect’s feature may be a new, numerically different instance actualized from potency.

distinctions.whyItMatters: Almost every “counterexample” to PPC (sponge cakes, helium, a boy giving a black eye) assumes PPC requires formal presence. It doesn’t. And when we apply PPC to God, we mean that creatures’ perfections are in him eminently, not that God is literally spongy, material, or changeable.

distinctions.name: Univocal vs. equivocal vs. analogical

left.label: Univocal or equivocal
left.desc: Univocal: exactly the same sense (Fido and Rover are dogs) — applied to God it makes him a big creature. Equivocal: unrelated senses (the two bats) — applied to God it leaves our words empty.

right.label: Analogical
right.desc: Related but not identical senses, grounded in real relations or proportional likeness (good wine, good man; seeing a tree, seeing a theorem). Literal, yet flexible enough to span radically different kinds of reality.

distinctions.whyItMatters: This is how we can speak truly and positively about a God who is utterly unlike creatures, avoiding both anthropomorphism and agnosticism. It also dismantles Plantinga’s objection, which assumes God’s power and knowledge must be distinct because ours are.

distinctions.name: Analogy of attribution vs. analogy of proper proportionality

left.label: Attribution
left.desc: The perfection is intrinsic only to the primary analogate; secondary analogates get the name by relation to it (food and complexion called “healthy” because of George’s health).

right.label: Proper proportionality
right.desc: The perfection is intrinsic and formal in every analogate, though realized in proportionally different ways (life in plants, animals, humans, angels).

distinctions.whyItMatters: Both apply to God. By proper proportionality, being is really in God and in creatures, each in its own way. By attribution, God is the primary analogate of being and creatures are beings by relation to him as their cause. Attribution alone would risk saying God is “good” only in the sense that he causes goodness.

distinctions.name: Proper vs. metaphorical proportionality

left.label: Proper (nonmetaphorical)
left.desc: The form or nature is literally present in each analogate: plants and angels are both really alive.

right.label: Improper (metaphorical)
right.desc: The form is literally present in only one analogate and figuratively in the other: the zoo animal is a lion; brave George only “is a lion.”

distinctions.whyItMatters: Metaphor is a kind of analogy, but analogy is not all metaphor. When classical theists say God-talk is analogical, they are not saying it is poetry. Plantinga’s charge that analogy means “nonliteral” runs these together.

distinctions.name: Real change vs. Cambridge change

left.label: Real change / real property
left.desc: Something intrinsic to the thing itself is altered: Socrates grows hair; a person gains knowledge.

right.label: Cambridge change / Cambridge property
right.desc: What is true of the thing changes only because something else changed: Socrates becomes shorter than Plato because Plato grew; God becomes Creator because the world comes to be.

distinctions.whyItMatters: This single distinction answers Morris’s necessary/contingent-properties objection to simplicity and the “creating is changing” objection to immutability. God has contingent Cambridge properties, but no contingent real ones.

distinctions.name: Classical theism vs. theistic personalism

left.label: Classical theism
left.desc: God is absolutely simple: not an instance of any kind, not composed of attributes, the source of being rather than a being among beings. Personal in having intellect and will, analogically understood.

right.label: Theistic personalism (neo-theism)
right.desc: God is the unique member of the kind “person,” like us but without our limits; attributes are distinct; some (process theists) even allow change in God.

distinctions.whyItMatters: The difference is not personal vs. impersonal. It is whether God is the uncaused, necessarily unique First Cause or a supremely impressive creature-like being that could in principle have rivals and would need a cause. Only the classical God is what the five proofs conclude to.

distinctions.name: Everlasting duration vs. timeless eternity

left.label: Everlasting (longevity)
left.desc: Existing through all past time and all future time — endless succession, adding moments forever.

right.label: Timeless eternity
right.desc: Existing outside time entirely, with no before and after in one’s life; causing the whole temporal order in a single act.

distinctions.whyItMatters: Having no beginning or end is only the first step; immutability and simplicity push further to timelessness. Getting this right defuses objections that treat eternity as a moment (the Socrates–Obama simultaneity puzzle) or God’s causing as a series of acts.

distinctions.name: Imagining vs. conceiving (and possible worlds vs. essences)

left.label: Imagination-first modal method
left.desc: Picture scenarios (a lone green marble, then nothing) and read off what is possible or necessary from what we can picture or conceive in “possible worlds.”

right.label: Essence-first modal method
right.desc: Start from what actually exists, discover its nature, and infer what is possible or necessary for it — the Aristotelian-Thomistic procedure.

distinctions.whyItMatters: Schrader’s empty-world argument depends on the first. But neither numbers nor God can be pictured, and the second method is how the proofs establish God’s necessity. Picturing nothing tells us nothing about a being whose essence is existence.

distinctions.name: Temporal vs. ontological priority

left.label: Temporal priority
left.desc: A cause that comes earlier in time, like a match struck before the fire it starts. Removing a first moment removes the need for this kind of cause.

right.label: Ontological priority
right.desc: A cause the effect depends on here and now for its being, regardless of time, like the current on which a lamp’s light depends. A composite needs such a cause for its parts to be combined at all.

distinctions.whyItMatters: It blocks the move “maybe God (or the universe) is composite but has always existed.” Everlastingness answers only the temporal question. It is also why Feser’s arguments are about what sustains things now, not about a beginning.

illustrations.title: Three ways to give you $20
illustrations.body:
I can hand you a bill from my wallet (the effect is in me **formally**), wire money from my account so you can withdraw one (**virtually** — the total cause is me plus the account), or, if I somehow control a Federal Reserve printing press, have a genuine bill printed for you (**eminently** — I have something more basic than a bill: the power to make bills).

Use it to show that PPC never required the cause to *look like* the effect. God has creaturely perfections eminently, the way the press “has” $20 bills.

illustrations.title: The black eye and the hot iron
illustrations.body:
A boy does not need a black eye to give one to his neighbor (a Thomist writer’s point), and a hot body does not pass the very same heat it contains to what it warms. Instead, by its power it makes an actual new heat that was only potential in the heated thing (Aquinas).

The lesson: PPC is not an “heirloom” theory in which properties are passed down like jewelry. It says the effect cannot exceed the *powers* of its total cause.

illustrations.title: Seeing a tree, seeing a theorem
illustrations.body:
“I see the tree” and “I see that the Pythagorean theorem is true” use “see” in neither the same nor unrelated senses. The eyes are to the tree as the intellect is to the theorem — a similarity of *relations*. When we spell out each case (light hitting the retina; grasping logical relations among concepts), they aren’t two species of one genus.

So too with being: a man’s existence is to his essence as an angel’s is to its essence as God’s is to his — though in God, existence and essence are one.

illustrations.title: Zeus alone on Olympus
illustrations.body:
Imagine every Olympian god but Zeus vanished. Zeus would now be the *only* god — but his nature would be unchanged. He would still be the kind of thing there could be many of, a member of a pantheon with a single remaining member. The same is true of Odin alone in Asgard.

That is what denying divine simplicity does to God: even if in fact there is only one, he becomes one *instance* of a kind — unique by luck, not in principle — and a being that needs a cause. Feser’s verdict: a superangel, not God.

illustrations.title: Socrates gets shorter without shrinking
illustrations.body:
Socrates stays the same height while Plato grows; suddenly “Socrates is shorter than Plato” is true. Something new is true of Socrates, but nothing in Socrates changed — a Cambridge change.

When the world begins, “God is Creator” becomes true. The real change is entirely in the world coming to be. That is how an immutable God can have a contingent description without any contingent real feature.

illustrations.title: The nine-foot professor
illustrations.body:
Every college professor who has ever lived has been under nine feet tall. It would still be a fallacy to conclude that no *possible* professor could be taller: height is only accidentally connected to professorship.

Likewise, every agent we know changes when it acts (my fingers move as I type), and every living thing we know changes as it lives. But change is only accidentally connected to acting and living. What acting essentially is: bringing about an effect. What teaching essentially is: causing someone to learn — whether by lectures, books, or otherwise.

illustrations.title: The author and the whole story
illustrations.body:
An author might conceive an entire novel — beginning, middle, and end — in a single flash of insight. For the characters, chapter 10 comes after chapter 1. But the author did not think up chapter 1 first and chapter 10 later.

This is how God, outside time, causes a temporal world in one act in which things exist at t1, t2, t3. “God causes X to exist at t1” does not mean “at t1, God causes X.”

illustrations.title: Erasing “2 + 2 = 4”
illustrations.body:
Picture a universe containing only a chalkboard with “2 + 2 = 4” on it. Now picture it erased. Have you shown that 2 + 2 = 4 might have been false? Obviously not — you pictured numerals, not numbers, and numbers aren’t the sort of thing you can picture present or absent.

Schrader’s lone green marble works the same way: picturing it gone tells us nothing about God, who can no more be pictured than numbers can.

illustrations.title: Five roads to one summit
illustrations.body:
Five climbers ascend a mountain by five different faces — one by the scree of change, one by the ridge of composition, one by the glacier of abstract truths, one by the cliff of essence and existence, one by the path of sufficient reason. Each arrives at a summit that, on inspection, has the same features: no potency, no parts, existence itself, necessity. Since a mountain can only have one highest point with those features (unity), they are all standing in the same place.

A course analogy for the convergence argument; it also shows why the attributes are *mutually entailing* rather than a checklist.

illustrations.title: The light and the stained-glass window
illustrations.body:
Sunlight passing through a stained-glass window appears red here, blue there, gold elsewhere. The colors are really distinct in the glass, yet they are one light at the source. Our concepts of God’s power, knowledge, and goodness are like the colored panes: distinct in our minds because we meet those perfections separately in creatures, but corresponding to one undivided reality in God.

A course analogy for simplicity, with a caveat: God is not a physical light, and the analogy illustrates how distinct concepts can be true of one simple reality — it does not prove it.

objections.title: The “heirloom” objection: helium and sponge cake
objections.objection: PPC pictures causation as passing heirlooms down the line: the cause has a property and hands it to the effect. But nature is full of novelty. Helium has properties the hydrogen it came from lacked. A sponge cake is spongy, yet none of its ingredients — eggs, flour, butter — is spongy. So effects routinely contain what their causes lacked, and PPC is false.
objections.reply:
Feser makes two points here (the third, on triviality, is the next objection).

1. **Wrong target: material cause vs. total cause.** By Cottingham’s own admission, the examples look only at the *materials*. PPC says the effect’s features are in its **total** cause — the materials plus agents, powers, processes, and conditions (for the cake: the baker, the mixing, the oven’s heat). Restricting PPC to ingredients and then refuting that restricted version is a straw man.
2. **Wrong mode: formal presence isn’t required.** The heirloom reading assumes the feature must be in the cause *formally*. Defenders of PPC explicitly deny this. As one Thomist put it, a boy needn’t have a black eye to give one; as Aquinas put it, a hot body doesn’t transfer its own numerically identical heat but, by its power, actualizes a new heat that was potential in the thing heated. The effect’s features can be in the total cause **virtually** or **eminently**.
objections.pushback: If they say, “Then PPC just means the cause had the power to produce the effect — isn’t that obvious?” — agree that it is close to obvious once stated correctly. That is its strength, not its weakness. The work it does in natural theology comes from applying an obvious principle to the question of what could produce *existence itself*, intellect, and so on. If they press that emergent properties are genuinely “new,” point out that novelty of *instance* (a new heat, a new sponginess) is not the same as something from nothing: the total cause had the power to produce it, which is all PPC claims.

objections.title: “Potentially present” makes PPC trivial
objections.objection: Grant that sponginess doesn’t come from nothing — it emerges from the chemistry of mixing and baking. That still doesn’t show it was “present” in the materials. And if the defender says it was there *potentially*, PPC is rescued only by being made trivially true: of course whatever happens was possible beforehand.
objections.reply:
1. Feser happily accepts the language of potentiality. As the Aquinas passage says, the characteristics that end up in the effect were in it potentially, and in the $20 example the virtual and eminent cases involve real potentialities — the account’s capacity to be drawn on, the press’s capacity to print.
2. But appealing to potentialities is not trivial. Such explanations may be only *minimally* informative, but minimal information is still information. Saying your $20 came from my bank account’s power to be drawn on genuinely explains something.
3. The proof that PPC isn’t vacuous: naturalists use it to reach substantive conclusions. Churchland argues that because humans arise from wholly material causes by wholly material processes, humans are wholly material — an inference that assumes a wholly material total cause can only yield a wholly material effect. Dualists accept the same principle and argue in reverse from the immateriality of intellect. A trivial principle couldn’t settle anything, yet both sides treat this one as decisive.
objections.pushback: If they say, “The Churchland point shows only that some philosophers use it, not that it’s true,” reply that the question here was whether it is *trivial*, and a principle that carries real argumentative weight for both materialists and dualists is not. Its truth rests on PC and PSR: a feature of an effect not accounted for by anything in its total cause would be an actualization with no actualizer and a fact with no explanation.

objections.title: Evolution gets more from less
objections.objection: Evolution shows that simpler life forms give rise to more complex ones. The complex effect contains more than the simple cause — a straightforward counterexample to the claim that the effect can’t exceed its cause.
objections.reply:
1. Even on the standard naturalistic account (not just theistic versions), a simpler organism doesn’t produce a more complex one all by itself. Every species is a variation on genetic material that has existed since life began.
2. New variations arise when existing genetic material, a mutation (from a replication copying error, or from radiation or chemical damage), and environmental circumstances combine, so that the trait is advantageous in that setting. None of these factors alone would suffice; together they are the total cause.
3. So evolution *respects* PPC: the new variation’s features are present, in some way, in the combined factors.
4. Feser adds Paul Davies’ point: to deny that a new life form’s information comes from some combination of prior factors — including the environment, not only inheritance — would conflict with the second law of thermodynamics, according to which order and information tend to decrease in a closed system.
objections.pushback: If they say, “But the overall trend is from simple to complex,” reply that PPC is about the *total* cause at each step, and the naturalistic account itself insists the environment and physical processes supply what the genome alone lacks. If they go further and say information can simply appear from nothing, they are now contradicting both PSR and (per Davies) thermodynamics — a heavier cost than accepting PPC.

objections.title: “These are medieval relics no modern philosopher accepts”
objections.objection: Proportionate causality and “action follows being” are Scholastic slogans. Modern philosophy moved past them, and you can’t build an account of God on discarded medieval metaphysics.
objections.reply:
1. Both principles follow from PSR and PC, which earlier chapters defended at length; they stand or fall on their merits, not on their age.
2. Contemporary naturalists implicitly rely on them. Churchland’s argument for materialism assumes PPC.
3. Searle’s criticism of property dualism relies on *agere sequitur esse*: if a mental property is really over and above the brain, it can’t be a property of the brain and must be a separate entity; if it is a property of the brain, it can’t be over and above it. Others find it mysterious how a wholly material brain could yield immaterial properties — the same principle again.
4. Even a materialist who rejects Aquinas’ premise that thought is immaterial can accept his conditional: *if* intellect is immaterial, its subject must be immaterial.

So what looks like a relic is something many secular philosophers are committed to.
objections.pushback: If they grant the naturalists use it but still say it could be false, ask for a clear case where an activity really outruns the nature of its subject with nothing else making it do so. Feser’s own qualification (the puppet moves only because the puppeteer moves it) shows that apparent exceptions involve an outside agent, which confirms the principle rather than refuting it.

objections.title: Deny actuality or deny potentiality (Heraclitus and Parmenides)
objections.objection: Feser’s argument that being is analogical needs both actuality and potentiality to be real. But a Parmenidean can deny potentiality (change is illusion), and a Heraclitean can deny actuality (there is only flux, nothing stable). Either way the argument collapses.
objections.reply:
1. **Against Parmenides**: denying potentiality means denying change, which chapter 1 showed can’t be done coherently (even the experience of thinking through an argument is a succession).
2. **Against Heraclitus**: pure flux is just as incoherent.
- There would be no persisting self, so the person who reaches the conclusion wouldn’t be the one who entertained the premises.
- There would be no single, stable argument to present to critics or repeat to oneself.
- Change is always change *toward* something: a melting ice cube moves toward liquidity and flatness — new actualities, however temporary.
- A thing changes in the ways it does because of what it actually is: the ice melts because it is water, not wood or glass.

So premises 1 and 2 cannot coherently be denied.
objections.pushback: If they suggest a softer view — “there are only events, no enduring things” — ask what makes a given event the kind of event it is and why it tends toward some outcomes rather than others. Any answer smuggles actuality back in. And for Parmenideans: the claim that change is an illusion needs the illusion itself to change (appear, then disappear), which is still change.

objections.title: Act and potency differ only in how we talk
objections.objection: Grant that we talk about what a thing actually is and what it could become. That is a distinction in our concepts or language, not in reality. So premise 3 — that potentiality is *really* distinct from actuality — is false, and the analogy of being loses its basis.
objections.reply:
1. We already have at least one real case: chapter 4 argued that essence and existence are really distinct in things and relate as potency to act.
2. More generally, if the distinction were merely conceptual — two ways of describing one and the same reality — then that single reality would be either an actuality (and potentiality would be unreal) or a potentiality (and actuality would be unreal).
