That would amount to denying premise 1 or premise 2, which we have seen can’t coherently be done.
3. Hence premise 3 stands, and with premises 4–6 (same sense would collapse the distinction; unrelated sense would make potency unreal; the three uses exhaust literal usage) the conclusion follows: potency has being in a sense analogous to act.
objections.pushback: If they say, “There’s just the actual thing, and ‘potential’ describes what it would do in various circumstances,” ask what grounds those truths. If nothing in the actual ice cube grounds its capacity to melt (which a lump of wood lacks), the difference between ice and wood becomes an inexplicable brute fact. If something does ground it, that something is not the same as the ice’s current solidity — which is the real distinction.

objections.title: God-talk is either anthropomorphic or empty
objections.whoRaises: Typical skeptic; Humean-style critics; also strictly apophatic theologians from the other side
objections.objection: Either words like “exists,” “powerful,” and “good” mean the same when applied to God as to us — making God a big human — or they mean something entirely different, in which case we don’t know what we’re saying. So either theology is anthropomorphic, or it says nothing. The most one can honestly say is what God is not.
objections.reply:
1. Feser agrees that univocal predication can’t work. The proofs conclude to something purely actual, simple, immaterial, immutable, eternal; words formed for changeable material things can’t apply to it in the same sense.
2. But pure negative theology fails too. “God exists” and “God causes the world” are affirmative statements; if we could only deny things of God, we couldn’t even state the conclusions of the proofs. Negation is part of the story, not the whole of it.
3. Equivocation fails as well. If God’s “power” has nothing to do with power, what does it mean? Try completing “God has ‘power’ in the sense that he ___.” A univocal filler reintroduces anthropomorphism; an equivocal one just moves the mystery. The upshot would be agnosticism or even atheism — maybe not even meaningful speech.
4. The dilemma is false because there is a third, literal use of language — analogical predication by attribution and proper proportionality — which we already needed (for “being” said of act and potency) before any theology.
objections.pushback: If they say, “But you can’t tell me exactly what God’s knowledge is like,” agree: analogical concepts are applied indeterminately. But indeterminate is not empty. We know what we are affirming (a real perfection of which our knowledge is a limited likeness) and what we are denying (the limits and composition that go with it in us).

objections.title: Analogy is special pleading invented to save theology
objections.objection: The “analogy” doctrine looks like an ad hoc device: when theists can’t make sense of their claims literally, they declare their words analogical. We don’t need a special semantics anywhere else.
objections.reply:
1. The doctrine is **independently motivated**. Feser’s seven-step argument derives it from the act/potency distinction alone — which one could accept without ever accepting any argument for God.
2. Ordinary language is shot through with analogy that no one regards as special pleading: good wine and good people; healthy food and healthy people; seeing a tree and seeing a proof; life in plants and in animals.
3. Science does the same. Physics speaks of entities with both wave-like and particle-like properties and of space itself being curved, stretching common-sense concepts far beyond their home; this seems intelligible only analogically. We should expect at least as much stretching when describing the cause of there being a material world at all.
4. And analogical predication is literal: nonunivocal does not mean nonliteral.
objections.pushback: If they respond that physics can back its analogies with mathematics and experiment, reply that theology backs its analogies with demonstrative argument: the proofs tell us *which* features are removed (potency, composition, limitation) and *why* the perfection must be present (PPC). That is a disciplined constraint, not a blank check.

objections.title: The First Cause might have potency in its activity
objections.objection: Grant that the first cause’s *existence* involves no actualization — that’s what lets it stop the regress. Why couldn’t its *activity* still involve potentiality — say, its activity of actualizing other things? Then it would be uncaused in existence yet not purely actual, and the arguments for unity and the other attributes would fail.
objections.reply:
1. **Agere sequitur esse.** Action reflects being. If a thing exists in a purely actual way, how could its acting be less than purely actual? Existence is the most fundamental thing about a being; everything else follows from it. There is nothing in a purely actual nature from which potentialities for activity could arise.
2. **Composition.** Such a being would have parts — an actual part and a potential part. Chapter 2 showed that composites need a cause of the combining of their parts, and that cause must be extrinsic (an intrinsic one would cause itself). This holds even if the thing always existed: the need is for an *ontologically* prior cause, not a temporally prior one. But a first cause with a cause of its own isn’t first and can’t end the hierarchical regress.
3. So the First Cause is purely actual in activity as well as existence.
objections.pushback: If they say, “Why not just say God is uncaused and composite — a brute fact?” point out that this abandons the principle the proofs rest on (composites need causes) at the precise moment it becomes inconvenient, and it would leave us with a being that is ultimate only by stipulation. It would also undermine the arguments that got us to God in the first place.

objections.title: Why not two (or many) gods?
objections.whoRaises: Polytheist; skeptic probing the leap to monotheism
objections.objection: Even if there must be a purely actual cause, why only one? Perhaps there are several, each purely actual, distinguished in some way — or perhaps each proof reaches a different ultimate being.
objections.reply:
1. For there to be more than one thing of a kind, there must be a distinction between individual and species (as matter distinguishes two humans) or between species and genus (as rationality distinguishes humans within the genus animal).
2. Such distinctions require parts — genus plus difference, matter plus form — and parts entail potentiality: matter is potentially this or something else; a genus is potentially one species or another; parts only potentially compose a whole until actualized.
3. A purely actual being has no potency and hence no such parts, so it can’t be one member of a kind that could have others. It is unique in principle.
4. Nor can we distinguish two purely actual beings by other kinds of parts, such as substance and accidents: any composition brings potency.
5. And the five proofs don’t reach five beings: pure actuality, simplicity, subsistent existence, and necessity each entail the others, so they all describe the same unique reality.
objections.pushback: If they propose that two gods might differ by a mere relation (e.g., by their positions), ask what in each god grounds the different relation. If nothing intrinsic differs, they’re not two; if something intrinsic differs, it is a part or a limitation, and that brings potency. Two purely actual beings would be indistinguishable in every intrinsic respect — which is just one being described twice.

objections.title: Theistic personalism: a personal God need not be simple
objections.whoRaises: “Theistic personalists” / “neo-theists” (Brian Davies’ and Norman Geisler’s labels): Alvin Plantinga, Richard Swinburne, Charles Hartshorne and process theologians
objections.objection: Divine simplicity is a Greek philosophical import that makes God unintelligible. Better to think of God as a person like us — with distinct attributes of knowledge, power, goodness — only without our limitations: the unique member of the kind *person* at its maximum. Process theists add that, like any person, God changes in response to the world.
objections.reply:
1. The dispute isn’t about personhood. Classical theists attribute intellect and will to God and so regard him as personal. The issue is whether being personal puts God *in a genus* and makes him composite.
2. If God belonged to a kind, he would be unique only as a matter of contingent fact — like Zeus alone on Olympus or Odin alone in Asgard, whose natures would be unaltered. Monotheism would be a lucky accident.
3. If God had distinct parts or attributes, something would have to combine them, so he would need a cause and wouldn’t be the First Cause. Even if immaterial, he would be a superangel, and worshiping him would be idolatry.
4. Changeability (the process view) implies potency, and so composition.
5. Crucially, none of the five proofs supports such a being. Each concludes to a wholly noncomposite cause. So one cannot accept the proofs and reject simplicity; denying simplicity is implicitly atheism. That is why the tradition across paganism, Judaism, Islam, and Christianity — and the Catholic Church at Lateran IV and Vatican I, as well as Luther and Calvin — treated it as nonnegotiable.
objections.pushback: If they say, “But the God of Scripture seems to be a person who responds and changes,” note that this module deals with metaphysics; the classical tradition reads such language analogically, with Part B (ch6b) explaining how intellect, will, and love belong to God without composition. If they say simplicity makes God impersonal, point out that it is compatible with — indeed required for — God’s being the *source* of personal perfections, which he has eminently.

objections.title: Plantinga: simplicity makes God a single property — an abstract object
objections.whoRaises: Alvin Plantinga, Does God Have a Nature?
objections.objection: Simplicity says God is identical with each of his properties. Then each property is identical with every other, so God has just one property — flatly contrary to the obvious fact that he has several, such as power and mercy. Worse, if God is identical with a property, then God *is* a property, and properties are abstract objects. So God would be an abstract object, which is absurd for a being who knows and acts.
objections.reply:
Feser says Plantinga reads the doctrine through three assumptions of his own, each of which classical theists reject.

1. **Univocity.** Plantinga takes “wise” or “powerful” to mean the same of God and of Socrates. But predication of God is analogical: what we call power and knowledge in God is *analogous* to ours. That they are distinct in us doesn’t show they are distinct in him.
2. **Platonism about properties.** Plantinga treats properties as abstract objects in a third realm that things exemplify. For Aquinas, a thing’s essence, properties, and accidents are concrete constituents *of* the thing (Wolterstorff’s “constituent ontology”). So identifying God with his wisdom doesn’t identify him with an abstract object; no classical theist ever said God is a “property.”
3. **An overbroad notion of “property.”** Plantinga counts anything predicable as a property: being human, wise, barefoot, married to Xanthippe, Plato’s teacher, even being Socrates. Aquinas distinguishes the **essence** (rational animality), **properties** proper that flow from it (the capacity for amusement), **contingent accidents** (skin color), and mere **relations** (being Plato’s teacher). Lumping them together is what makes it sound as if simplicity would make God’s creating humans as essential to him as his wisdom.

The odd consequences come from these assumptions, not from simplicity. Plantinga also misreads analogy as nonliteral (it is literal) and misses the real stakes: not Platonic participation, but that a composite God would be caused and only contingently unique.
objections.pushback: If they ask, “So are God’s power and mercy the same thing or not?” answer: in God there is one simple reality; we form distinct concepts of it because we know it through distinct effects in creatures, and each concept truly (analogically) describes that one reality. The concepts are distinct; what they apply to in God isn’t divided. That no more makes the concepts synonyms than “morning star” and “evening star” are synonyms.

objections.title: Plantinga’s fallback: “call them characteristics”
objections.objection: Fine — Aquinas uses “property” more narrowly than I do. But that is merely verbal. Whatever we call them, God has many *characteristics* — power, mercy, being Creator — and simplicity still has to say they are all identical.
objections.reply:
1. This misses the point. Aquinas’ distinctions are not a semantic preference for using “property” in a restricted way.
2. They mark objective, extralinguistic metaphysical differences between a thing’s essence, its proper properties, its contingent accidents, its intrinsic accidents, and its relations to other things.
3. Once those differences are respected, simplicity only identifies God’s real, intrinsic perfections — not his relations to creatures (which are Cambridge properties; see Morris’s objection). The alleged implication that God’s contingent relations are identical with his essence never arises.
objections.pushback: If they insist that all true predications must correspond to some item in God, ask whether “Socrates is shorter than Plato” corresponds to an item in Socrates when only Plato has grown. It plainly doesn’t, and neither does “God is Creator” require a new item in God.

objections.title: Necessary and contingent properties can’t be identical
objections.whoRaises: Thomas Morris, Our Idea of God (see also Christopher Hughes)
objections.objection: Some things are true of God necessarily (he is omnipotent) and some only contingently (he created the world, though he needn’t have). The only good way to capture this is to say God has both necessary and contingent properties. But a necessary property can’t be identical to a contingent one. So not all God’s properties are identical, and simplicity is false.
objections.reply:
Setting aside the loose use of “property,” Feser follows Barry Miller, who builds on Peter Geach.

1. Distinguish **real** properties from mere **Cambridge** properties. Socrates growing hair is a real change; Socrates becoming shorter than Plato because Plato grew is a Cambridge change, giving Socrates only a Cambridge property.
2. Simplicity doesn’t deny that God has contingent properties of every sort — only contingent **real** ones. And it doesn’t say all God’s properties are identical — only his **real** ones.
3. Being Creator is a Cambridge property: it involves the world coming into existence, not a change in God.
4. So Morris is right that omnipotence (real, necessary) and having created the world (Cambridge, contingent) aren’t identical. But simplicity never implied they were.
objections.pushback: If they reply, “But creating is like Socrates *causing* Plato to grow, and that does change Socrates,” Feser’s answer (his footnote) is that this assumes the changes we undergo when acting must occur in any agent — a fallacy of accident. What is essential to causing is producing an effect in another, not changing oneself. If they then raise the modal-collapse worry, see that objection below.

objections.title: To act is to change
objections.whoRaises: Common objection to immutability (and Feser’s footnote on creation as Socrates-changing-Plato)
objections.objection: Acting always involves a change in the agent, not just in what it acts upon. When I type, the screen changes — but so do my fingers, my nervous system, and my thoughts. So if God creates, he changes, and an immutable God couldn’t create or do anything.
objections.reply:
1. It’s true that the agents we experience change in the course of acting. But inferring that every *possible* agent must do so commits the **fallacy of accident** — like reasoning that because every professor so far has been under nine feet tall, no possible professor could be taller. The link is contingent, not essential.
2. What is essential to acting, as Brian Davies points out, is bringing about an effect in another thing, not undergoing change oneself. Teaching essentially means causing someone to learn — not specifically lecturing or writing books. Creating essentially means causing the world to exist; nothing in that requires the Creator to change.
3. And God’s becoming Creator is a Cambridge change: the real change is in the world.
4. Immutability is also demanded independently: a purely actual being has no potency to actualize, and a simple being lacks the parts that real change (changing in one respect while staying the same in others) requires.
objections.pushback: If they say, “But I can’t imagine acting without changing,” agree — and note that imagination is tied to the material, changing agents we know. The question is whether *acting as such* entails change, and nothing in the concept of producing an effect does. We even have partial models: a magnet or the sun can produce effects without itself being altered in doing so (a course illustration; the analogy is imperfect since these things do change in other ways).

objections.title: An unchanging God can’t be alive
objections.objection: Living things grow, feed, move, and learn — life *is* change. A changeless God would be static, frozen, dead — more like a stone than a living being.
objections.reply:
1. This is another fallacy of accident: the living things we know change, but it doesn’t follow that every possible living thing must.
2. On the traditional Aristotelian account, what is essential to life is operating from an **internal principle** rather than being wholly moved by external forces (immanent rather than merely transient causation). An animal is alive because much of what it does flows from its own nature; a stone isn’t, because it does things (like breaking a window) only when something acts on it.
3. God acts without being acted upon by anything at all. Other living things are partly dependent — they must eat and breathe. So God has life in the fullest possible way.
4. The stone comparison gets it backward: the stone is the most dependent, God the least.
objections.pushback: If they say “life without change is inconceivable,” ask which is more alive: something that needs constant input from outside to keep functioning, or something whose activity is wholly from itself and lacks nothing. Change in creatures is a sign of their incompleteness — they change to acquire what they lack.

objections.title: Causing at t1 and at t2 means acting in time
objections.objection: Feser says God causes the existence of everything at every moment. Then God causes something to exist at t1, and causes something to exist at the later time t2. So he acts at t1 and again at t2 — which means he is in time.
objections.reply:
1. The inference is invalid. From *God causes it to be the case that X exists at t1* it doesn’t follow that *at t1, God causes X to exist* (a point Feser takes from Brian Davies). The temporal index belongs to the effect, not to the act.
2. God doesn’t perform a sequence of acts — creating at t1, conserving at t2, conserving again at t3. From outside time, in one act, he causes a temporal world in which X exists at t1, t2, t3, and so on.
3. Compare an author who conceives a whole story in a single flash of insight (an image Feser borrows from Stephen Barr): within the story, the middle follows the beginning; the author didn’t devise them one after the other.
objections.pushback: If they say “causing is always simultaneous with or prior to its effect, so it must be at a time,” reply that this generalizes from temporal causes (fallacy of accident again). If they say “then God can’t respond to prayers or events,” that belongs to Part B (knowledge and will), but in brief: God’s single timeless act includes the whole history, prayers and responses together, as the author’s single conception includes the plot’s every twist.

objections.title: The simultaneity argument: Socrates would be simultaneous with Obama
objections.objection: If God causes Socrates to exist in 469 B.C., Socrates’ existence must be simultaneous with God’s eternity; if God causes Obama to exist in A.D. 1961, Obama’s existence must be simultaneous with God’s eternity too. Simultaneity is transitive, so Socrates’ existence would be simultaneous with Obama’s. That is absurd, so timeless eternity is incoherent.
objections.reply:
1. The objection treats eternity as if it were a **point in time**, since only a point in time can be simultaneous with another point in time.
2. But the entire claim is that God does not exist at any point in time; he exists outside time altogether (Feser cites Davies and Paul Helm).
3. So the first two premises are false as stated: temporal events are not “simultaneous with” eternity in the ordinary, transitive sense of simultaneity.
objections.pushback: If they say, “Then what is the relation between God and a temporal event?” answer: causal dependence — the event exists because God causes it — not temporal location. A novel’s events all depend on the author’s one conception without being simultaneous with each other.

objections.title: Necessity is linguistic convention
objections.whoRaises: J. N. Findlay; Bertrand Russell (1948 BBC debate with Frederick Copleston)
objections.objection: Necessity belongs to statements, not to things. “All bachelors are unmarried” is necessary only because it is analytic — true in virtue of what the words mean — and it tells us about our linguistic conventions, not about the world. Extralinguistic reality can’t be necessary. God is supposed to be part of extralinguistic reality. So a “necessary being” is a confused notion.
objections.reply:
1. **Conventionalism is false on independent grounds.** It confuses **sentences** (linguistic items) with **propositions** (not linguistic). “Snow is white” and “Schnee ist weiss” express one proposition, which would be true even if no language had ever existed. So the conventionality of sentences doesn’t make propositions — or their necessity — conventional.
2. That example is contingent, but truths of mathematics and logic (2 + 2 = 4; everything is identical to itself) are necessary, and it is notoriously hard to argue plausibly that they are conventions (chapter 3).
3. **The objection begs the question.** The proofs claim to show that there is an extralinguistic cause of the existence of things that exists necessarily, and they give an account of that necessity unrelated to convention: pure actuality, absolute simplicity, identity of essence and existence. Merely asserting that all necessity is linguistic presupposes the arguments are wrong without showing that they are.
objections.pushback: If they retreat to “at least necessity *de dicto* is all we understand,” ask whether they understand the claim that a thing whose essence is its existence can’t fail to exist. That is intelligible and not about words. If they say it’s still an ontological-argument trick, clarify: Feser isn’t deriving existence from a definition; the proofs establish God’s existence from the world first, and necessity follows from what that cause turns out to be.

objections.title: Schrader’s empty world
objections.whoRaises: David Schrader, “The Antinomy of Divine Necessity”
objections.objection: Imagine a world with nothing in it but a single green marble. Now imagine even the marble gone. You have imagined a world in which nothing exists — not even God. So there is a possible world without God, and God doesn’t exist necessarily.
objections.reply:
1. This works only if everything that exists or could exist — God included — is the kind of thing you can form a **mental image** of, present or absent. It isn’t (Feser cites Brian Leftow).
2. Compare: picture a universe containing only a chalkboard with “2 + 2 = 4” on it, then picture it erased. That shows nothing about whether 2 + 2 = 4 is necessary, because numbers aren’t imageable objects. You can picture numerals (“2,” “4,” or “II,” “IV”), but numerals are labels, not numbers.
3. What we can form an image of is simply irrelevant to what we can strictly conceive.
4. The same holds of God, who is wholly immaterial. You can’t picture God existing, let alone not existing. Mental imagery tells us nothing about God’s modal status, any more than it does about mathematics.
objections.pushback: If Schrader’s defender says, “I didn’t mean picture — I mean I can *conceive* a world with nothing,” move to the next objection’s reply: conceivability of worlds isn’t the right starting point for modal knowledge, and assuming God is absent from some conceivable world simply assumes he isn’t necessary.

objections.title: Conceivability of possible worlds is our guide to necessity
objections.whoRaises: Schrader, and much contemporary modal metaphysics
objections.objection: Even without mental images, we can coherently conceive a possible world containing nothing at all. Conceivability is our best guide to possibility. So it is possible that God not exist, and he is not a necessary being.
objections.reply:
1. From the Aristotelian-Thomistic point of view, this method gets things **backward**. We don’t first survey possible worlds and then read off what is possible or necessary for things.
2. Rather, we start with *actual* things, determine their essences, and from those draw conclusions about what is possible for them and necessarily true of them.
3. In God’s case the right procedure is: establish that God exists, determine his nature, and infer from that what is possible and necessary for him. That’s what the preceding chapters did: God is purely actual, absolutely simple, subsistent existence depending on nothing else — and so exists necessarily, and hence (if we use possible-worlds talk) in every possible world.
4. Schrader’s objection doesn’t show anything wrong with this reasoning; it simply assumes something is wrong with it, so it begs the question.
objections.pushback: If they say, “But surely an empty world is at least prima facie conceivable,” reply that apparent conceivability is defeasible: one can seem to conceive that some complex arithmetical claim is false until one works through the proof. Likewise, the ‘empty world’ seems conceivable only until one understands that a being whose essence is existence can’t fail to exist.

objections.title: “Who made God?”
objections.whoRaises: Popular skeptic (e.g., the “Who designed the designer?” line); not an objection Feser discusses in this section
objections.objection: If everything needs a cause, God needs one too. If God doesn’t need one, why does the universe? Positing God just pushes the question back a step.
objections.reply:
Using this module’s results (Feser takes up the objection directly in chapter 7):

1. The proofs never say *everything* needs a cause. They say that what has potentiality needing actualization, parts needing combination, an essence distinct from its existence, or contingent existence needs a cause.
2. This chapter shows that God has none of these features: he is purely actual, simple, subsistent existence, and necessary. He not only *needs* no cause; he *could not* have one (the eternity argument).
3. The universe, by contrast, is made of composite, changeable, contingent things. The asymmetry isn’t special pleading; it follows from a principled difference.
4. And if we suppose God had a cause, then the being we are talking about is not the First Cause, and the regress would continue to the being that is uncaused — which would then be God.
objections.pushback: If they say, “Then why not stop at the universe as the uncaused thing?” ask whether the universe (or its fundamental constituents) has parts, potentialities, or contingent existence. Everything physics tells us says it does — even fundamental particles have distinct attributes and come to be and pass away. So it can’t play the role of the First Cause.

objections.title: Modal collapse: if God is simple, isn’t everything necessary?
objections.whoRaises: Contemporary critics of divine simplicity (e.g., R. T. Mullins); not raised in this chapter
objections.objection: If God is simple, his act of creating is identical with his necessary essence. Then creating is as necessary as God’s existence, and the world exists necessarily — God couldn’t have refrained from creating. That contradicts both freedom and the contingency of the world.
objections.reply:
This chapter doesn’t address the objection by name, but it supplies the key tools; the fuller answer, involving divine will and freedom, belongs to Part B (ch6b).

1. Simplicity identifies God’s **real** perfections with his essence. Being Creator is a **Cambridge** property: the difference between a world where God creates and one where he doesn’t is a difference in the *world*, not an extra real feature in God (Geach/Miller, via Feser).
2. So the objection’s premise — that God’s creating is an intrinsic element of God identical with his essence — is exactly what the classical theist denies. What is identical with God’s essence is his one act of being, knowing, and willing; that this act has *this* world as a term is a contingent truth grounded in the world’s dependence on God.
3. By the same reasoning Feser uses for timeless causing: “God causes X” reports a relation of dependence in X, not a new real item in God.
objections.pushback: If they press, “But then what explains why God’s one act has this world as its term rather than none?” acknowledge that this is where the harder questions about divine freedom begin, and point to Feser’s treatment of will and freedom in ch6b. Note that this is a live contemporary debate among theists; honesty about that strengthens rather than weakens your case.

misconceptions.myth: PPC says a cause must literally resemble or contain its effect, so a creator of material things must be material.
misconceptions.correction: PPC allows an effect’s features to be in the cause formally, virtually, or eminently. God contains creaturely perfections eminently — as the one with power over the printing press “has” $20 bills without having any in his wallet.

misconceptions.myth: Calling God-talk “analogical” means it is metaphorical, poetic, or not literally true.
misconceptions.correction: Analogies of attribution and proper proportionality are literal uses of language. Only improper (metaphorical) proportionality is figurative. Nonunivocal does not mean nonliteral: God really exists and really knows, in ways analogous to ours.

misconceptions.myth: Divine simplicity means God has only one attribute and all our words for him are synonyms.
misconceptions.correction: Our concepts of God’s power, knowledge, and goodness are distinct, because we know them through distinct effects; each truly applies to the one undivided divine reality. Simplicity concerns what is in God, not the number of concepts we use.

misconceptions.myth: Simplicity makes God an abstract object, like a Platonic property.
misconceptions.correction: That follows only if one assumes, with Plantinga, that properties are abstract Platonic entities. For Aquinas, a thing’s essence and attributes are concrete constituents of it; and God is not a “property” at all but subsistent existence itself.

misconceptions.myth: Classical theists deny that God is personal; theistic personalists affirm it.
misconceptions.correction: Both ascribe intellect and will to God. The disagreement is whether being personal puts God in a genus alongside humans and angels and makes him composite. Classical theists say no.

misconceptions.myth: An immutable God is inert, frozen, or lifeless, and cannot act.
misconceptions.correction: Acting essentially is producing an effect, and living essentially is acting from an internal principle; neither requires change. God, wholly unacted upon, is maximally active and has life in the fullest sense.

misconceptions.myth: God’s eternity means he has existed for an infinitely long time and will go on forever.
misconceptions.correction: That is mere everlastingness. Feser argues that God is strictly timeless: no succession, no temporal stages, no moments added. Eternity is not a point or stretch of time.

misconceptions.myth: If God becomes Creator, something in God must have changed.
misconceptions.correction: Becoming Creator is a Cambridge change, like Socrates becoming shorter than Plato when only Plato grew. The real change is the world coming to be.

misconceptions.myth: Each of the five proofs reaches a different ultimate being, and one needs a sixth argument to show there is only one.
misconceptions.correction: The attributes established — pure actuality, simplicity, subsistent existence, necessity — entail one another, and pure actuality entails uniqueness. The five proofs are five routes to one God.

misconceptions.myth: Divine necessity means God’s existence follows from the definition of the word “God.”
misconceptions.correction: Feser does not use an ontological argument. The proofs first establish from the world that a First Cause exists; its necessity follows from its nature (pure actuality, simplicity, essence identical to existence), which is a real, extralinguistic feature.

misconceptions.myth: PPC rules out genuine novelty: nothing new can ever appear in nature.
misconceptions.correction: New instances of features arise all the time (a new heat, a new sponginess, a new biological variation). PPC denies only that they come from nothing in the total cause.

misconceptions.myth: The analogy of being is a special theory invented only to protect theology from criticism.
misconceptions.correction: Feser derives it from the act/potency distinction alone, and ordinary language and physics use analogical terms constantly.

misconceptions.myth: Divine unity just means God is internally harmonious or undivided in purpose.
misconceptions.correction: In this chapter, unity means uniqueness: there is and could be only one God, because a purely actual being can’t be one member of a kind.

explain.tweet: The five proofs don’t reach five gods. A purely actual cause can’t have parts, so it can’t be one of a kind, can’t change, can’t be material, can’t be in time, and can’t fail to exist. Deny simplicity and you don’t get a humbler God — you get a creature.
explain.elevator: Once you’ve shown there’s a First Cause that is pure actuality — no unrealized potential at all — a lot follows. Anything with parts has potential, so this cause has no parts. Without parts, there’s nothing that could make two of it, so there’s only one. Change is potential being realized, so it can’t change. Matter is full of parts and potential, so it isn’t material. And existing in time means changing, so it’s timeless. That’s the classical God, and every proof lands on him.
explain.twoMinute:
Here’s the problem this chapter solves. Say you accept an argument that there’s some ultimate cause of the world. Fine — but why call it God? Why one? Why not an impersonal force, or a committee of gods, or a very powerful alien?

Feser’s answer is that the proofs don’t just get you *a* cause; they get you a cause of a very specific sort. It has to be **purely actual** — no potential waiting to be realized — because anything with unrealized potential needs something else to realize it, and then it wouldn’t be first. And from that one feature, the rest follows almost like geometry.

Anything with parts has potential, because the parts have to be combined. So the First Cause has **no parts**: it’s simple. How do you get two of anything? Two dogs differ by their matter; dogs differ from cats by some added feature. Both require parts. So nothing could make there be two First Causes — it’s **one**, necessarily. Change is potential becoming actual, so it **can’t change**. Matter is made of rearrangeable parts, so it’s **immaterial**. Being in time means adding moments and changing state, so it’s **timeless**. And a being whose very essence is to exist can’t fail to exist: it’s **necessary**. Those five descriptions — pure act, simple, existence itself, necessary, the mind behind necessary truths — turn out to be one thing seen from five angles.

Two tools make this work. First, a cause can’t give what it doesn’t have — though it can have it in a higher way, like someone who can print money rather than someone who has cash. Second, our words apply to God **analogically**: “exists” and “knows” are true of God literally, but not in exactly the same way they’re true of us — the way “seeing” a tree and “seeing” a proof are both really seeing.

And the objections? “If God creates, he changes” — no, the change is in the world, the way you can become ‘shorter than your brother’ just because he grew. “A changeless God is dead” — no, life means acting from within, and nothing is more self-active than God. The upshot: if you try to make God more like us — with parts, in time, changing — you don’t get a friendlier God. You get a creature, and the proofs no longer point to it.
explain.eli12:
Imagine the very first domino that starts everything falling — except it isn’t pushed by anything, and it keeps everything going right now, not just at the start. What would it have to be like?

It can’t have any “not yet” in it — nothing it’s waiting to become — because then something else would have to make it become that. Things with pieces always have a “not yet” (the pieces could come apart or be arranged differently). So the first cause has no pieces at all.

Now, how can there ever be two of something? Two cookies from the same batch are made of different bits of dough. Chocolate chip and oatmeal cookies differ by what’s added. Both need pieces. The first cause has no pieces, so there can’t be two of it. There’s just one.

Can it change? Changing means becoming something you weren’t yet — but it has no “not yet.” So no. Is it made of stuff, like atoms? Stuff has pieces, so no. Does it get older? Getting older is changing, so no — it’s outside of time, like an author who thinks up a whole story all at once.

When we say it “knows” or is “powerful,” we mean something real, but bigger than our knowing and power — like how “seeing” a picture and “seeing” a math answer are both really seeing, just different kinds.

explain.keyAnalogy: **The author and the story.** An author who conceives a whole novel in one flash stands outside the story’s timeline, isn’t changed when a character is born or dies, is the source of everything in the book without being one of its characters, and has every character’s traits “eminently” in his imagination without himself being a pirate or a princess. Use it to illustrate timeless causation (the author doesn’t write chapter 1 “before” chapter 10 in the relevant sense), Cambridge change (a character’s birth changes the story, not the author), and the difference between the First Cause and the greatest *character* (theistic personalism makes God the hero of the novel instead of its author). Be explicit about the limits: real authors think in time and are composite; the analogy illustrates relations, not God’s inner nature.

persuade.coreInsight:
The click happens when someone sees that **the divine attributes are not a wish list but a single consequence viewed from different sides**. Once a cause is purely actual — with no unrealized potential — it follows by strict reasoning that it has no parts, can’t be one of many, can’t change, can’t be material, can’t be in time, and can’t fail to exist. These aren’t separate claims stacked up by piety; each is what “no potential at all” means in a different department.

It usually fails to click for one of two reasons. First, people keep **picturing God as a very big person inside the universe** — a being among beings — so every attribute sounds like an arbitrary superpower (“how can a person be timeless?”). The fix is to keep returning to what the proofs actually concluded: not a super-being, but the source of being itself. Second, people assume that our words must apply to God **in exactly the same way** or not at all, so “God knows” sounds either anthropomorphic or empty. The analogy of being — which they already use whenever they talk about “seeing” a solution — dissolves this.

audiences.startingPoint: Assumes causes and effects are physical, emergent novelty is everywhere, and theology’s concepts are vague.
audiences.approach: Start with PPC as a principle they already use: conservation laws, “you can’t get information from nothing,” Churchland’s own inference to materialism. Correct the heirloom misreading with the $20 example and the evolution account (genes + mutation + environment). Then show that the attributes are *derived*, with the same rigor as a proof in physics: no potency → no parts → one, unchanging, immaterial. Use the physics point that science also speaks analogically (curved space, wave-particle duality).
audiences.openingQuestion: Do you think a new biological trait can appear with no contribution from genes, mutation, or environment — literally from nothing?
audiences.avoid: Don’t lead with Church councils or Scripture, and don’t overclaim that thermodynamics proves God; Davies’ point supports PPC, not theism directly.

audiences.who: Committed Christian or theist who pictures God as a person like us
audiences.startingPoint: Loves a relational, responsive God; suspects simplicity, immutability, and timelessness are cold Greek imports.
audiences.approach: Affirm that classical theists say God is personal — intellect and will are ascribed to him. Then show the stakes: a God with parts is unique only by accident (Zeus alone on Olympus) and needs a cause (a superangel). Point out that the whole tradition — Augustine, Anselm, Aquinas, Maimonides, Avicenna, Luther, Calvin, Lateran IV, Vatican I — held simplicity. Frame immutability as fullness, not inertness: God doesn’t change because he lacks nothing.
audiences.openingQuestion: If God were made of parts, what would hold those parts together — and wouldn’t that be more ultimate than God?
audiences.avoid: Don’t make them feel their prayer life is naive; save the details of God’s knowledge, will, and love for Part B rather than implying the classical God is indifferent.

audiences.startingPoint: Trained on Plantinga, possible worlds, and property talk; finds simplicity incoherent.
audiences.approach: Take Plantinga’s argument seriously and isolate its three assumptions (univocity, Platonic properties, an undiscriminating notion of property). Introduce constituent ontology, the essence/property/accident/relation distinctions, and Geach’s Cambridge properties. On necessity, contrast the essence-first modal method with conceivability-first; ask whether numbers can be ‘imagined away.’
audiences.openingQuestion: When Socrates becomes shorter than Plato because Plato grew, has Socrates acquired a new property?
audiences.avoid: Don’t dismiss contemporary metaphysics wholesale or pretend the modal-collapse debate is settled; acknowledge it as live and point to where the resources are.

audiences.startingPoint: Thinks different traditions’ ultimate beings could be many, or that ‘one God’ is just a cultural preference.
audiences.approach: Walk through the argument for unity: how do you get more than one of anything? Show that multiplicity requires parts, and parts require potency, which the First Cause lacks. Then show the convergence: five independent routes, from different starting points, reach one and the same reality. Note that pagan philosophers (Aristotle, Plotinus) reached this conclusion too — it isn’t sectarian.
audiences.openingQuestion: What makes two things two, rather than one thing described twice?
audiences.avoid: Don’t caricature polytheistic traditions; the target is the metaphysics of ‘god as one of a kind,’ not people’s devotion.

audiences.who: Apophatic mystic or ‘God is beyond all words’ believer
audiences.startingPoint: Holds that nothing positive can be said of God; any description is idolatry.
audiences.approach: Agree that negative theology is a real and indispensable part of the truth — immateriality, immutability, timelessness all tell us what God is not. Then show that pure negation can’t even say that God exists or causes, and so would undercut the very reasons for believing in God. Offer analogy as the way to affirm without reducing God to our size.
audiences.openingQuestion: If we can say nothing positive about God, can we say that God exists?
audiences.avoid: Don’t treat their humility as confusion; present analogy as honoring transcendence, not taming it.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Suppose I grant your five arguments each prove some ‘first cause.’ Why think it’s one thing, let alone God?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Because of what kind of cause they prove. Take the first: it has to be purely actual — no unrealized potential — or it would need something else to actualize it. Now ask: how do you ever get two of anything?

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Two electrons are two because they’re in different places, I suppose.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Right — there’s something about each that differs: location, matter, some added feature. Two things of a kind differ by some part or aspect beyond the kind. But that means composition, and composition means potential — the parts could be otherwise combined. A purely actual cause has none of that. There’s nothing that could make a second one.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Maybe the first cause is purely actual in its existence but has potential in its activity. It could have options about what to do.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Two problems. What something does reflects what it is — a being whose existence is pure act has no source for merely potential activity. And if it had an actual part and a potential part, it would be composite, and composites need something to unite their parts. Then it wouldn’t be first.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Composites need a cause only if they began. Maybe it’s always been composite.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Even a thing that has always existed needs an account of why its parts are combined at all. That’s a question of ontological priority, not temporal priority — like asking what keeps a structure together right now, not when it was built.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Fine. But when you say this thing ‘knows’ or is ‘powerful,’ you’re just projecting human traits onto a metaphysical abstraction.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: If I meant ‘knows’ exactly as you know, yes. If I meant something totally unrelated, I’d be saying nothing. But there’s a third, everyday option. When you say you ‘see’ a proof, you don’t mean your eyes, and you’re not speaking nonsense — seeing a proof is to your intellect as seeing a tree is to your eyes. That’s analogy, and it’s literal.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Convenient. You invent a semantics just for God.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: It isn’t invented for God. Physics needs it for curved space and wave-particle duality, and it’s forced on us by the distinction between potential and actual being before God even comes up: potentiality is real, but not real in exactly the way actuality is.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Plantinga — a theist — says simplicity makes God identical to a property, so God would be an abstract object. That seems fatal.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Only if properties are Platonic abstract objects, if ‘power’ means the same in God as in us, and if every predicate names a property on a par with every other. Classical theists reject all three. A thing’s nature and attributes are real constituents of it, not items in a Platonic heaven. And no classical theist says God is a property; he’s subsistent existence itself.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: But God has some features necessarily and some contingently — he’s necessarily powerful but only contingently a creator. Those can’t be identical.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Agreed — and simplicity doesn’t say they are. When Plato grows and Socrates becomes shorter than him, something new is true of Socrates without anything changing in him. ‘Being Creator’ is like that: the real change is in the world. Simplicity identifies only God’s real, intrinsic perfections.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Still, to create is to do something, and doing is changing. I change when I type.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Every agent you’ve met changes while acting, just as every professor you’ve met is under nine feet tall. Neither is essential. What’s essential to acting is producing an effect. What’s essential to teaching is causing learning, not lecturing in particular.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Then your God is frozen — no life, no activity.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Life, classically, is acting from within rather than being pushed from outside. A stone does things only when thrown. We’re partly self-moving but need food and air. God acts with no input at all. That’s not less life; it’s the fullest life.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: And timelessness? If God keeps things in existence now and tomorrow, he’s acting now and tomorrow.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: ‘God causes X to exist tomorrow’ doesn’t mean ‘tomorrow, God causes X.’ Think of an author conceiving a whole novel in one flash: within the story, chapter 10 comes after chapter 1, but the author didn’t produce them in that order.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Last one. I can imagine a world with nothing in it at all — not even God. So God isn’t necessary.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: You can imagine a blank. But you can’t imagine God any more than you can imagine the number four — only numerals. Erasing ‘2 + 2 = 4’ from a mental chalkboard doesn’t make arithmetic contingent. And the right way to find out what’s necessary is to start from what exists and what its nature is. A being whose essence just is existence can’t fail to exist.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: I’m not convinced the proofs work. But I see that if they do, you don’t get a bearded sky-king; you get something much stranger.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: That’s exactly right — and much more defensible. Every attempt to make God more like a big person makes him less like the First Cause, and the arguments stop pointing to him.

socratic: If I don’t have a $20 bill but can print one, do I lack what it takes to give you $20?
Can a boy give someone a black eye without having one himself? What does that tell you about ‘a cause can’t give what it doesn’t have’?
When you say ‘I see the answer,’ are you using ‘see’ in the same sense as ‘I see the tree’? In a totally unrelated sense?
Is a possibility something, or nothing? If something, is it real in the same way that what’s actual is real?
What makes two coins two coins, rather than one coin counted twice?
If a being had parts, what would explain why those parts are combined? Could that explanation lie within the being itself?
If Zeus were the only god left on Olympus, would his nature be any different? Would he be God in the sense the proofs require?
When your younger brother outgrows you, have you changed?
Every professor you’ve met has been under nine feet tall. Could there be a nine-foot professor? What does that suggest about ‘every agent changes when it acts’?
Is a being that needs food and air more alive, or less, than one that needs nothing?
Can you picture the number four — not the numeral, the number? If not, what does picturing ‘nothing’ tell you about whether numbers or God could fail to exist?
If God had existed for an infinite amount of time, would he still be adding new moments to his life? Would that be a change?
If something has always existed, does that by itself explain why its parts are held together right now?
If ‘God is powerful’ means something wholly unrelated to power, what are we asserting when we say it?

traps.trap: Presenting the attributes as a list of superlatives (‘God is the most powerful, the oldest, the biggest…’).
traps.fix: Show each attribute as a consequence of pure actuality and simplicity. Always give the derivation, not just the label; the interlocking is what persuades.

traps.trap: Saying analogical language is ‘just a metaphor’ or ‘symbolic.’
traps.fix: Insist that attribution and proper proportionality are literal. Use ‘seeing’ a proof and ‘life’ in plants and angels as examples of literal but non-identical senses.

traps.trap: Defending simplicity as ‘God has only one property.’
traps.fix: Explain that we have many true concepts of God, grounded in many kinds of effects, all applying to one undivided reality; and that contingent relations like ‘Creator’ are Cambridge properties, not identical with his essence.

traps.trap: Conceding that immutability means God is inert or unresponsive.
traps.fix: Reframe: God doesn’t change because he is fully actual, not because he is inactive. Acting is producing effects; life is self-origination of activity. Save the details of knowledge and will for Part B, but don’t concede ‘static.’

traps.trap: Treating timelessness as ‘God lives for infinitely long.’
traps.fix: Distinguish everlasting duration from strict timelessness, and use the author analogy to explain single-act causation of a temporal world.

traps.trap: Answering ‘necessary being’ objections with an ontological argument.
traps.fix: Make clear that Feser’s necessity is derived from what the proofs established from the world; it isn’t read off the definition of a word. Point out that Findlay and Schrader beg the question against those proofs.

traps.trap: Defending PPC as ‘the effect must be like the cause’ and getting refuted by sponge cakes.
traps.fix: Lead with ‘total cause’ and the formal/virtual/eminent distinction; offer the $20 example before any critic raises a counterexample.

connections.note: The introduction promised that the proofs reach the God of classical theism, not a cosmic designer or ‘god of the gaps.’ This module delivers on that promise by deriving the classical attributes and defining classical theism by its commitment to simplicity.

The master premise here — God is pure actuality — is chapter 1’s conclusion, and PPC was first introduced there. Unity, immutability, immateriality, and eternity are all unpacked from pure act; the Parmenides/Heraclitus discussion returns to chapter 1’s defense of change.

Chapter 2’s thesis that composites need an extrinsic cause (even if everlasting) drives the unity and simplicity arguments; chapter 2 also first introduced analogical predication and the physics analogy. Here the One is shown to be identical with the Unmoved Mover.

The Augustinian proof’s divine intellect is identified with the other proofs’ First Cause via necessity. The necessity section also leans on chapter 3’s case that mathematical and logical truths are not mere conventions.

The real distinction of essence and existence supplies a case of real act/potency distinction for the analogy argument; subsistent existence itself is shown convertible with pure actuality and simplicity, and God becomes the primary analogate of being.

The rationalist proof argued directly for a necessary being; this module shows why necessity entails and is entailed by pure actuality and simplicity, and defends the coherence of necessary existence against Findlay, Russell, and Schrader.

Part B continues the derivation: omnipotence, omniscience, goodness, will, love, incomprehensibility, conservation and concurrence, and miracles. It relies on this module’s tools — agere sequitur esse (for omnipotence and concurrence), PPC (for intellect and goodness), analogy (for all positive attributes) — and answers the questions about knowledge, freedom, and responsiveness that timelessness and immutability raise.

Chapter 7’s replies to “If everything has a cause, what caused God?”, “Maybe the universe itself is the uncaused cause,” “Even if there is a first cause, why think it is God?”, and “The cosmological argument presupposes the ontological argument” all lean on this module: only what has potency, parts, or an essence distinct from existence needs a cause; the universe has all three; the First Cause has the classical attributes; and its necessity is derived from the world, not from a definition.

Dawkins’ claim that a designer would be more complex than what it explains is answered by divine simplicity; the “one god further” jibe (Zeus, Thor, and the rest) is answered by this module’s point that the classical God is not a member of any kind — Zeus alone on Olympus would still be just a god; and the charge that the God of the philosophers isn’t the God of ordinary believers draws on the analogy of being and the personal (intellect-and-will) character of the classical God.
The capstone’s synthesis of the five proofs rests on the convergence argument here: five starting points, one purely actual, simple, necessary, eternal God.

quiz.q: In Feser’s $20 illustration, I have no bill on me but wire $20 from my bank account so you can withdraw it. The effect is in the total cause:
options: Formally
Eminently
Virtually
Accidentally
quiz.explanation: Wiring from the account is the virtual case: the total cause (me plus my account) has the effect’s content in another mode. Formal would be handing over a bill I hold; eminent would be having the power to print bills.

quiz.q: What is Feser’s first reply to Cottingham’s sponge-cake and helium counterexamples?
options: The examples consider only the material ingredients, whereas PPC concerns the total cause.
Sponginess and helium’s properties are illusions, so nothing new appears.
PPC applies only to living things, not to cakes or chemistry.
Baking and fusion are not genuine causation, just correlation.
quiz.explanation: Cottingham admits his examples concern the materials only. PPC says the effect’s features are in the total cause — agents, powers, and processes included — so attacking a materials-only version is a straw man. Feser never denies the novelty is real.

quiz.q: According to Feser, PPC follows from which principles?
options: Agere sequitur esse and the analogy of being
The second law of thermodynamics and conservation of energy
The ontological argument and the PSR
The principle of causality and the principle of sufficient reason
quiz.explanation: A feature of an effect not found in its total cause would be a potential actualized by nothing (violating PC) and a fact without explanation (violating PSR). Davies’ thermodynamics point supports the evolution reply but is not the ground of PPC.

quiz.q: Paul Churchland argues that because humans arise from purely material beginnings by purely material processes, they are purely material. What does Feser take this to show?
options: That PPC leads straight to materialism and should be rejected
That even naturalists implicitly rely on PPC
That dualism has been refuted by evolutionary biology
That agere sequitur esse applies only to formal causes
quiz.explanation: Churchland’s inference assumes a wholly material total cause yields a wholly material effect. The dualist accepts the same principle but reverses the inference from the immateriality of intellect. The point is that PPC is shared ground and not trivial.

quiz.q: Why, on the standard naturalistic account itself, is a new evolutionary variation not a counterexample to PPC?
options: Because natural selection is directly guided by God at every step
Because existing genetic material, a mutation, and environmental circumstances together form a total cause containing what the variation has
Because complex organisms actually contain no more information than simple ones
Because PPC applies only to inorganic chemistry
quiz.explanation: Feser stresses that even without theism, no simple organism produces a complex one on its own; the combination of genes, mutation (copying error, radiation, chemical damage), and environment is the total cause. He does not claim complexity doesn’t increase.

quiz.q: How does Feser relate agere sequitur esse to PPC?
options: It is a principle about final causes that has nothing to do with PPC
It is a rule of logic about predication rather than a metaphysical principle
It says that a thing’s being follows from its actions
It applies to formal causes (natures) what PPC says about efficient causes
quiz.explanation: PPC: an effect cannot exceed its total efficient cause. Agere sequitur esse: a thing’s activities cannot exceed its nature (formal cause). Option 2 reverses the direction — action follows being, not being action.

quiz.q: A puppet’s wooden arms dance across the stage. Does this violate agere sequitur esse?
options: No — the principle rules out a thing exceeding its nature on its own, and the puppeteer is making the arms move.
Yes — it shows the principle has exceptions and is only a rule of thumb.
No — because dancing is within the nature of wood.
Yes — unless we say the puppet has a soul.
quiz.explanation: Feser’s footnote: a thing can in a sense ‘go beyond’ its nature when something else makes it do so. What the principle forbids is a thing doing so by itself. Wood can’t dance on its own.

quiz.q: “This wine is good” and “George is a good man” use “good”:
options: Univocally
Equivocally
Analogically
Only metaphorically, never literally
quiz.explanation: The goodness of wine and of a man are not the same, but not unrelated either — the analogical middle ground. Analogy is not the same as metaphor.

quiz.q: Why is “healthy” said of George, his food, and his complexion an analogy of attribution?
options: Because health exists formally but differently in all three
Because George is only figuratively healthy
Because the three uses are entirely unrelated
Because health exists intrinsically only in George, and the others are called healthy by their relation to his health
quiz.explanation: George is the primary analogate; food is called healthy as a cause of health, complexion as a sign of it. Option 0 describes proper proportionality instead.

quiz.q: What distinguishes proper proportionality (“life” said of plants and angels) from metaphorical proportionality (“George is a lion”)?
options: In proper proportionality the feature exists only in the primary analogate
In proper proportionality the form or nature is literally present in each analogate; in the metaphorical case it is literally present in only one
Metaphorical proportionality is univocal, while proper proportionality is equivocal
There is no real difference; both are figures of speech
quiz.explanation: Plants and angels really are alive, each in its own way; George has courage that grounds the comparison, but lionhood is literally only in the zoo animal. Option 0 describes attribution.

quiz.q: Why, according to Feser, can “being” not be a genus?
options: Because being is too vague a concept to classify anything
Because only material things belong to genera
Because a specific difference must lie outside its genus, and the only thing outside being is nonbeing, which cannot differentiate anything
Because God is the only being, so there is nothing to classify
quiz.explanation: We can grasp rationality without grasping animality, but we can’t grasp substance or attribute without grasping them as beings. Nothing extrinsic to being could serve as a differentia. So being is predicated analogically, not as a genus.

quiz.q: In Feser’s seven-step argument that being is analogical, which premise does the Heraclitean (on a traditional reading) deny?
options: That actuality is real
That potentiality is real
That univocal, equivocal, and analogical usage exhaust the literal options
That essence and existence are really distinct
quiz.explanation: Heraclitus holds that only change is real, with nothing stable — denying actuality. Parmenides denies potentiality (and change). Feser argues both denials are incoherent.

quiz.q: According to Feser, what would follow if we confined talk about God to univocal and equivocal terms?
options: Agnosticism or even atheism, since no positive content could be given to what we say about God
Pantheism, since God would be identical to the world
Polytheism, since each term would name a different god
Nothing problematic, since negative theology is sufficient
quiz.explanation: Univocal terms can’t apply to a radically different being, leaving only negations (which can’t even say that God exists or causes). Equivocal terms leave the words empty. The result is agnosticism or atheism — hence the need for analogy.

quiz.q: A critic says the First Cause might have no potency in its existence but some potency in its activity. Which is one of Feser’s replies?
options: Activity and existence are the same word, so the suggestion is merely verbal
Only material things have activities, so the First Cause is inactive
Such a being would be composite — an actual part plus a potential part — and composites need an extrinsic cause, even if they always existed
The critic is right, and God has potency in his activity but not in his being
quiz.explanation: Feser’s two replies: agere sequitur esse (purely actual being can’t act in a less than purely actual way) and composition (an ontologically prior cause would be needed, making it not first).

quiz.q: Why can’t two purely actual beings be told apart by one having an accident the other lacks?
options: Because accidents exist only in material things
Because any composition, including substance plus accident, entails potentiality, so neither would be purely actual
Because purely actual beings have all accidents at once
Because two such beings would be distinguished by location instead
quiz.explanation: Footnote 17: appealing to other kinds of parts doesn’t help, since anything composed of parts of any kind mixes act and potency. Location would likewise require parts or limitation.

quiz.q: How does Feser show that the purely actual actualizer (ch. 1) and the One (ch. 2) are the same being?
options: By appeal to Church teaching on the Trinity
By noting that both proofs start from observations of change
By showing both are material causes
By showing that pure actuality and absolute simplicity entail each other
quiz.explanation: Parts entail potency, so the purely actual is simple; a simple thing, being actual, can’t have potency without having an actual part and a potential part. Mutual entailment identifies the two.

quiz.q: What is the point of Feser’s remark that Zeus or Odin would have the same nature even if they were the sole occupants of Olympus or Asgard?
options: That pagan gods are fictional
That monotheism is a later development of polytheism
That God’s immateriality distinguishes him from Zeus
That denying simplicity makes God a member of a kind — unique only in fact, not in principle
quiz.explanation: A God who falls under a genus is just the only member of a pantheon. Immateriality alone wouldn’t fix this: an immaterial composite being would be a superangel.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT one of the assumptions Feser says Plantinga reads into the doctrine of divine simplicity?
options: That God is personal
That properties are Platonic abstract objects
That terms apply to God and creatures univocally
That anything predicable of a thing counts as a property
quiz.explanation: Classical theists also regard God as personal (intellect and will), so that isn’t the problem. The three assumptions Feser identifies are univocity, Platonism about properties, and an overbroad notion of property.

quiz.q: Socrates becomes shorter than Plato only because Plato grows. By analogy, God’s becoming Creator of the world is:
options: A real change in God’s will
A change in God’s essence
A mere Cambridge change: the real change is in the world
Impossible, since God cannot create
quiz.explanation: Following Geach and Miller, being Creator is a Cambridge property. This answers Morris’s objection to simplicity and the ‘creation is change’ objection to immutability.

quiz.q: “When I type, my fingers and nervous system change, so any agent changes when it acts.” Feser says this reasoning:
options: Is sound, so God does not act
Commits the fallacy of accident
Commits the fallacy of composition
Begs the question in favor of theism
quiz.explanation: Like inferring that no possible professor could be over nine feet tall. What is essential to acting (per Davies) is producing an effect in another, not changing oneself.

quiz.q: On the traditional Aristotelian account Feser uses, what is essential to being alive?
options: Growth and reproduction
Having a material body
Undergoing continual change
Operating from an internal principle rather than wholly from external forces
quiz.explanation: An animal acts largely from its own nature; a stone acts only when acted upon. God, acting without being acted on at all, has life in the fullest way.

quiz.q: Why does the Swinburne–Kenny simultaneity objection (Socrates would be simultaneous with Obama) fail?
options: Because simultaneity is not transitive
Because Socrates and Obama might in fact coexist in eternity
Because it treats timeless eternity as if it were a point in time
Because God did not cause Socrates to exist
quiz.explanation: Only a point in time can be simultaneous with another point in time. The claim is precisely that God is not at any point in time. Feser does not deny that temporal simultaneity is transitive.

quiz.q: Which best captures Feser’s response to the claim (Findlay; Russell) that all necessity is linguistic convention?
options: He concedes the point but says God is necessary by definition anyway
Conventionalism confuses sentences with propositions, mathematical necessity resists it, and the objection begs the question against the proofs’ account of necessity
He argues that language itself is necessary
He appeals to religious experience to show God is necessary
quiz.explanation: “Snow is white” and “Schnee ist weiss” express one proposition, true even without language; 2 + 2 = 4 isn’t a convention; and the proofs ground God’s necessity in pure actuality, simplicity, and identity of essence and existence.

quiz.q: Schrader imagines a world with one green marble, then imagines it gone. Which parallel does Feser use to expose the mistake?
options: Imagining “2 + 2 = 4” on a chalkboard and then erasing it
Imagining Socrates becoming shorter than Plato
Imagining an author writing a story in a single flash
Imagining a $20 bill printed on demand
quiz.explanation: Erasing the numerals shows nothing about the necessity of arithmetic, because numbers can’t be pictured. Likewise God, being immaterial, can’t be pictured present or absent.

quiz.q: Why does Feser hold that God’s eternity is strict timelessness rather than mere endless duration?
options: Because the Bible says God is outside time
Because physics shows time had a beginning
Because an everlasting God would be too powerful
Because a temporal God would change (adding moments, acting differently, acquiring new knowledge) and would have distinct stages, i.e., parts
quiz.explanation: Timelessness follows from immutability and simplicity. Feser notes that even Craig, who rejects both, agrees an immutable God would be timeless.

quiz.q: A friend suggests the First Cause might be two beings that differ only in that one has a certain accident the other lacks. What would Feser reply?
options: Any composition, including substance plus accident, brings potentiality, so neither would be purely actual.
Accidents cannot exist in immaterial beings, so the suggestion is meaningless.
Two such gods are possible, but Ockham’s razor tells us to posit only one.
Accidents are Cambridge properties, so they cannot distinguish anything.
quiz.explanation: Footnote 17: appealing to any kind of parts fails, because parts entail potency. Feser’s argument is a strict demonstration of uniqueness, not an appeal to simplicity of theory.

quiz.q: Which distinction does Cottingham’s sponge-cake objection ignore?
options: Real vs. Cambridge change
The material factors vs. the total cause (and formal vs. virtual or eminent presence)
Univocal vs. equivocal predication
Imagining vs. conceiving
quiz.explanation: The objection looks only at ingredients and assumes formal presence. PPC concerns the total cause and allows virtual or eminent presence.

quiz.q: Plantinga’s charge that simplicity makes God an abstract object depends on ignoring which view of properties?
options: Ontological vs. temporal priority
The formal/virtual distinction
Constituent ontology, on which a thing’s nature and attributes are concrete constituents of it
Immanent causation
quiz.explanation: Only if properties are Platonic abstract objects would identifying God with his wisdom make him abstract. Classical theists hold a constituent ontology — and deny God is a property at all.

quiz.q: In the argument that being is analogical, why does denying that potentiality is really distinct from actuality amount to denying one of the first two premises?
options: Because essence and existence are identical in creatures
Because potentiality is just a kind of actuality
Because Parmenides proved that change is impossible
Because a merely conceptual distinction means the one underlying reality is only actual or only potential
quiz.explanation: If there is only one reality described two ways, then either only actuality or only potentiality is real — denying premise 1 or 2, which cannot coherently be done.

quiz.q: Which two authors does Feser credit with the labels “neo-theism” and “theistic personalism”?
options: Norman Geisler and Brian Davies
Alvin Plantinga and Richard Swinburne
Peter Geach and Barry Miller
Nicholas Wolterstorff and Thomas Morris
quiz.explanation: Geisler speaks of neo-theism; Davies of theistic personalism, classifying Plantinga, Swinburne, and Hartshorne that way.

quiz.q: Mia’s old teacher retires, and that day Mia becomes “a former student of a retired teacher” without anything in her altering. What is this, and which issue does it illuminate?
options: A real change in Mia; it shows God changes when he creates
A Cambridge change in Mia; it shows how God can become Creator without real change
A fallacy of accident; it bears on God’s eternity
An analogy of attribution; it bears on God’s simplicity
quiz.explanation: What is true of Mia changed only because something else changed — exactly the Socrates/Plato pattern Feser uses for creation and for Morris’s objection.

quiz.q: Why does Feser say that even a composite thing that had always existed would need a cause?
options: Because nothing can literally exist forever
Because the second law of thermodynamics rules out an eternal universe
Because the question is why its parts are combined at all, which requires an ontologically prior cause even with no temporally prior one
Because anything eternal must have had a first moment
quiz.explanation: Composites depend on a uniting principle here and now; everlasting duration removes only a temporal cause, not an ontological one.

quiz.q: Which councils does Feser cite as teaching divine simplicity as binding doctrine?
options: Nicaea (325) and Chalcedon (451)
Trent (1545–1563) and Vatican II (1962–1965)
Constantinople I (381) and Ephesus (431)
Fourth Lateran (1215) and First Vatican (1869–1870)
quiz.explanation: Feser names Lateran IV and Vatican I, and adds that Luther and Calvin also affirmed simplicity.

quiz.q: Which parts of the module’s reasoning would be undermined if the real/Cambridge property distinction were rejected?
options: The defense of simplicity against Morris and of immutability against the creation objection
The argument that being is analogical
The immateriality argument from fundamental particles
The derivation of PPC from PC and PSR
quiz.explanation: Both replies rely on God’s being Creator as a Cambridge property. The analogy argument and immateriality argument do not depend on it.

quiz.q: What does Feser mean in saying that a man’s existence is to his essence as God’s existence is to his essence?
options: God’s existence is caused, as a man’s is
The relations are proportionally similar, grounding analogical predication of “being,” though in God existence is identical to essence
“Being” is said of God and man univocally
God and man fall under the same genus
quiz.explanation: This is proper proportionality: the relation differs (identity in God, actualization of potency in man) but is similar enough to ground one analogical concept.

quiz.q: A student argues: “Every mind I know learns things over time, so if God has a mind he must learn over time.” Which of Feser’s tools best answers this?
options: The principle of proportionate causality
The analogy of attribution
The fallacy of accident: a feature of the minds we know need not belong to every possible mind
The sentence/proposition distinction
quiz.explanation: It generalizes a contingent feature of our minds to all possible minds, as in the nine-foot-professor example; the same pattern answers the acting and life objections.

quiz.q: Why, according to Feser, can mental imagery not settle whether numbers exist necessarily?
options: Because numbers are material and too small to picture
Because numbers exist only in human minds
Because mathematics is a set of conventions
Because numbers are abstract and cannot be pictured; images of numerals are only labels
quiz.explanation: Picturing “2 + 2 = 4” erased shows nothing about arithmetic. The same holds for God, who is immaterial.

quiz.q: What does Feser’s mention of fermions and bosons show?
options: Even fundamental particles have distinct attributes and come to be and pass away, so they involve parts and potentiality
That matter can be purely actual
That physics has refuted Aristotelian matter
That physics speaks of particles analogically
quiz.explanation: Even without an Aristotelian view of matter, material things at every level exhibit composition and potency, so God cannot be material.

quiz.q: Why does Feser insist that simplicity, not immateriality alone, is needed to distinguish God from a Zeus or an Odin?
options: Because Zeus and Odin are material, which already rules them out
Because an immaterial being with parts would still be one of a kind and in need of a cause — a superangel
Because immateriality entails polytheism
Because simplicity entails having a body
quiz.explanation: Immateriality alone leaves open composition, membership in a kind, and dependence. Only simplicity secures uniqueness and ultimacy.

quiz.q: What role does William Lane Craig play in the eternity section?
options: He raises the simultaneity objection to timelessness
He coined the term “Cambridge change”
Though he rejects immutability and timelessness, he agrees that an immutable God would be timeless
He argues that God is both everlasting and immutable
quiz.explanation: Feser cites Craig’s concession to show that the inference from immutability to timelessness is recognized even by critics.

quiz.q: Someone says: “Since God is simple, ‘God is merciful’ and ‘God is powerful’ must be synonyms.” What is the best response on Feser’s view?
options: Our concepts differ because we know God through different effects, but they apply analogically to one undivided reality.
Correct — they are synonyms, since simplicity allows only one concept of God.
Mercy is a Cambridge property, so the problem disappears.
Power is a Cambridge property, while mercy is real.
