quiz.explanation: Simplicity concerns what is in God, not how many concepts we have. Distinct concepts can truly describe one simple reality; power and mercy are not mere relations.

quiz.q: In replying to Findlay, which example does Feser use to show that a proposition is not a sentence?
options: “All bachelors are unmarried”
“2 + 2 = 4” written on a chalkboard
“George is a lion”
“Snow is white” and “Schnee ist weiss” expressing the same proposition
quiz.explanation: The same proposition in two languages — true even if no language existed — shows that the conventionality of sentences doesn’t make propositions conventional.

shortAnswer.q: State the principle of proportionate causality, explain the formal/virtual/eminent distinction, and use it to answer Cottingham’s sponge-cake objection.
shortAnswer.model:
PPC says that whatever is in an effect must be present in some way in its **total** cause, because a cause can’t give what it lacks. It may be present **formally** (I hand you the $20 bill I have), **virtually** (I wire $20 from my account), or **eminently** (I can have a genuine bill printed — a power more basic than having one). PPC follows from PC and PSR.

Cottingham says a cake is spongy though no ingredient is. But (1) he considers only the materials, while PPC concerns the total cause — baker, mixing, heat; (2) he assumes the heirloom reading (formal presence), which PPC’s defenders reject — a boy needn’t have a black eye to give one; heat actualizes a new heat in what it warms; (3) saying the feature was there *potentially* isn’t trivial — minimally informative, but not empty. Naturalists like Churchland use PPC to reach substantive conclusions.
rubric: Defines PPC in terms of the total cause and grounds it in PC and PSR
Correctly explains all three modes with an example
Identifies the material-cause vs. total-cause straw man
Rejects the heirloom (formal-only) reading
Answers the triviality charge

shortAnswer.q: What does agere sequitur esse mean, why is it true, and how does Feser use it to show God has no potentiality even in his activity?
shortAnswer.model:
“Action follows being”: what a thing does flows from and cannot exceed what it is (unless something else makes it act beyond its nature, as a puppeteer moves a puppet). It is the formal-cause counterpart of PPC and follows from PSR: an activity outrunning its nature would be unexplained. Naturalists like Searle rely on it against property dualism.

Applied to God: a critic suggests the First Cause is purely actual in existence but has potential in activity. But existence is the most fundamental thing about a being, and activity reflects it; nothing in a purely actual nature could be the source of merely potential activity. Feser adds a second argument: such a being would be composite (actual part plus potential part), and composites need an extrinsic cause, even if everlasting — so it wouldn’t be first.
rubric: Correct statement of the principle
Mentions the puppet qualification or ‘on its own’
Grounds it in PSR
Applies it to the potential-activity suggestion
Gives the composition argument as a second reply

shortAnswer.q: Reconstruct Feser’s argument that “being” is analogical and defend its most controversial premise.
shortAnswer.model:
1. Actuality is real. 2. Potentiality is real. 3. They are really distinct. 4. If potentiality were real univocally with actuality, they wouldn’t be distinct. 5. If it were real only equivocally, it wouldn’t be real at all. 6. The three uses exhaust literal usage. 7. So potentiality is real in a sense analogous to actuality’s.

The most contested premise is probably 3. Feser’s defense: the real distinction of essence and existence (ch. 4) is a clear case of real potency/act distinction; and if the distinction were merely conceptual, the one underlying reality would be either actual only or potential only, denying premise 1 or 2 — which can’t coherently be done (against Parmenides, change is real; against Heraclitus, pure flux undermines the persisting reasoner, the stable argument, the directedness of change, and the fact that things change according to what they actually are).
rubric: All seven steps in correct order
Explains why univocal would collapse the distinction
Explains why equivocal would make potency unreal
Defends one premise with Feser’s actual reasoning
Notes the argument is independent of theism

shortAnswer.q: Why can’t our language about God be purely univocal, purely equivocal, or purely negative — and how does analogy solve the problem?
shortAnswer.model:
God as the proofs conclude to him is purely actual, simple, immaterial, immutable, and eternal — radically unlike the composite, changeable things our words were made for, so univocal predication would make him a creature. Purely negative (apophatic) theology can’t even say God exists or causes the world, since those are affirmative; it would undercut the proofs. Equivocal language leaves the words without content: any attempt to explain what God’s “power” means either uses a univocal term (the first problem again) or an equivocal one (compounding the problem). The result would be agnosticism or atheism.

Analogy — by attribution and proper proportionality — allows literal, positive, but non-identical predication. It is independently motivated (being said of act and potency; ‘seeing’ a tree vs. a theorem; physics’ curved space), so it isn’t ad hoc.
rubric: Explains failure of univocity
Explains why negative theology can’t be the whole story
Explains failure of equivocity (the fill-in-the-blank point)
Identifies agnosticism/atheism as the result
Presents analogy as literal and independently motivated

shortAnswer.q: Explain Feser’s argument for divine unity.
shortAnswer.model: For there to be more than one thing of a kind, there must be a distinction between the individual and its species (two humans differ by their matter) or between the species and its genus (humans differ from other animals by the specific difference rationality). Such distinctions require metaphysical parts, and parts involve potentiality: matter is potentially this or that; the genus animal is potentially rational or not; parts only potentially make up a whole. God is purely actual, so he has no such parts, and so he can’t be a member of a kind that could have other members. He is unique in principle. Nor can one distinguish two purely actual beings by other parts (substance/accident), since any composition brings potency. So the proofs lead to monotheism.
rubric: States the requirement of individual/species or species/genus distinction
Uses the rational-animal example or equivalent
Links parts to potency
Concludes uniqueness in principle, not just fact
Mentions the substance/accident loophole

shortAnswer.q: Show how Feser establishes that the five proofs all reach one and the same God.
shortAnswer.model: He shows the key descriptions are mutually entailing. Pure actuality ⇔ simplicity (parts entail potency; a simple actual thing can’t have potency without having parts). Pure actuality ⇔ subsistent existence (essence distinct from existence is potency to act; subsistent existence can’t depend on actualization or its existence would be derived). Simplicity ⇔ subsistent existence directly. All three ⇔ absolute necessity (a contingent being needs potency actualized and parts combined; a necessary being has neither). So the Unmoved Mover (ch. 1), the One (ch. 2), the necessary divine intellect (ch. 3), subsistent existence (ch. 4), and the necessary being (ch. 5) coincide — especially given unity, which rules out more than one purely actual being.
rubric: Identifies mutual entailment as the method
Gives at least three of the entailments with reasons
Includes necessity and thus chs. 3 and 5
Invokes unity to rule out several such beings

shortAnswer.q: What is theistic personalism, and why does Feser think denying divine simplicity is implicitly atheism?
shortAnswer.model:
Theistic personalism (Davies’ label; Geisler says “neo-theism”) treats God as the unique member of a species under the genus person — like us but without our limits — and denies simplicity (Plantinga, Swinburne, Hartshorne). The dispute isn’t whether God is personal; classical theists ascribe intellect and will to God.

If God fell under a genus, he’d be unique only by fact (Zeus alone on Olympus); if he had parts, something would need to combine them, so he’d need a cause and wouldn’t be first — a superangel, and worship of him idolatry. Every proof concludes to a wholly noncomposite cause, so nothing supports such a being. Classical theism and simplicity go together; denying simplicity denies the ultimacy definitive of God, which amounts to atheism. Since the proofs show atheism false, simplicity is true.
rubric: Defines theistic personalism accurately
Notes the dispute isn’t personal vs. impersonal
Explains the uniqueness point (genus → contingent uniqueness)
Explains the ultimacy point (parts → cause)
Notes the proofs support only a simple cause

shortAnswer.q: Present Plantinga’s objection to divine simplicity and Feser’s reply.
shortAnswer.model:
Plantinga: simplicity says God is identical to each of his properties, so all are one property — contrary to God’s having power and mercy — and God would be a property, hence an abstract object.

Feser: Plantinga reads in (1) univocal predication — but God’s power and knowledge are only analogous to ours, so their distinctness in us doesn’t transfer (and analogy is literal, not metaphorical); (2) Platonic properties — but for Aquinas essence and attributes are concrete constituents of a thing (constituent ontology), and no classical theist says God is a property; (3) an overbroad notion of property — ignoring the differences among essence, proper properties, contingent accidents, and relations (rational animality; capacity for amusement; skin color; being Plato’s teacher). The odd results come from these assumptions. Calling everything “characteristics” misses that the distinctions are metaphysical, not verbal. And Plantinga misses the real stakes: a composite God would be caused and only contingently unique.
rubric: States the objection fairly
Identifies Plantinga’s three assumptions
Uses analogy to answer the distinct-attributes point
Uses constituent ontology and the essence/property/accident/relation distinctions
Notes the causal-dependence and uniqueness stakes

shortAnswer.q: Explain the distinction between real and Cambridge properties and show how it answers both Morris’s objection to simplicity and the ‘creation is change’ objection to immutability.
shortAnswer.model:
A real property/change involves something intrinsic to the thing (Socrates grows hair); a Cambridge property/change is one where what is true of a thing changes only because something else changed (Socrates becomes shorter than Plato because Plato grew). Geach named it; Miller applied it.

Morris: God has necessary properties (omnipotence) and contingent ones (having created), which can’t be identical. Reply: simplicity identifies only God’s real properties and denies only contingent real properties; being Creator is a Cambridge property, so it needn’t be identical to omnipotence.

Immutability: creating seems to be a transition in God from not creating to creating. Reply: becoming Creator is a Cambridge change; the real change is in the world. Added: inferring that every agent must change in acting is a fallacy of accident — acting essentially is producing an effect in another.
rubric: Correct definition with the Socrates–Plato example
States Morris’s objection
Applies the distinction to simplicity
Applies it to immutability
Mentions the fallacy of accident for the acting objection

shortAnswer.q: Derive God’s timeless eternity and answer the two objections Feser considers.
shortAnswer.model:
Whatever begins or ends has parts that combine or separate (especially essence and existence), is potential, and is contingent; God has none of these features, so he neither begins nor ends. More strongly, a temporal God would add moments, act differently at different times, and acquire new knowledge (“now it is t2”) — change, contrary to immutability — and would have distinct life-stages — parts, contrary to simplicity. So God is timeless (Craig agrees an immutable God would be).

Objection 1 (Swinburne, Pike): causing X at t1 and at t2 means acting at t1 and t2. Reply: “God causes X to exist at t1” doesn’t entail “at t1, God causes X”; God in one timeless act causes a temporal world, like an author conceiving a whole story at once.

Objection 2 (Swinburne, Kenny): simultaneity with eternity is transitive, making Socrates simultaneous with Obama. Reply: this treats eternity as a point in time.
rubric: No beginning/no end argument
Timelessness from immutability
Timelessness from simplicity
Answers the temporal-causation objection with the scope distinction
Answers the simultaneity objection

shortAnswer.q: Answer the conventionalist objection and Schrader’s objection to God’s necessary existence.
shortAnswer.model:
Conventionalism (Findlay; Russell): necessity is analytic truth by linguistic convention, so reality, including God, can’t be necessary. Replies: it confuses sentences with propositions (“Snow is white”/“Schnee ist weiss”; true even without language); mathematical and logical necessities resist conventionalist treatment; and it begs the question against the proofs, which give an extralinguistic account of God’s necessity (pure actuality, simplicity, essence = existence).

Schrader: imagine a world with one green marble, then with nothing — even God is absent. Replies: (1) God, like numbers, isn’t imageable; erasing “2 + 2 = 4” from a chalkboard doesn’t make arithmetic contingent; imagination is irrelevant to strict conception. (2) Modal method: start with actual things and their essences, not with conceivable worlds; having established God’s nature, we infer that he exists necessarily — in every possible world. Schrader assumes, without showing, that this reasoning fails.
rubric: States conventionalism and the sentence/proposition reply
Explains why the conventionalist objection begs the question
States Schrader’s argument
Imagery vs. conception reply, with the numbers example
Essence-first modal method reply

shortAnswer.q: Why is “being” not a genus, and why does that matter for talk about God?
shortAnswer.model: A genus (animal) is divided into species by specific differences that lie outside it: we can grasp rationality without grasping animality. But we cannot grasp substance, attribute, or anything else without grasping it as a being, and the only thing outside being is nonbeing, which cannot differentiate anything. So being is not a genus, and “being” is not predicated univocally; it is predicated by proportional similarity (existence : essence in each thing). This matters because it lets us say God is a being without making him one species among others. It also blocks the theistic-personalist picture of God as the top member of a kind.
rubric: Explains how genus and differentia work
Explains why nothing outside being can differentiate it
Concludes that being is analogical (proportional similarity)
Connects this to God’s not falling under a genus

shortAnswer.q: How does Feser show that PPC and agere sequitur esse are not Scholastic relics?
shortAnswer.model: Both follow from PSR and PC, which were defended earlier. More strikingly, contemporary naturalists use them. Churchland argues that humans are wholly material because their total cause is wholly material, which assumes PPC. The dualist accepts the same principle and reverses the inference from immaterial intellect. Searle argues against property dualism in a way that assumes agere sequitur esse: an immaterial property can’t be a property of a material brain; if it is over and above the brain, it is a separate thing. Even a materialist can accept Aquinas’ conditional that if intellect is immaterial, its subject is immaterial.
rubric: Grounds both principles in PSR/PC
Churchland example for PPC
Dualist mirror-image point
Searle example for agere sequitur esse

shortAnswer.q: Explain why divine immutability implies neither inactivity nor lifelessness.
shortAnswer.model: Objectors say acting requires changing (I change when I type) and that life is change. Feser replies that both commit the fallacy of accident: features that accompany action and life in the things we know are treated as essential to action and life as such. It is like inferring that no possible professor could be over nine feet tall. What is essential to acting, as Davies notes, is producing an effect in another; teaching is causing someone to learn, however it is done. What is essential to life, on the Aristotelian view, is acting from an internal principle rather than being moved from outside. God acts on everything and is acted on by nothing, so he acts, and he lives in the fullest way.
rubric: States both objections
Identifies the fallacy of accident with an example
Gives the essence of acting (Davies)
Gives the Aristotelian account of life and applies it to God

shortAnswer.q: Show why God must be immaterial on both an Aristotelian and a non-Aristotelian view of matter.
shortAnswer.model: Aristotelian view: material substances are composites of substantial form and prime matter, and matter as such is potentiality for form (prime matter is pure potentiality). A simple being has no such composition, and a purely actual being has no potentiality, so God is not material. Non-Aristotelian view: by anyone’s account, material things have parts, from visible components down to molecules, atoms, and subatomic particles, and these can be rearranged, which implies potentiality. Even fundamental particles, though not made of smaller particles, have distinct attributes and come into being and pass away. Either way, what is material is composite and potential, and God is neither.
rubric: Aristotelian argument (form and matter; matter as potency)
Non-Aristotelian argument (parts and rearrangement)
Fundamental particles point
Conclusion drawn from pure actuality and simplicity

shortAnswer.q: Why is Feser’s account of divine necessity not an ontological argument, and what modal method does it use?
shortAnswer.model: An ontological argument infers God’s existence from the concept or definition of God. Feser instead first establishes, from features of the world (change, composition, abstract objects, essence/existence, PSR), that a First Cause exists. He then determines its nature: purely actual, simple, subsistent existence. Only then does he infer that it exists necessarily, since contingency requires potency to be actualized and parts to be combined. This is the Aristotelian-Thomistic modal method: start with actual things, discover their essences, and infer what is possible or necessary for them — rather than starting from what we can imagine or conceive in possible worlds (Schrader’s method), which gets things backward.
rubric: Defines the ontological argument’s strategy
Notes Feser’s necessity is derived after existence is proven from the world
Links necessity to pure actuality/simplicity
States the essence-first modal method and contrasts it with conceivability-first

flashcards.back: Whatever is in an effect is in its total cause in some way — formally, virtually, or eminently — because a cause can’t give what it lacks.
Handing over a bill I have / wiring $20 from my account / being able to get a genuine bill printed on the Federal Reserve press.
The principle of causality (no unactualized actualization) and the PSR (no unexplained feature).
Helium’s properties absent in hydrogen; a sponge cake’s sponginess absent in eggs, flour, and butter.

(1) He looks only at material factors, not the total cause (straw man); (2) the heirloom reading assumes formal presence, which PPC denies (black eye; Aquinas on heat); (3) ‘potentially present’ is minimally informative, not trivial.
Churchland: wholly material causes → wholly material humans. The dualist runs the same principle backward from immaterial intellect.

flashcards.front: Why isn’t evolution a counterexample to PPC?
flashcards.back: Genes + mutation (copying error, radiation, chemical damage) + environment together are the total cause. Davies: denying this would clash with the second law of thermodynamics.
“Action follows being”: activities flow from and can’t exceed a thing’s nature (on its own). The formal-cause counterpart of PPC; follows from PSR.
If a mental property is over and above the brain, it’s a separate thing, not a brain property; if it’s a brain property, it isn’t over and above. An implicit use of agere sequitur esse.
Fido and Rover are dogs / the flying bat and the baseball bat / good wine and a good man.
Health is intrinsically in George (primary analogate); food (cause) and complexion (sign) are called healthy by relation to him.
Proper: form literally in each (life in plants, animals, humans, angels). Metaphorical: form literally in one only (the zoo lion vs. brave George).
A differentia must lie outside its genus; the only thing outside being is nonbeing, which can’t differentiate anything.
Eyes : tree :: intellect : Pythagorean theorem — both ‘seeing.’ Likewise, existence : essence in man, angel, and God.

flashcards.front: The seven-step argument for analogical being (short)
flashcards.back: Act is real; potency is real; they’re really distinct; univocal sameness would erase the distinction; equivocal sense would make potency unreal; only analogy remains; so potency has being analogously to act.

flashcards.front: Heraclitus’ view and why it fails
flashcards.back: Only change is real (no actuality). Fails: no persisting reasoner, no stable argument, change is always toward something (the melting ice cube), and things change according to what they actually are (water, not wood).
It can’t even say that God exists or causes the world — both affirmative — so it would undercut the proofs.
“God has ‘power’ in the sense that he ___” can’t be filled in: a univocal filler brings back anthropomorphism, an equivocal one deepens the mystery. Result: agnosticism or atheism.
Wave-particle entities and curved space stretch ordinary concepts; such talk seems intelligible only analogically. Expect the same for the cause of all material reality.

flashcards.front: Two replies to ‘potency in God’s activity’
flashcards.back: (1) Agere sequitur esse: purely actual being can’t act in a less than purely actual way. (2) Actual + potential parts = composite = needs an extrinsic (ontologically prior) cause.
Many of a kind requires individual/species or species/genus distinctions → parts → potency. God has no potency → no parts → can’t be one of many → unique in principle.

flashcards.front: Five proofs, one God — the method
flashcards.back: Show pure actuality, simplicity, subsistent existence, and necessity each entail the others.
A god who is one of a kind would be unique only by fact; denying simplicity turns God into the sole member of a pantheon — a superangel.
God as the unique member of the genus person, without our limits, not simple (Plantinga, Swinburne, Hartshorne). Labels: Davies (‘theistic personalism’), Geisler (‘neo-theism’).
Aristotle, Plotinus, Maimonides, Avicenna, Averroes, Athanasius, Augustine, Anselm, Aquinas; Lateran IV (1215), Vatican I (1869–70); Luther and Calvin.
Univocal predication; Platonic properties in a ‘third realm’; ‘property’ covering anything predicable.
Rational animality / capacity to be amused / skin color / being Plato’s teacher.
Wolterstorff’s term: a thing’s essence and attributes are concrete constituents of it, not Platonic entities it participates in.
God has necessary (omnipotence) and contingent (having created) properties, which can’t be identical — so simplicity fails.
Geach’s term: what is true of X changes only because something else changed (Socrates shorter than Plato). God’s becoming Creator is one.
No potency to actualize (pure act); no parts to lose while others remain (simplicity).
Concluding no possible professor could exceed nine feet because none has — like concluding every agent must change in acting.
Acting essentially = producing an effect in another. Teaching essentially = causing someone to learn, not lecturing specifically.
Operating from an internal principle (immanent causation) rather than wholly from outside (like a thrown stone). God has life most fully.
Aristotelian: matter + form composite, matter = potency. Any view: material things have rearrangeable parts; even fermions and bosons have distinct attributes and come to be and pass away.
No beginning or end is only the first step; immutability and simplicity require strict timelessness — no succession, no stages.

flashcards.front: Reply to ‘causing at t1 and t2’ (Swinburne, Pike)
flashcards.back: “God causes X to exist at t1” ≠ “at t1 God causes X.” One timeless act causes a temporal world — like an author conceiving a whole story at once.

flashcards.front: Reply to the simultaneity objection (Swinburne, Kenny)
flashcards.back: It treats eternity as a point in time; only points in time can be simultaneous.

flashcards.front: Findlay/Russell on necessity — and the replies
flashcards.back: Necessity is linguistic convention. Replies: sentences ≠ propositions; math and logic resist conventionalism; the objection begs the question against the proofs’ account of necessity.
Imagine a marble, then nothing, not even God. Replies: God (like numbers) can’t be imaged — the erased chalkboard; and modal truths follow from essences of actual things, not from imagined worlds.

flashcards.front: Step 8: what does it claim and why?
flashcards.back: Potentiality is really (not just conceptually) distinct from actuality. Essence/existence is one real case, and a merely verbal distinction would leave only act or only potency real.

flashcards.front: Step 10: what does it claim and why?
flashcards.back: If potency were real only in an equivocal sense, it wouldn’t be real at all, since “real” in a wholly unrelated sense just means unreal.

flashcards.front: Step 13: what does it claim and why?
flashcards.back: Positive, literal talk about God must be analogical: univocal talk makes God a creature or leaves only negations; equivocal talk is empty.

flashcards.front: Step 15: what does it claim and why?
flashcards.back: A purely actual being can’t act in a merely potential way, because action follows being and nothing in a purely actual nature could ground potential activity.

flashcards.front: Step 16: what does it claim and why?
flashcards.back: Actual existence plus potential activity would make God composite, and composites need an ontologically prior cause even if everlasting.

flashcards.front: Step 19: what does it claim and why?
flashcards.back: Parts of any kind bring potentiality: matter could be otherwise, a genus is open to several species, and parts only potentially compose a whole.

flashcards.front: Step 25: what does it claim and why?
flashcards.back: Pure actuality, simplicity, and subsistent existence entail, and are entailed by, absolute necessity, since contingency requires potency actualized and parts combined.

flashcards.front: Step 29: what does it claim and why?
flashcards.back: Simplicity identifies God’s real attributes, not his Cambridge properties (e.g., being Creator), which involve real change only in creatures.

flashcards.front: Step 33: what does it claim and why?
flashcards.back: A simple being can’t change, because real change means changing in one respect while staying the same in others — which requires parts.
A God in time would change (new moments, acts, knowledge) and would have temporal stages (parts); so an immutable, simple God is timeless.

flashcards.front: Step 50: what does it claim and why?
flashcards.back: Modal truths about a thing are known from the essence of what actually exists, not from imagined possible worlds — the Aristotelian-Thomistic method.

flashcards.front: Objection: “Plantinga — simplicity makes God a property.” One-line reply
flashcards.back: Only on univocity, Platonic properties, and an overbroad sense of “property”; classical theists hold a constituent ontology and never call God a property.

flashcards.front: Objection: “Morris — necessary and contingent properties can’t be identical.” One-line reply
flashcards.back: Simplicity identifies only real properties; being Creator is a contingent Cambridge property, so it needn’t equal omnipotence.

flashcards.front: Objection: “To act is to change.” One-line reply
flashcards.back: Fallacy of accident: acting essentially is producing an effect in another, not changing oneself (Davies).

flashcards.front: Objection: “A changeless God is lifeless.” One-line reply
flashcards.back: Life is acting from an internal principle; God, acted on by nothing, has life most fully.

flashcards.front: Objection: “Why not two gods?” One-line reply
flashcards.back: Being one of many requires parts, parts entail potency, and pure act has none — so a second God is impossible, not just absent.

flashcards.front: Objection: “Plantinga — just call them ‘characteristics.’” One-line reply
flashcards.back: Aquinas’ distinctions (essence, property, accident, relation) are metaphysical, not verbal, so relabeling changes nothing.

flashcards.front: Objection: “Analogy is special pleading.” One-line reply
flashcards.back: It is independently required by act/potency, by ordinary speech (“seeing” a proof), and by physics (curved space).
Attribution: perfection intrinsic only to the primary analogate (healthy George). Proper proportionality: intrinsic and formal in each (life in plants and angels).
Temporal: earlier in time. Ontological: the effect depends on it for its being here and now. Everlasting composites still need ontologically prior causes.
Classical: God is simple, not in any genus, the source of being. Personalist: God is the unique member of the kind “person,” composite, possibly changing.

flashcards.front: What does the boy with the black eye show?
flashcards.back: A cause needn’t formally have what it gives; PPC isn’t an heirloom theory.

flashcards.front: What does Aquinas’ hot body example show?
flashcards.back: Heat isn’t handed over numerically; the agent’s power actualizes a new heat that was potential in the patient.

flashcards.front: What does the stone and its color show?
flashcards.back: Substance and attribute are both real but not in the same way — being is said of them analogically.

flashcards.front: What does the melting ice cube show?
flashcards.back: Change is always toward new actualities, and a thing changes according to what it actually is (water, not wood) — against Heraclitus.
Though he rejects immutability and timelessness, Craig agrees an immutable God would have to be timeless.

teachBack:
**Challenge: the “one master key” talk.** Explain to a curious friend who has heard of the five proofs but not of this chapter why the First Cause must be one, simple, unchanging, immaterial, timeless, and necessary — in **under ten minutes**, using **no Latin and no names of philosophers**.

Constraints:

- Start from a single premise: the First Cause has no unrealized potential. Derive every attribute from it (and from ‘no parts’) out loud. If you find yourself just asserting an attribute, stop and supply the reason.
- Use exactly three illustrations: the $20 bill (to show a cause can have things ‘in a higher way’), Socrates getting shorter than Plato (Cambridge change), and the author with the whole story (timelessness).
- Your friend must interrupt you with three objections: “Why not two gods?”, “If God creates, doesn’t he change?”, and “Isn’t ‘God knows’ either anthropomorphic or meaningless?” Answer each in under a minute.

Check yourself afterward:

1. Could your friend repeat the unity argument (how you get two of anything → parts → potency)?
2. Did you explain analogy as literal, using an everyday example like ‘seeing’ a proof?
3. Did you distinguish timelessness from living forever?
4. Did you say why denying simplicity makes God a creature rather than just a ‘different’ God?
5. Did you avoid claiming these attributes follow from the definition of ‘God’ rather than from what the proofs established?

If you stumbled on any, reread the matching summary section and the corresponding stage of the argument, then try again with a different listener.
videoPrompt: Audience: thoughtful beginners, including skeptics, who wonder why a First Cause should be one God with the classical attributes. Emphasize, in order: the three tools — proportionate causality (the $20 bill: formally, virtually, eminently), “action follows being,” and the analogy of being (“seeing” a tree vs. a theorem); pure actuality as the master key; unity and the convergence of all five proofs; simplicity, and why denying it makes God like Zeus alone on Olympus; immutability via Cambridge change (Socrates shorter than Plato); immateriality; timelessness (the author conceiving a whole story at once); necessity versus conventionalism and the imagined empty world. Correct misconceptions: analogy isn’t metaphor, simplicity isn’t one concept, immutable isn’t inert, eternal isn’t very old. Tone: clear, calm, serious, fair to critics.

readingGuide.beforeYouRead:
The first five chapters of Feser’s book each argued, by a different route, that everything depends on an ultimate cause. This chapter asks the obvious follow-up questions: **what must that cause be like**, and **are the five arguments pointing to the same thing?** Feser’s answer is that the cause must be one, without parts, unchanging, not physical, outside time, and incapable of not existing — the traditional idea of God — and that all five arguments reach this same God.

Why care? Because most everyday objections to belief in God are really about God’s nature: “Why only one God?” “Who made God?” “How can an unchanging God do anything?” “Isn’t God just a big person in the sky?” This chapter answers each of these directly. It also shows why the traditional idea of God is very different from the “sky person” many skeptics (and many believers) picture.

What will you be asked to accept? Mainly three general rules, which Feser defends before using: (1) a cause can’t give what it doesn’t in some way have; (2) what a thing does depends on what it is; and (3) some words apply to very different things in related but not identical senses — the way you can “see” a tree and “see” the answer to a puzzle. With these in hand, Feser works out God’s characteristics one by one, and replies to philosophers who have objected.

Reassurance about the hard parts: pages 176–184 (on how words apply to God) and 184–189 (on why there can be only one God) are the most abstract. It is normal to need two passes. Use this module’s plain summaries first, then read, then return to the deep dives. The later sections (on change, matter, time, and necessity) are shorter and more concrete, with memorable examples — a man becoming “shorter” than his brother without shrinking, an author who conceives a whole story at once, a math equation erased from a chalkboard. You don’t need any prior philosophy: every technical term you meet is in this module’s vocabulary list.

knowFirst.plain: What a thing actually is right now versus what it really could become. Cold coffee is actually cool and potentially hot.
A cause can’t give what it doesn’t have in some way — though it may “have” it as money in the bank or as the power to make it, not just in hand.
Latin for “action follows being”: what a thing does depends on what it is.
Using a word in related but not identical senses, like “good wine” and “a good person.” It is still literal, not a figure of speech.
Being fully real with no untapped potential at all. Chapter 1 argued the ultimate cause must be like this.
The idea that God has no parts of any kind — not physical pieces, and not even distinct ingredients like separate power and knowledge.
A new truth about something that involves no change in it, like becoming “shorter than your brother” because he grew.
Assuming that a feature that usually goes along with something is essential to it, like assuming all possible professors must be under nine feet tall.
Existing outside time altogether, not just for an endlessly long time.
A contingent thing could fail to exist; a necessary being can’t fail to exist because of what it is.

questionsToHold: What exactly did each of the five proofs conclude, and how much does each conclusion already tell us about the cause’s nature?
Can a cause really contain something without resembling it? Where in the chapter does that matter?
How can we say true things about a God who is utterly unlike anything we experience?
What makes two things two — and why would that rule out a second God?
Why does Feser think that a God made of parts wouldn’t really be God at all?
How can something act and live without ever changing?
What’s the difference between existing forever and existing outside time?

map.what: A one-page summary of the five arguments and the plan for the chapter: first general principles, then God’s attributes.
map.tip: Use it to check you remember each proof’s conclusion; jot them in a list you can refer back to.

map.what: The rule that a cause can’t give what it lacks, the $20 illustration of formal, virtual, and eminent presence, and replies to Cottingham’s sponge-cake and “triviality” objections.
map.tip: Slow down on the $20 example — the three modes return throughout. The quoted passages from Coffey and Aquinas are worth rereading.

map.what: Naturalists like Churchland rely on the principle; evolution respects it once genes, mutation, and environment are counted together.
map.tip: Read quickly; the point is that the principle is shared ground, not that evolution needs God.

map.what: “Action follows being,” its link to natures (formal causes), Aquinas’ soul argument, and Searle’s critique of property dualism.
map.tip: Don’t get stuck on the philosophy-of-mind dispute; Feser explicitly doesn’t settle it. Note footnote 10 on the puppet.

map.what: Univocal, equivocal, and analogical uses of words; attribution vs. proportionality; why “being” isn’t a genus; seeing a tree vs. seeing a theorem.
map.tip: The hardest stretch. Read it twice and make a three-row table (attribution / proper proportionality / metaphor) with Feser’s examples.

map.what: The seven-step argument that being is analogical, its defense against Parmenides and Heraclitus, and why God-talk must be analogical rather than purely negative or equivocal.
map.tip: Number the seven premises in the margin. The fill-in-the-blank passage about “power” (p. 183) is the heart of the section.

map.what: Closing the loophole of potential activity, then the argument that nothing could make a second purely actual being.
map.tip: Focus on the question “what makes two things two?” Read footnote 17 — it closes an important loophole.

map.what: Why pure actuality, simplicity, subsistent existence, and necessity entail each other, so all five proofs reach the same God.
map.tip: Draw arrows between the four descriptions as you read each “if and only if.”

map.what: Why simplicity is inseparable from God’s uniqueness and ultimacy, the Zeus/Odin illustration, the tradition that held it, and the rise of “theistic personalism.”
map.tip: Mark the Zeus-and-Odin sentence; it’s the most quotable illustration in the chapter.

map.what: Replies to Plantinga (God as a “property”) and Morris (necessary vs. contingent properties), using analogy, the essence/property/accident distinctions, and Cambridge properties.
map.tip: The Plantinga discussion is long; keep a list of his three assumptions. Footnotes 27 and 32 add important replies.

map.what: Why God can’t change, why creating is only a Cambridge change, and why acting and living don’t require change (the nine-foot professor).
map.tip: Connect back to the Socrates–Plato example from p. 196 before reading.

map.what: God isn’t material on either an Aristotelian or an everyday-physics view of matter.
map.tip: Short and straightforward; notice the point about fundamental particles.

map.what: God neither begins nor ends, and is timeless rather than merely everlasting; replies to the temporal-causation and simultaneity objections (the author analogy).
map.tip: Pause on the sentence distinguishing “God causes X to exist at t1” from “at t1 God causes X.”

map.what: Replies to the claim that necessity is only linguistic (Findlay, Russell) and to Schrader’s imagined empty world.
map.tip: The chalkboard example on p. 204 makes the key point; the last page (205) explains Feser’s method for knowing what is necessary.

State Plantinga’s objection and Feser’s reply in three sentences.

Explain the difference between God’s existing forever and God’s existing outside time, using the author analogy.
